#163478. Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1553 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the earliest moments after the Big Bang, the universe was filled with an extraordinarily hot mixture of particles known as quark-gluon plasma.
  • Scientists can briefly recreate these conditions using powerful particle accelerators.
  • One way to explore this mysterious fluid is to observe how heavy quarks behave as they travel through it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the earliest moments after the Big Bang, the universe was filled with an extraordinarily hot mixture of particles known as quark-gluon plasma. Temperatures reached trillions of degrees, and quarks and gluons raced through this primordial soup at nearly the speed of light. This extreme state of matter existed for only a few microseconds before quarks began combining into the more stable protons and neutrons that eventually helped form the matter around us.

Scientists can briefly recreate these conditions using powerful particle accelerators. By colliding ions at speeds approaching that of light, they produce tiny droplets of quark-gluon plasma about the size of an atomic nucleus. Each droplet survives for only tens of septillionths of a second, giving researchers an incredibly brief opportunity to investigate the substance that filled the newborn universe.

One way to explore this mysterious fluid is to observe how heavy quarks behave as they travel through it. Although these particles are not part of the surrounding plasma being studied, their movements can reveal crucial details about its microscopic structure. This approach builds on a principle first described by Albert Einstein in 1905.

However, Einstein's original framework has limitations under the extraordinary conditions found in quark-gluon plasma. When particles approach the speed of light, interactions occur that his theory does not fully account for.

MIT Physicists Extend Einstein's Century-Old Theory.

Recent findings suggest that researchers at MIT and the University of California at Santa Barbara (UCSB) have now developed a theoretical framework that goes beyond Einstein's original description. Their work predicts how a fluid affects particles traveling at relativistic speeds, including the forces that accelerate, slow, and redirect them.

It has been revealed that the researchers believe their calculations could help scientists better understand how heavy quarks move through quark-gluon plasma. By comparing their predictions with results from particle accelerator experiments, physicists may be able to uncover upcoming details about the internal structure of this ancient form of matter and the conditions that prevailed shortly after the Massive Bang.

Recent findings suggest that "Our result reveals a upcoming source of information carried by heavy quarks in rare, unusually large changes in their motion," claims Jean Du Plessis, a graduate student in MIT's Center for Theoretical Physics, a Leinweber Institute. "How often those large changes occur depends on the microscopic nature of the plasma, raising the possibility that they could provide a new way to learn what the quark-gluon plasma is actually like inside.".

Sources indicate that du Plessis conducted the research with Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at UCSB. Their findings were published in Physical Review Letters.

How Pollen in Water Inspired Einstein's Discovery.

The origins of this research stretch back nearly two centuries to an observation made by botanist Robert Brown. In 1827, Brown noticed that pollen grains suspended in apparently motionless water moved unpredictably, constantly shifting and drifting despite the absence of any visible disturbance. Scientists eventually named this phenomenon "Brownian motion.".

Einstein provided a scientific explanation in 1905, showing that these seemingly random movements were caused by tiny, invisible interactions between particles suspended in a fluid and the atoms and molecules surrounding them.

In a recent development, he demonstrated that two competing effects govern the movement of a particle through a fluid. The first is drag, which resists the particle's movement and slows it down. The second consists of countless random pushes from the surrounding atoms and molecules. Although individual microscopic particles are extremely small, their combined activity can deliver enough energy to make larger particles move unpredictably.

Einstein's theory established a relationship between these effects, allowing scientists to learn about the microscopic properties of a fluid by studying the motion of particles inside it.

Over the following decades, researchers applied this principle to many different fluids, including quark-gluon plasma. They generally expected particles traveling through such plasma to experience a balance of drag and random impacts resembling the behavior of pollen grains in water.

Sources indicate that in conventional Brownian motion, the likelihood of different forces follows a bell-shaped curve. Moderate pushes are the most common (the highest point of the bell), while unusually strong pushes in either direction are much less likely (the tail ends of the bell). Over time, the balance of drag and random motion allows a particle to reach the same temperature as its surroundings.

But this familiar description becomes incomplete when particles move at speeds approaching that of light.

Recent findings suggest that "Einstein highlighted that the drag and the random kicks must balance in just the right way for a particle eventually to come to the same temperature as its surroundings," Du Plessis explains. "For the types of fluids he was thinking about, he was correct. But for particles that are moving at relativistic velocities, this relationship breaks down. And we've known for 20 years that something is missing. So we have to go beyond the work that Einstein did.".

Unexpected Forces Reveal Hidden Physics in Quark-Gluon Plasma.

To investigate what Einstein's traditional model was missing, Du Plessis and Scheihing-Hitschfeld calculated how a heavy quark would respond to the forces inside a fluid while moving close to the speed of light.

Their calculations focused on the strong nuclear force, one of nature's fundamental forces, which governs interactions between quarks and gluons and holds them together.

Sources indicate that the team began with a relatively simple model consisting of a gas of quarks and gluons that interacted only weakly with one another. Starting with these weaker interactions made it possible to calculate the forces acting on a heavy quark passing through the gas.

Recent findings suggest that they then determined how those forces would change the quark's momentum as it moved. A stronger push produces a larger change in momentum, so the calculations allowed the researchers to predict the likelihood of impacts of different strengths.

At first, the resulting probability curve looked similar to the bell-shaped distribution associated with Einstein's theory. For small changes in momentum, the familiar pattern still held. But when the researchers examined larger changes, they discovered a striking difference.

Instead of the expected symmetrical curve, the distribution was tilted, with unequal probabilities for extreme changes in opposite directions. Powerful impacts occurred more frequently than the traditional Brownian model predicted, and unusually large slowdowns were more likely than similarly large increases in speed.

"The usual Brownian picture assumes that large kicks become exceedingly rare," Du Plessis indicates. "For heavy quarks, however, these rare kicks are more common than the bell curve predicts, and are not equally likely in opposite directions: A large kick that slows the quark down more than expected from drag is more likely than an equally large kick that leaves it moving faster than expected.".

A Universal Pattern Could Reveal the Universe's First Fluid.

The researchers next examined whether this unusual behavior depended on the particular particles making up the plasma.

They repeated their calculations using plasmas containing different types of particles and found that the same tilted distribution appeared regardless of the composition.

Sources indicate that even more intriguingly, they recognized the same underlying pattern in an earlier calculation involving strongly coupled plasma, where particles interact much more intensely with one another. Despite the substantial differences in microscopic behavior between the two types of plasma, the probability distributions shared the same distinctive structure.

This suggested that the researchers had identified a potentially universal feature of how fast-moving particles interact with fluids, rather than an effect confined to one particular model.

"This is the first time that this seemingly universal structure was realized and really formalized," Du Plessis says. "This gives a concrete path forward for how to better understand the quark-gluon plasma, using heavy quarks.".

The discovery could offer physicists a valuable new tool for investigating the extraordinarily hot matter that dominated the universe immediately after the Major Bang. By studying the rare, extreme changes in the movement of heavy quarks, scientists may be able to learn more about the interactions occurring deep inside quark-gluon plasma.

Sources indicate that the results also point toward an key characteristic of this primordial substance. Rather than behaving like a relatively loose collection of particles, the universe's first fluid may have been governed by much stronger interactions than a conventional Brownian motion model would indicate.

Industry observers note that du Plessis suggests that primordial quark-gluon plasma was likely "more strongly interacting than this Brownian motion way of modeling it would suggest. It's more like a liquid and less like a gas.".

By extending a theory Einstein developed more than a century ago, the researchers have opened a promising newly introduced approach to studying one of the most extreme states of matter in nature and potentially uncovering what the universe was like during its first fleeting moments.

Sources indicate that the research received partial support from the Office of Nuclear Physics within the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation, and the Simons Foundation.

Discounts on already budget-oriented laptops are often sparse. That’s been true for the Dell XPS 13 ever since it relaunched a few months ago, holding steady at a starting price of either $700 or $750. But for Black Friday, Dell’s dropped the price by $200 to just $550. It’s astounding that you can get a laptop of this caliber for that price, especially given how premium it feels. The chassis is well-built and highly portable; the display is both bright and colorful, and the trackpad feels great to use. However, this $550 model comes with only 8 GB of RAM, which might be a sticking point for many people. You can upgrade to 16 GB, but it’s not on sale for Black Friday.

Back in June, Apple raised the price of the MacBook Air to $1,299. It felt inevitable, but as a laptop reviewer, it still crushed my spirits. The M5 MacBook Air is the laptop most people should buy, but at $1,299, I knew it was a stretch for most budgets. That’s what makes this Amazon discount feel so impactful. It brings the MacBook Air down to $1,049, making it the first time it’s been close to its original price since June.

Sources indicate that the MacBook Neo is already cheap, so Apple has no incentive to cut the price—even though the laptop has been out for seven months. But finally, the MacBook Neo’s price has dropped by $50, bringing it down to $649. That’s a great deal, especially if you’re looking for an affordable laptop that feels premium, with a metal chassis and quality display. The 8 GB of RAM is limiting, but if your needs aren’t overly heavy, the MacBook Neo should do the trick—especially at this price.

In a recent development, these days, you’ll be hard-pressed to find a laptop under $1,000 without major compromises. That’s even more uncommon for a laptop with a larger screen. But the IdeaPad Slim 5x is just that. It’s a 15-inch laptop with great performance, long-lasting battery life, lots of ports, a solid trackpad, and a high-resolution OLED screen. It even comes packed to the brim with 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. It’s not as thin as the 15-inch MacBook Air, but it’s hundreds of dollars cheaper.

It has been revealed that it might be well over two years old, but I still recommend the 2024 Surface Laptop. The price is down to $900 right now, which is a good deal for these specs, performance, and battery life. You’re limited to the blue color option (also known as Sapphire), but it’s the best price I’ve seen on this laptop so far this year. My favorite feature will always be the 3:2 aspect ratio screen, which gives the display a taller shape for more vertical space to work with.

In a recent development, there is a newer version that uses the Snapdragon X2 Plus/Elite chips, but I find it quite expensive. The IdeaPad Slim 5x listed above is the better option if you’re OK with a larger device, since it uses those next-generation Snapdragon chips and twice the storage. But if you’re sold on the Surface Laptop's more premium design, this is the one to get.

Industry observers note that with the MacBook Neo selling for $600, you might look at something like the HP OmniBook 5 with suspicion. Even on sale for $700, being $100 more than the MacBook Neo doesn’t seem like a great position for an entry-level Windows laptop. And while this laptop is often on sale, this is $100 cheaper than I’ve seen it over the past few weeks.

But the HP OmniBook 5 is a special device, with its OLED display, very thin chassis, and 16 GB of RAM. It very much looks like a laptop that should cost hundreds more. Battery life is great, too, thanks to the Snapdragon X chip inside. The 16 GB of RAM is still the main selling point here—if it was any less, I would recommend the XPS 13 in nearly every scenario (but it’s not on sale right now). It’s only real downfall is the touchpad. It feels frustratingly clumsy to use, making precise movements difficult.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Engineers and analysts searching for the root cause of the technical issues behind Friday's nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration have been able to replicate the situation that was overwhelming parts of the air traffic system, people familiar with the investigation told CNBC.

While replicating the glitch in a lab in Florida is progress, those investigating the matter have yet to determine exactly why two routers in question failed, according to the people, who requested anonymity to talk about an ongoing situation. Finding the root cause is critical to the FAA determining if there may be an issue with other routers that form the backbone of communications for the national air transportation network.

Recent findings suggest that the ground stop lasted for more than four hours Friday, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford have remarked there is no indication the routers failed due to a cyberattack.

The incident in question happened shortly after L3Harris Technologies, the primary contractor supporting the FAA telecommunications network, installed a new router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas.

L3Harris said that it, in partnership with other tech companies, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement remarked. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.".

Investigators mentioned within eight minutes of its installation, the router began to transmit too much data within the FAA network.

That surge of data, 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilized aircraft communications and radar feeds, Duffy remarked.

Since the ground stop, Duffy has increased the amount of money he wants to upgrade the national air traffic system. After originally asking for $30 billion to build a digital network that will incorporate artificial intelligence, Duffy has now asked Congress for $50 billion.

#163472. A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1108 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1108 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space.
  • According to recent reports, new research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes.
  • The discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

According to recent reports, new research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

The discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.

A Hidden Population of Black Holes.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," indicates LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.".

In a recent development, chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.

Recent findings suggest that despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.

A Mysterious Gap in Black Hole Masses.

Sources indicate that to investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.

Recent findings suggest that even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising newly introduced questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

"We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred says. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.".

The researchers also examined how rapidly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).

According to recent reports, taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.

Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths.

It has been revealed that finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.

According to recent reports, "We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred says. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.".

By studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The fresh findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.

According to recent reports, the research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.

#163471. Astronomers watch a red giant star greedily devour a stellar 'Bao bun' before erupting: 'We couldn't quite believe our luck'

Astronomers watch a red giant star greedily devour a stellar 'Bao bun' before erupting: 'We couldn't quite believe our luck'

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star.
  • In a recent development, that isn't a random comparison.
  • According to recent reports, A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star.

In a recent development, that isn't a random comparison. The cannibal star, which is 350 times bigger than the sun, is nicknamed "Major Bao," while its unfortunate companion had the nickname "Little Bao." The cute cosmic monikers come from the fact that this destructive merger event has been designated AT2025abao.

According to recent reports, A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao. This cannibalistic event was tracked by a wide array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA space missions NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. The conclusion of the event AT2025abao was marked by a massive eruption witnessed in Oct. 2025 by two instruments at Caltech's Palomar Observatory: the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Wide-field INfrared Transient ExploreR (WINTER).

Sources indicate that "The excitement was real," team member Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University noted in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "We couldn't quite believe our luck. With detailed observations for several years before the merger, for the first time, we now have an unprecedented glimpse of the conditions that lead to such cosmic events.".

The story of AT2025abao began when astronomers detected a bright flash in the nearby Andromeda galaxy, a region where scientists hadn't expected to see a cosmic explosion.

Industry observers note that responding to this unexpected flash, Karambelkar and colleagues set about investigating its cause with a plethora of telescopes. This led to them seeing a slow and continuous brightening over the course of two years,.

They determined the cause of the flash was a rare stellar merger, the luminous red nova now designated AT2025abao. They linked this to a star called WNTR23bzdiq / WTP19aalzlk that had been observed steadily brightening since 2019 after being stable for the preceding 30 years. Thus, the team determined that at the heart of the event is a red giant, a star that puffs out to hundreds of times its original size after it runs out of hydrogen in its core. The team theorizes that Massive Bao, with a mass seven times greater than the sun, expanded so rapidly and violently that it swallowed its smaller companion star. The unfortunate star, Little Bao, then spiraled into Big Bao's core in fewer than 10 orbits.

Sources indicate that "A couple of years back, we discovered a star that was gradually brightening. We took a closer look to discover a red giant, or a star that has started to expand toward the end of its life, just like our sun will one day," Karambelkar remarked. "Steady brightening was unusual, but even if something was stirring, no one expected to see an explosion in their lifetime, as these stars remain relatively stable for thousands of years.".

An important clue to how this cataclysmic and cannibalistic event proceeded was provided by SPHEREx in July 2025, which found that before the eruption, Big Bao was fading in optical light but brightening in infrared. This indicated that Big Bao was cooling down and spewing out dense clouds of gas and dust that were enveloping the red giant star.

According to recent reports, when Little Bao crashed into the core of Big Bao, it caused stellar material to be ejected at speeds of around 1.8 million miles per hour. This matter crashed into the envelope of gas and dust previously spewed by Big Bao, and this caused the flash of light seen on Oct. 17, 2025.

Recent findings suggest that one of the final pieces of this story was provided by the JWST on Dec. 24, 2025. The powerful space telescope measured the total mass of dust and gas around Big Bao prior to the eruption since two months earlier.

This helped determine that Little Bao had a mass of around 70% of the sun's mass.

"It was kind of symbolic how the year was coming to an end as we managed to bring together the puzzle pieces from the story of Massive and Little Bao," Karambelkar noted. "But in my mind, this felt like a closure of just one chapter in a story that is just starting. We learned so much about AT2025abao, but we also learned much about conducting coordinated, multi-facility, multi-team astronomical discoveries.".

Recent findings suggest that the team's research was published on Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

Japanese anime master Masaaki Yuasa’s latest studio, ame pippin, has revealed first look images and a clip from the highly-anticipated animated feature Daisy’s Life, a tale of grief and healing now delayed to a 2027 theatrical release in Japan.

It has been revealed that the first title from Yuasa’s new studio ame pippin unveiled images to The Hollywood Reporter of the main characters from the animated adaptation of Banana Yoshimoto’s novel, The Life of Daisy, and original illustrations by Yoshitomo Nara. In one image, the young protagonist Daisy and her closest friend, Dahlia, are standing together in a lush forest. Related Stories Movies Golden Globes Category Chaos: When 'The Drama' Is a Comedy... Movies Golden Globes: 'I Play Rocky' Submitted as Comedy (Exclusive).

It has been revealed that the second image demonstrates both animated characters seated together at the roots of a tree, bonding over yakisoba, a Japanese stir-fried noodle dish. Their friendship helps frame the story of Daisy, who, as a child, lost her mother, her only family, in a tragic accident and now grieves that death as she struggles with a upcoming life with her aunt. Studio ame pippin on Thursday unveiled a short clip from Daisy’s Life on X.

It has been revealed that “On a long, lonely night during the rainy season, she (Daisy) plays the recorder by herself. As if drawn by the sound, Dahlia appears and becomes the friend who supports Daisy through her isolation. Years later, while Daisy is living and working at her aunt and uncle’s yakisoba restaurant, a letter arrives from Brazil. It speaks of the mysterious connection between two lonely souls separated by distance and time,” a synopsis from the producers of Daisy’s Life states about the young girl’s life changing one sleepless night.

The film is the first animated feature from ame pippin, the animation studio founded by Yuasa in 2025. Daisy’s Life also marks the first animated adaptation of books by Yoshimoto, a popular Japanese writer whose literary work has been published in 30 countries, with over seven million copies in print.

Published in 2000, Yashimoto’s The Life of Daisy novel centers around Daisy (Hinagiku) and explores the themes of death and loss through Daisy’s relationships with her mother and childhood best friend, Dahlia.

Recent findings suggest that director Yuasa is known for classic films like The Tatami Galaxy and Ping Pong the Animation, and in 2013 co-founded Science SARU with Eunyoung Choi. He directed an episode of Adventure Time and The Night Is Short, Walk on Girl.

Yuasa left Science SARU in 2020 after Keep Your Hands Off Eizouken! and directed Inu-Oh, which earned both Golden Globe and Annie nominations. Character designer Izumi Murakami created the animated characters for Yuasa’s Daisy’s Life adaptation, while production designer Tomotaka Kubo created the film’s settings that envelop Daisy and Dahlia’s time together.

Visual development artist Batiste Perron, color designer Ayaka Nakamura, director of photography Yoshihiro Sekiya and editor Kiyoshi Hirose are also part of Yuasa’s creative team.

The Japanese-French co-production is from ame pippin and Miyu Productions, with Fumie Takeuchi, Emmanuel-Alain Raynal and Pierre Baussaron sharing producer credits.

Yuasa is guest curating the Drawn Universes: Visions in Animation program at the Toronto Film Festival’s Lightbox complex through Dec. 29, and on Saturday night will participate in an informal conversation at the festival’s Lightbox facility in Toronto.

#163468. DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth

DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (970 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions?
  • Researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA.
  • Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions? Scientists have spent decades trying to answer this fundamental question, including how the earliest biological systems endured an environment that would have been dangerous to many living organisms today.

Researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA. Their findings could help explain how early genetic material survived intense ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.

The research was led by Dr. Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar. Their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), provides new insight into a longstanding mystery surrounding molecular evolution and the origins of life.

Why DNA's Evolution Has Puzzled Scientists.

One of the major changes in the evolution of genetic systems involved the transition from RNA, which is typically a single-stranded molecule, to DNA as the primary means of storing genetic information. An important difference between the two molecules is that DNA uses a chemical building block called thymine in place of uracil, which is found in RNA.

This substitution has puzzled researchers for decades. Thymine is more susceptible to certain forms of ultraviolet (UV) damage, making its adoption seem like an evolutionary disadvantage. The problem would have been especially significant on early Earth, before a protective ozone layer developed and shielded the planet's surface from much of the Sun's harmful radiation.

Why would evolution favor a component that appeared to make genetic material more vulnerable under such harsh conditions? Rentzepis and his colleagues set out to investigate whether thymine might offer an advantage that had previously been overlooked.

It has been revealed that to explore this possibility, the researchers exposed thymine and uracil to carefully controlled UV radiation intended to reproduce conditions on primordial Earth. They analyzed the molecules using biophotonics, a field that examines biological materials through their interactions with light. Their experiments employed several techniques, including absorption, fluorescence, and Raman spectroscopy.

DNA's Surprising Defense Against UV Damage.

The results revealed an unexpected possibility. Although thymine can be vulnerable to UV radiation, it appears to favor types of molecular damage that are more readily reversed. This suggests that an key advantage of thymine may lie not in preventing damage, but in limiting its consequences and making recovery easier.

Recent findings suggest that "We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form, suggesting that early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight not by avoiding damage, but by controlling it and making it easier to self-repair," stated Khosh Abady. "In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule.".

Sources indicate that this finding offers a possible explanation for why thymine became a fundamental component of DNA despite its apparent weakness. By concentrating UV damage in parts of the molecule where it could be more easily reversed, thymine may have helped protect the integrity of early genetic systems.

The discovery also suggests that surviving the extreme conditions of early Earth may have depended on more than simply resisting environmental threats. The ability to manage and recover from damage could have played an important role in the evolution of the molecular systems that eventually supported life.

Fresh Possibilities for Pathogen Detection and UV Disinfection.

Beyond its implications for understanding life's beginnings, the research could have practical applications in several scientific and technological fields.

The team established a new set of reference measurements describing how these molecules respond to light. These measurements could eventually help researchers identify harmful microorganisms more efficiently and assess the effectiveness of systems that use UV radiation to disinfect water and other materials.

"The distinct spectral signatures we measured could support applications in faster, more sensitive pathogen detection and in monitoring whether UV disinfection has effectively inactivated microorganisms, particularly in water-treatment systems," said Khosh Abady.

These potential applications demonstrate how investigating fundamental questions about molecular evolution can also provide tools for addressing modern challenges in health and environmental safety.

Could the Building Blocks of Life Have Come From Space?

With these findings in hand, Rentzepis and his team strategy to investigate an even earlier chapter in life's history. Their next goal is to understand the forces and chemical processes that brought thymine, uracil, and other essential components of primitive genetic systems together.

A central question is whether these ingredients originated entirely on Earth or whether some arrived from beyond our planet. Meteorites may have delivered organic compounds that later became incorporated into the chemical systems from which life developed.

It has been revealed that "We hope to explore whether life's chemical building blocks formed and assembled entirely on Earth or whether some were delivered to our planet from elsewhere by meteorites and later incorporated into early genetic systems," said Khosh Abady. "We are grateful to Texas A&M University and our research sponsors for supporting this work and enabling us to explore fundamental questions about life's origins.".

By examining how DNA's molecular components respond to radiation and how those components may have first assembled, the researchers hope to uncover more of the chemical history that made life on Earth possible.

China Renaissance, a top dealmaker in the country’s tech industry, said it would suspend trading of its shares and delay the release of its annual results because it still can’t get in touch with its founder.

Bao Fan, 52, started the boutique investment bank in 2005 and has been unreachable since the middle of February, according to the firm. Shares in China Renaissance have plunged since Bao went missing, at one point dropping as much as 50%.

China Renaissance mentioned in late February that it had learned Bao was “cooperating in an investigation” being carried out by certain authorities in the country. It gave no other details.

Chinese media have reported Bao might be assisting in an investigation related to a former executive at China Renaissance.

In a filing on Sunday, China Renaissance noted auditors couldn’t complete their work or sign off on their report because of Bao’s absence. The board was also unable to give an estimate about when it would be able to approve its audited results for 2022 or dispatch its annual report by an April 30 deadline as required by Hong Kong’s listing rules.

Missing Chinese billionaire CEO assisting authorities in investigation, organization indicates.

Trading in the company’s shares was suspended from Monday as a result.

It has been revealed that bao is known as a veteran dealmaker who works closely with top technology companies in China. He helped broker the 2015 merger between two of the country’s leading food delivery services, Meituan and Dianping. Today, the combined manufacturer’s “super app” platform is ubiquitous in China.

His team has also invested in US-listed Chinese electric vehicle makers Nio (NIO) and Li Auto and helped Chinese internet giants Baidu (BIDU) and JD.com (JD) complete their secondary listings in Hong Kong.

It has been revealed that over the weekend, China’s top anti-graft watchdog launched an investigation into Liu Liange, former party secretary and chairman of Bank of China, according to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the State Supervision Commission. The bank is state-owned and one of the country’s four biggest lenders.

According to recent reports, liu is suspected of “serious violations of discipline and law,” the statement remarked. He is among the most senior financial executives targeted in a broader financial crackdown by President Xi Jinping.

In January, Wang Bin, former party chief and chairman of China Life Insurance, was charged by national-level prosecutors with taking bribes and hiding overseas savings.

Just weeks after making her Christmas debut with “Take Me Home (4 Christmas),” the 23-year-old pop star has returned with a second holiday offering, “Miss This Christmas,” exclusively through Amazon Music.

According to recent reports, rodrigo debuted “Miss This Christmas” live during her concert at Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena on Monday (Nov. 23), introducing it to the crowd as a “really sad Christmas song” and noting that “no one’s ever really heard it before,” according to Rolling Stone.

According to recent reports, the track was also included as the B-side on the vinyl edition of “Take Me Home (4 Christmas),” which arrived in early November. The holiday tune peaked at No. 32 on the Billboard Hot 100 in mid-November.

While “Take Me Home (4 Christmas)” leans into festive pop with a nostalgic feel, “Miss This Christmas” takes a more melancholy approach, exploring the heartache of missing someone during the holiday season.

“Happy Christmas to the lonely/ Broken hearts that feel just like me,” Rodrigo sings before adding, “Yeah, next year’s gonna look real different/ Tell your folks I’ll miss their Christmas.”.

The song was co-written with Dan Nigro.

The new release arrives during a particularly busy stretch for Rodrigo, who earned seven nominations at the 2027 Grammy Awards, including album of the year for her third studio album, you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love.

Sources indicate that “I am over the moon!!!!!” Rodrigo wrote on Instagram after the Grammy noms were announced. “I love this album so much and for it to be recognized in this way is the biggest honor.”.

You seem pretty sad for a girl so in love also recently earned its fifth nonconsecutive week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200.

Furner also said Walmart is seeing encouraging adoption of its artificial intelligence agent, named Sparky, especially ahead of the holiday season. He said it's led to customer basket increases of 40% on average.

In a recent development, in October, Walmart announced it was launching a joint membership option with Walmart+ and Sam's Club as it leans further into convenience. Both stores will still offer stand-alone memberships, as well.

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1564 w)

Welcome to the Repair Café, Where Neighbors Fight Throwaway Culture

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
  • On an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk.
  • That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

On an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk. Some carried broken lamps, glitching electronics, or cracked furniture. Others walked in with toolboxes, multimeters for testing electric currents, and cans of WD-40. Beneath extension cords dangling from the rafters, they sorted themselves into smaller groups: the volunteer electricians, tailors, luthiers, carpenters, and at least one cutler (knife sharpener), commandeering nearby worktables and passersby as needed.

That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.

In a recent development, “This is so interesting,” a giddy Pettus stated, inspecting for the first time the joints, one of them broken, that held together the chair she’d owned for decades. “You never even know how furniture is put together.”.

This is Decatur’s semi-regular repair café, one of a few hundred meetings like it across the United States. More Americans than ever are turning to these community gatherings to fix what they already own, resisting the influence of companies that sell everything from hiking boots to smartphones and hot water boilers and that push for replacement over repair. One consequence of this throwaway economy is an increase in greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing that threatens to intensify climate change.

Yet, organizers and volunteers consider repair cafés to be more than a relatively small climate solution. As inflation rises and wages stagnate, the meetups connect people to a movement with the ambitious goal of changing the fundamentals of America’s consumer economy.

At the Decatur repair café, volunteers, wearing green shirts with “I can probably fix that” printed on the back, offered their skills free of charge as patrons observed. A young father of a toddler and squirmy baby watched as a volunteer replaced a switch on a favorite mid-century modern lamp worn out by the older child’s repeated clicking. Murmurs of excitement rippled around the building as the acrid smell of a spot welding project wafted through.

Pettus’ broken chair held in its wood her family’s story. Soon after she and her husband were married in 1996, they began a search for a dining room set. Pettus wanted the chairs to be comfortable for her entire family, but one of her brothers is nearly 7 feet tall, and another just a few inches shorter. “We are not a tiny family,” Pettus said. “We are a substantial family.”.

Pettus also thought of one of her children who’d interned at the Environmental Protection Agency and shared his concerns with Pettus about pollution and climate change. Then, after months of the broken chair cluttering the family’s house, Pettus was running Saturday morning errands when she passed the Decatur repair café. She drove the half-mile home to grab the chair and decided to give it a second chance.

“When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it’s very lonely,” noted Martine Postma, director of Repair Café International, a Netherlands-based network of 4,000 cafés. “ It’s easier to just go on the internet and order a upcoming item which will come to your doorstep in 24 hours, but that’s also a very lonely, disconnected activity.”.

Postma, a former journalist with the demeanor of an unflappable librarian, founded her organization in 2010 after the birth of her second child magnified her fears about the planet’s future. “Markets are flooded with trash—with cheap products that we don’t need and that do not work,” Postma stated. “They break, and they contribute nothing to our well-being. They just contribute waste.”.

In a recent development, repair cafés appear to be inspiring people to use their stuff longer. In 2025, they prevented nearly 2 million pounds of waste—the equivalent of more than 100 fully loaded Boeing 747 aircraft—according to Repair Café International, and reduced greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to the average consumption of about 1,000 Dutch families.

Sources indicate that postma, Pettus, and millions of others often smack into obstacles when they try to fix their own stuff. Broken products are increasingly difficult to repair, according to a report from the Federal Trade Commission titled “Nixing the Fix.” The report details how Americans are incentivized to “replace products before the end of their useful lives” by companies that decide to make repairs less safe, limit the availability of parts, lock software and firmware, or even “disparage” independent repair.

Sources indicate that in 2023, California, Colorado, Minnesota, and Newly introduced York passed “right to repair” legislation meant to encourage repair over replacement. A year later the European Union passed a similar directive. Postma and other organizers consider the cafés a natural place for activism to push for right-to-repair measures, although Postma hopes for more sweeping changes in Europe, like a tax on raw materials. She argued it would limit emissions and bolster repair shops, even if it increases the cost of products.

“ I feel for the objects around me. I feel sorry for them if they’re broken,” she said. “I want to make repairing a normal thing in everyday life once more.”.

According to recent reports, according to Postma, repairing goods is more common in relatively poor countries where replacing them can be especially difficult and expensive. It’s in wealthy countries that repair cafés are thriving, but they’re not at all uniform. Each reflects the surrounding area and its socioeconomics.

Sources indicate that on a Sunday afternoon in the Collier Heights neighborhood of Atlanta, volunteers brought most of their own tools to the basement of a building owned by a Seventh-Day Adventist Church, setting them on white plastic folding tables atop a light pink carpet. The café looked much different from the one a 30-minute drive across the city in Decatur. The median annual household income in the mostly Black Collier Heights neighborhood is roughly $40,000 lower than in Decatur. Many people who brought items wanted them fixed less for sentimental reason, and more so they could keep using them.

In a recent development, gale Pines walked in with a red air fryer that had stopped working after they used it to dehydrate ginger. When their oven ran, Pines said, it heated the entire kitchen. So, while in nursing school, they cooked many of their evening meals in the air fryer, most often chicken nuggets and fries.

It has been revealed that pines recently graduated but had trouble finding a job and couldn’t afford to buy a newly introduced $100 air fryer. “It’s just hard to exist,” Pines noted. “I don’t really have a very significant support network outside of my friends.”.

In a recent development, one of Pines’ housemates told them about Collier Heights’ repair café. They keep a bag of broken electronics in the garage that they’d prefer not to send to a landfill. “Being in the height of climate collapse we can’t just keep buying fresh stuff all the time, both for the economy and for our material scarcity,” Pines said.

In a recent development, when a volunteer at the Collier Heights repair café opened up the air fryer, they swiftly discovered the problem: a bad capacitor. Another volunteer had brought a replacement part, and the two of them made the fix as Pines watched, impressed, but unable to follow the relatively complex repair. Pines felt OK that they hadn’t learned how to fix the air fryer themself.

“ To just be around people that want to help other people with the skills that they have, that’s value that is really notable to me and something that I try to do as well,” Pines remarked. “If somebody in my community has a question about their medication or something and can’t afford to go to the doctor, I’m happy to answer any questions that people have.”.

It has been revealed that another volunteer, Lew Lefton, said he thought that the satisfaction humans draw from making and fixing things has largely been lost, but apocalyptic threats like climate change and artificial intelligence have driven many people toward rediscovering more basic, human skills that are key to survival. People who come to a repair café have a different way to view the future, according to Lefton, especially if they learn something or volunteer themselves. “If the world ends,” he said, “at least I’ll know how to fix a motor.”.

According to recent reports, back in Decatur, Pettus left the repair café with a newly sturdy chair. A screw and some glue fixed the crack around the joint, but the chair still needed upholstery work. Someone Pettus met at the café, who had provided one of the sets of hands that held her chair together as the glue set, advised her on where to buy fabric. Pettus thought she might bring the chair back to the repair café for help reupholstering its seat cushion.

“The beauty of it,” Pettus noted, “was that I actually was able to learn more about the chair. It was a great experience to know that—I’m not gonna say I birthed it, I of course did not—but I actually had something to do with helping to get it put back together.”.

A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today.
  • Industry observers note that the findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes.
  • According to recent reports, in a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today. Now, scientists studying his extraordinary lifespan have uncovered genetic clues that may explain how he has remained so resilient for nearly two centuries.

Industry observers note that the findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes. His body also appears to have avoided some of the genetic changes that normally accumulate with age, helping preserve important biological functions.

According to recent reports, in a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging. These variants influence several essential processes, including repairing damaged DNA, limiting inflammation, controlling insulin activity, and suppressing cancer.

According to recent reports, jonathan is an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea) believed to have hatched in 1832. That means he was already alive during the lifetimes of Charles Darwin and Queen Victoria. Today, he holds the distinction of being both the oldest living giant tortoise and the oldest known living land animal.

A 194-Year-Old Tortoise With Remarkably Youthful Gene Regulation.

One of the most surprising discoveries came when scientists examined Jonathan's epigenome, the system of chemical markers that helps determine which genes are switched on or off. These regulatory mechanisms typically change as animals grow older, potentially disrupting notable cellular processes and contributing to age-related deterioration.

To investigate how Jonathan's biology has changed over time, the researchers compared his epigenome with those of younger giant tortoises belonging to the same species.

They found that the regulatory mechanisms associated with DNA repair and metabolism had remained remarkably stable. Despite Jonathan's advanced age, these genetic controls closely resembled those found in his much younger relatives.

The results suggest that maintaining stable gene regulation could be one of the factors helping giant tortoises withstand the biological stresses of aging for exceptionally long periods.

According to recent reports, this research also represents the first investigation of the epigenome of a giant tortoise. The project was led by Kallel, a US nonprofit organization focused on longevity research. Its scientists believe that examining the biology of animals capable of surviving for centuries could reveal notable fresh insights into the mechanisms of extreme longevity.

It has been revealed that "We found that the gene regulators involved in energy production and DNA repair have remained incredibly stable in Jonathan over almost two centuries," said Dr. Justin Gerlach at Peterhouse at the University of Cambridge, who was involved in the study.

In a recent development, he added: "There are few creatures that could tell us more about aging than the giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Seychelles islands. Working with a really old giant tortoise is such a privilege: you get a sense of the tortoise being your collaborator, not your study subject.".

According to recent reports, gerlach has spent several decades investigating giant tortoise ecology and conservation. However, this project marks his first examination of the biological mechanisms responsible for their exceptional lifespans.

Could Giant Tortoise DNA Reveal Secrets to Human Longevity?

The researchers hope Jonathan's genetic characteristics could eventually help scientists develop fresh approaches to slowing age-related decline and preventing chronic diseases in humans.

By identifying the biological systems that allow certain animals to remain healthy for extraordinarily long periods, researchers may be able to uncover protective mechanisms that could inform future medical treatments.

"Nature has already solved the puzzle of aging in remarkable ways, and Jonathan's genome provides a blueprint for cellular resilience," mentioned Stephen Clark, MD, PhD, founder of Kallel and senior author of the study.

Industry observers note that he added: "Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people. Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face, and through the generosity of philanthropic partners, we can democratize access to longevity medicine.".

Although the findings provide intriguing clues about extreme longevity, translating these discoveries into treatments for humans will require further research.

Nearly Two Centuries of Life on a Remote Atlantic Island.

According to recent reports, jonathan has spent most of his exceptionally long life on St. Helena, a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean. He lives on the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the island's governor.

Industry observers note that he arrived on St. Helena from the Seychelles 144 years ago as a gift to the governor. Jonathan was already fully grown when he reached the island, providing further evidence of his remarkable age.

The giant tortoises native to the Galapagos and Seychelles islands are among the last surviving representatives of a group of enormous reptiles that once played dominant ecological roles across many of the world's islands.

Today, these extraordinary survivors offer scientists a rare opportunity to investigate how evolution has equipped certain animals to withstand the effects of time. Jonathan's unusually stable genetic regulation provides a particularly intriguing window into the biology of aging and the possibility of extending healthy life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, training for a mission to space is hard work. But sometimes you have to take a minute and have a little fun with your crewmates.

Crowded together with the Orion spacecraft, the four astronauts that make up the Artemis III crew hold up three fingers, taking a brief pause in their rigorous training for some lighthearted crew bonding.

In the snapshot, the crew — from left to right, NASA astronauts Randy Bresnick (mission commander) and Frank Rubio (mission specialist), European Space Agency astronaut Luca Parmitano (mission pilot) and NASA astronaut Andre Douglas (mission specialist) — is spotted posing alongside the same Orion spacecraft that they will fly to space as part of their mission.

This brief moment of levity took place where the spacecraft right now resides at the Neil A. Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

It has been revealed that this crew has a serious mission ahead of them. The four astronauts will launch to low-Earth orbit around Earth where they plan to practice rendezvous and docking with both Blue Origin and SpaceX's lunar landing vehicles, Blue Moon and Starship, respectively.

Industry observers note that to prepare, the crew has to undergo months of critical training to both be physically ready while prepared to handle any situation that might come up during their mission. And while Artemis III isn't landing astronauts on the moon, it is a critical step toward that goal. If Artemis III goes to plan and NASA has a lunar landing vehicle that passes rendezvous and docking tests with the Orion spacecraft, Artemis IV might see astronauts land on the moon for the first time since the final Apollo mission in 1972.

Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing fresh details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System.
  • Upcoming research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed.
  • The Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing fresh details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System. The discoveries are challenging a scientific theory that has stood for decades and could also provide important clues about the conditions that influenced Earth's earliest history.

Upcoming research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed. Instead, evidence preserved in lunar rocks indicates that the frequency of these collisions decreased gradually over billions of years.

The Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past. While erosion, volcanic activity, and the movement of tectonic plates have destroyed much of Earth's earliest geological record, the lunar surface has retained evidence of ancient asteroid impacts dating back billions of years.

Why the Moon's Far Side Holds Key Clues.

It has been revealed that dr. Fred Jourdan, a research co-author affiliated with Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences and John de Laeter Centre, explained that lunar rocks preserve valuable information about the Solar System's earliest history. These natural records allow researchers to investigate events that took place soon after the planets formed.

It has been revealed that "The Moon is like a time capsule -- it has preserved a record of events that have been erased from Earth by erosion, plate tectonics and other geological processes," Dr. Jourdan noted.

"Samples collected from the Moon's far side are particularly significant because they allow us to compare two very different parts of the Moon for the first time. Until now, almost everything we knew came from the side facing Earth.".

"By analyzing these ancient rocks, we can better understand when major asteroid impacts occurred and how the early Solar System evolved. The far side preserves a cleaner record of those earliest impacts because it was much less affected by later geological events than the side facing Earth.

"These samples are helping us rewrite parts of the Moon's history and suggest the early Solar System experienced a long decline in asteroid impacts rather than a single catastrophic bombardment.".

Reconstructing Billions of Years of Asteroid Impacts.

According to recent reports, to investigate the Moon's bombardment history, the researchers examined tiny pieces of lunar rock for evidence of ancient collisions. Their analysis identified impact events dating from approximately 4.33 billion to 1.13 billion years ago, providing a record that spans more than three billion years.

These findings offer a new perspective on how asteroid impacts changed over time. Rather than supporting the idea of a relatively brief period of exceptionally intense bombardment, the evidence points to a much longer process in which impacts became progressively less frequent.

The implications extend beyond the Moon itself. According to Dr. Jourdan, reconstructing the history of lunar impacts can help scientists better understand the events that affected Earth during its earliest stages of development.

What Ancient Moon Rocks Reveal About Early Earth.

Industry observers note that "The Moon and Earth share a common history, but the evidence of early impacts has largely disappeared from our planet," Dr. Jourdan stated.

"Because the Earth and Moon formed together, every major impact recorded on the Moon tells us something about the conditions experienced by the young Earth.

"Studying lunar rocks allows us to look back billions of years and better understand the events that shaped the environments of both worlds and helps us understand the role asteroid impacts played in planetary evolution and the conditions that may have influenced the emergence of life on Earth.

"The findings come amid a newly introduced era of lunar exploration and science, with China's Chang'e-6 mission being the first to return samples from the Moon's far side.".

Recent findings suggest that the return of material from the lunar far side has given scientists an unprecedented opportunity to examine a region that was previously inaccessible to direct sampling. By comparing these rocks with samples from the Moon's near side, researchers can develop a more complete picture of the impacts that shaped the lunar surface and the wider Solar System.

The research was led by the State Key Laboratory of Deep Earth Processes and Resources at the Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The findings were published in Science Advances in a paper titled 'The bombardment history on the lunar farside revealed by 40Ar/39Ar geochronology of Chang'e-6 impact melt rocks'.

Recent findings suggest that gap Inc. on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14.

The retailer also stated Old Navy's turnaround is showing signs of progress, sending shares up more than 11% Friday.

Kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that.

Sources indicate that "I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter stated in a statement.

The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month.

"Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode.".

Industry observers note that dickson stated the manufacturer is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success.

While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson mentioned this newly introduced approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential.

In a recent development, gap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount.

In a recent development, net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the company mentioned. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%.

Gap also noted it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year.

The tech giant lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share.

Dickson noted in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season.

"We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson said.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

For the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior.

In a recent development, at Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the company attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing. `.

The firm's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson noted it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales.

"Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson mentioned.

The Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its new CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2.

In a recent development, banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the company attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount.

Dickson mentioned the brand has since introduced newly introduced products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country.

"We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he said. "There's some work to do here, but with peak selling still ahead, I'm confident that the team is focused on the right areas and [will] ultimately position Banana well for growth.".

The streaming business is in flux, and Black Friday deals can help explain it.

It’s not hyperbole: Netflix stock has been cut in half from its all-time high. Bundles are proliferating. And Skydance CEO David Ellison has made it clear that a merger of HBO Max and Paramount+ is a question of when, not if.

Black Friday streaming deals are an annual tradition at this point, but given the state of the business, they can also shed light on how the entertainment giants behind them are thinking about the future of their products.

HBO Max and Paramount+ are offering very different types of deals, even as their parent manufacturer Skydance, is actively preparing for a discount bundle set for early next year, and with a full merger of the services following later on.

Sources indicate that HBO Max is offering an aggressive 50 percent discount on its ad-supported tier, charging $5.49 per month for a full year. Paramount+, meanwhile, is offering both its premium and standard prepares for $2.99 per month, albeit only for the first two months.

With the bundle imminent and a merger coming (expect Paramount+’s tech stack to win out over HBO Max’s), the Black Friday deals are a last gasp before what is expected to be an aggressive discount campaign early next year.

The biggest new streamer to launch in the last year, Fox One, is offering a steep 75 percent discount, $5 for the first month, before it reverts back to $20 in month two.

Peacock, meanwhile, is offering generous discounts on both its select and premium plans, selling them for $2.99 and $8.99 per month for the first three months.

Disney, which has been leaning into bundles, is offering a year of Disney+ and Hulu for $5 per month, hoping to get viewers hooked on its two entertainment platforms (ESPN is the other) ahead of a full sunset of the Hulu standalone app (it is expected to continue as a standalone service within Disney+).

Apple TV, which is still trying to gain the scale that many of the other services already have, is offering an aggressive discount of over 50 percent, selling six months of the services for $6.99 per month, down from its typical price of $14.99 per month.

According to recent reports, and niche streamers are being more aggressive: Look at Starz, which is offering an astonishing deal: $11.99 for 12 months, putting the price at under $1 per month when buying the annual plan (a more modest discount is available on monthly intends), underscoring how it needs to gain scale, and fast. Crunchyroll, Sony’s anime-focused streamer, is also offering discounts of over 50 percent for six months, ranging from $3.99 for its base tier to $8.99 for its ultimate tier.

Sources indicate that and it’s a world where Netflix, the king of the crop, still feels as though it has no need to offer discounts of any sort. After all, when you have won the subscription streaming war, it’s better to keep those margins intact.
