Tech Report: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1148 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh research suggests the Milky Way produces stars in an unexpected location, revealing a surprising difference between our galaxy and most of its neighbors.
  • The discovery comes from research led by a University of Sydney PhD student, who found evidence that a massive rotating structure of stars near the galactic center is generating powerful shock waves through surrounding clouds of gas.
  • Published in Nature Astronomy, the study also casts doubt on the nature of the Norma spiral arm, a feature of the Milky Way named for the constellation Norma as seen from Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh research suggests the Milky Way produces stars in an unexpected location, revealing a surprising difference between our galaxy and most of its neighbors. The findings also raise questions about a familiar feature of the Milky Way, suggesting that part of what astronomers have long considered a spiral arm may actually be something else.

The discovery comes from research led by a University of Sydney PhD student, who found evidence that a massive rotating structure of stars near the galactic center is generating powerful shock waves through surrounding clouds of gas. These waves squeeze the gas together, creating conditions that allow latest stars to form in a region where such intense forces usually prevent their birth.

Published in Nature Astronomy, the study also casts doubt on the nature of the Norma spiral arm, a feature of the Milky Way named for the constellation Norma as seen from Earth.

Sources indicate that lead author Dr. Hillary Davis, who recently completed her PhD at the University of Sydney's School of Physics and Sydney Institute for Astronomy, said the research provides fresh insights into the structures near the galactic center and how gas moves around them.

"At its heart, star formation is a process we understand from everyday physics. Forces set matter in motion. In this case gas is compressed, and that compression can create the conditions for latest stars to be born on a massive scale," Dr. Davis said.

"In most similar galaxies, star formation very commonly occurs along spiral arms. What's extraordinary is seeing this happen in a different region of our Galaxy, where shocks are usually so strong that star formation is often suppressed.".

A Hidden Star Factory at the Heart of the Milky Way.

In a recent development, the Milky Way belongs to a class of galaxies known as barred spiral galaxies. Unlike galaxies with only a central concentration of stars and surrounding spiral arms, these systems contain an elongated structure of stars stretching across their central region. In our galaxy, this structure is called the Galactic bar.

As the bar rotates, its gravity influences nearby gas, driving it into powerful shock fronts. These fronts compress the gas in much the same way that a shock wave compresses air.

Industry observers note that studying this structure from Earth is particularly difficult because we are located inside the Milky Way rather than viewing it from the outside. Large amounts of cosmic dust also block our view of the galactic center.

"The Galactic bar cannot be easily observed because of a combination of our position in the Galaxy and dust obscuring our view," Dr. Davis mentioned.

"As a result, the bar's properties have been highly debated.".

Observations of other barred galaxies have shown that these shock fronts generally inhibit the formation of newly introduced stars, even in regions containing abundant gas. The intense conditions make it difficult for the gas to collapse into stars.

In a recent development, however, the upcoming findings indicate that the Milky Way may behave differently. Although it is not the only known example, our galaxy appears to belong to a relatively small group in which substantial star formation takes place along the shock fronts of the central bar.

"We believe that the Milky Way's bar has star formation occurring along its shock front, which is uncommon for most bars in nearby galaxies," Dr. Davis said.

A Milky Way Spiral Arm May Not Be What It Seems.

To investigate this unusual activity, the research team compared detailed computer simulations showing how galaxies change over billions of years with astronomical observations of regions where massive stars are forming.

It has been revealed that A crucial part of the evidence came from masers, naturally occurring sources that emit highly concentrated microwave radiation. These emissions are associated with the formation of massive stars and operate on a principle similar to lasers, but at microwave wavelengths.

By examining the positions of these masers, the researchers uncovered a striking match between actual observations and the locations of shock fronts predicted by their simulations.

It has been revealed that "We found that masers previously associated with the Norma arm closely align with the shock front predicted by our simulations," Dr. Davis said. "This suggests that at least part of the so-called Norma arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a region of star formation along the leading edge of the Galactic bar.

"This raises questions about the Galaxy's spiral structure, and the bar region of the Milky Way, which needs further investigation," she mentioned.

The possibility is significant because it suggests that some of the star formation previously attributed to the Norma spiral arm could instead be occurring along the central bar. If confirmed, this interpretation would change how astronomers understand the arrangement of stars and gas in that part of the Milky Way.

Upcoming Evidence Could Redraw the Milky Way's Map.

Beyond revealing an unusual location for star birth, the research also sheds light on the physical properties of the Galactic bar itself.

Astronomers have debated the structure's length, orientation, and rotation speed for decades, partly because the Milky Way's dust and our viewing position make direct measurements so challenging.

It has been revealed that "Our findings place further constraints on the size, angle and rotation speed of this central bar," Dr. Davis said.

The team's analysis indicates that the bar extends approximately 4.3 kiloparsecs, equivalent to about 14,000 light-years, outward from the galactic center along its long axis. This supports a picture of the Milky Way containing a relatively long bar that rotates slowly.

The results illustrate how increasingly sophisticated simulations can help scientists investigate regions of our galaxy that are difficult to observe directly. By comparing models spanning billions of years with the available astronomical evidence, researchers can narrow down the possible structures and processes shaping the Milky Way.

According to recent reports, "By comparing a upcoming generation of large-scale computerized galaxy simulations, evolving over billions of years, against a more limited set of observations, we now have a stronger understanding of the bar and star formation processes in the Milky Way," Dr. Davis mentioned.

The authors reported no competing interests. Research funding came from the Australian Research Council, the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation, the Swedish Research Council, the Swedish National Space Agency, the LMK Foundation and eSSENCE (Sweden).

Computing resources and data storage were provided through National Computing Infrastructure Australia, an NCRIS capability supported by the Australian Government, and LUNARC, the Centre for Scientific and Technical Computing at Lund University, Sweden.

Russia-Ukraine war extends to Baltic, Mediterranean

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • First there was an attack on a Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, off the Finnish coast, then on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel that was allegedly carrying weapons off the coast of Libya.
  • Intelligence agencies have long warned that Russia was preparing some form of provocation along NATO's eastern flank.
  • What are the risks of Russia's war in Ukraine escalating further and drawing in other regions?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

First there was an attack on a Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, off the Finnish coast, then on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel that was allegedly carrying weapons off the coast of Libya. These spectacular Ukrainian operations in regions far from the Ukrainian capital Kyiv have caused a stir. They came shortly after several suspected Russian missiles crashed in Poland, not far from where an international military exercise was underway.

Intelligence agencies have long warned that Russia was preparing some form of provocation along NATO's eastern flank.

What are the risks of Russia's war in Ukraine escalating further and drawing in other regions?

It is no secret that Russia has long since expanded its operations beyond Ukraine: With military provocation, hybrid operations and acts of sabotage, Moscow has attempted to put pressure on the countries that openly support Ukraine.

And Ukraine has also targeted Russia's military and economy beyond its borders.

Since the summer, attacks by both Russia and Ukraine have increased in the Black Sea. Not only have Russian and Ukrainian cargo ships been targeted, but also vessels from other countries, particularly Turkey.

It has been revealed that furthermore, in the past few years, Ukraine has managed to deal significant blows to Russia, deep within Russian territory, thanks to aerial and maritime drones. It has targeted military airfields and other strategic targets such as oil refineries, including one in Omsk, Siberia, as well as military vessels in the eastern Black Sea.

Russia has access only to a very narrow strip of the Baltic Sea coast, which is flanked by Finland and Estonia. Even ahead of the attack on the Sparta II, Ukraine had struck in the area multiple times, targeting oil terminals in the region around St. Petersburg, in Ust-Luga and Primorsk.

Russia uses the Baltic Sea to transport supplies to its Kaliningrad exclave and to export oil and other goods to the rest of the world, with the help of its "shadow fleet.".

Ukrainian special forces are also said to have carried out operations against Russian military facilities in Syria, well before the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. They are also reported to have lent support to local Tuareg fighters in Mali who were able to inflict heavy losses on the Malian army and allied Russian mercenaries.

Kyiv is thus attempting to harm Russia's military and economy worldwide, even if in military terms this does not help Ukraine directly.

The Russian corvette that was sunk was part of Russia's Black Sea Fleet but because of Turkey's blockade of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, it would not have been allowed to return to the Black Sea. Instead, it was escorting Russian cargo ships in the Mediterranean. Primarily, the attacks send a political message: Russian ships can no longer feel safe — anywhere in the world.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"We are not speaking about random shadow vessels which simply transport oil above the price cap and as a result bring revenues for the Russian treasury," security expert Elisabeth Braw from the Atlantic Council told DW. Sparta II was suspected of carrying military equipment, which Moscow denies.

Sources indicate that "Ukraine is showing that it knows exactly, and secondly that it's able to hit them wherever and whatever waters they are in," Braw continued. "And this is something I don't think Ukraine has been able to do at the beginning of the war.".

Officially, Kyiv's goal is to disrupt Russian logistics and supply routes, but military experts and politicians also see the attacks as a clear political signal to Western allies. They suspect that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is sending a clear message of strength with an eye toward possible future peace negotiations.

Sources indicate that in an interview on the German news outlet Tagesschau, security expert Joachim Weber from the University of Bonn suggested that Zelenskyy was paying less attention to the US, out of a sense of disappointment. He said that Ukrainian attacks in distant maritime areas were a sign that there was less inhibition and that Ukraine was ready to expand the conflict geographically to increase pressure on Russia, despite the risks.

Weber warned that war could become omnipresent if there was an increase in attacks on civilian vessels or ships that were considered suspicious in international waters. He noted that Russia was providing more military escorts for the ships of its shadow fleet. "The likelihood that an accidental exchange of fire between armed forces, coast guards or anyone could occur is rising.".

Braw pointed out that violations of the Law of the Sea were not only rising with regard to the Russia-Ukraine war but also in relation to other conflicts and playing out in "the South China Sea, the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.".

She noted about 90% of global trade today was conducted via the oceans and she feared that others might conclude it was not "really to their advantage" to follow the rules of international maritime law.

In a recent development, she added that they might find it "beneficial in the short term to violate maritime rules" for short-term gains. "That would make the world's oceans significantly less safe for everybody.".

This article was originally written in German.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, with 29 entries ranging from in-movie needle drops and ditties written for the dystopian movie to existing songs remixed for the occasion, it’s longer than any previous “Hunger Games” soundtrack album.
  • Noah Kahan joins Taylor Swift, Coldplay, Lorde and Olivia Rodrigo in a starry lineup of artists who have voiced the lead single for one of the franchise’s films.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The “Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” album is an absolute behemoth befitting the blockbuster movie.

According to recent reports, with 29 entries ranging from in-movie needle drops and ditties written for the dystopian movie to existing songs remixed for the occasion, it’s longer than any previous “Hunger Games” soundtrack album. (“Mockingjay Part 2” leads with 19 tracks, “Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” clocks in at 17 songs, the original “Hunger Games” logs 16, and “Catching Fire” and “Mockingjay Part 1” both have 15.).

Noah Kahan joins Taylor Swift, Coldplay, Lorde and Olivia Rodrigo in a starry lineup of artists who have voiced the lead single for one of the franchise’s films. Kahan’s folk-Americana style blends into the rest of the soundtrack, which runs the gamut from country to indie. The soundtrack also includes songs from the movie’s stars, Mckenna Grace, Whitney Peak and Katniss Everdeen herself, Jennifer Lawrence.

According to recent reports, writing lyrics for characters with lived experiences different from your own (i.e., fighting to the death in a televised cage match against other children) is no small task. Many of the “Sunrise on the Reaping” tracks capture the struggles of Haymitch Abernathy’s (Joseph Zada) games and the overarching resistance movement in Suzanne Collins’ franchise. Others are good, but could have been left on the cutting room floor (or saved for the artist’s own project).

If listening to nearly 30 songs seems daunting, Variety picked the 12 best moments that Hunger Games fans must dive into.

I imagine this is what most District 12 tributes think when their name is called on Reaping Day. Perhaps during the Quarter Quell Games that Haymitch enters, with twice as many tributes to face, the fight to the finish is even fiercer. And let’s not forget that classic Abernathy wisdom: “Nobody ever wins the Games, period. There are survivors … there’s no winners.” Stephen Wilson Jr.’s voice has a hint of twang and enough rasp to give this song the grittiness the situation demands; the bridge’s refrain of “I’ll keep running” builds into a final repetition with a desperate cry into an edgy final chorus that hammers that “last place” refrain until the end.

Recent findings suggest that this song feels inspired by Haymitch’s (Zada) promise to Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak) that he will eventually see the sun rise on his birthday without a Reaping. It also rings of Wiress, whose mentorship centered around the idea that “all machines can be broken,” and the role the other rebellious Victors played in Katniss’ eventual success in ending the Hunger Games for good. And Lizzy McAlpine nails the right tone of rebellion here, which doesn’t hurt either. Her voice bends, rather than breaks, to steal some of this track’s lyrics, which deftly handles the shift between the angstier chorus and the arching vocals of the verses.

In a recent development, sydney Rose clearly knows “Sunrise on the Reaping.” This is the song that perhaps most directly and accurately references the text: The mention of Lenore Dove’s geese with the birds chirping on the backing track, the boy “sent to slaughter,” the phone line the lovers speak through while Haymitch is in the Capitol, the liquor he finds respite in after the “biggest loss” that comes after thinking he had finally escaped the Arena. This song’s strength lies partly in its accuracy to the story and also in how gentle Rose’s vocals are over these lyrics, down to the devastating final line. It’s haunting, beautiful and it’s Haymitch mourning his lost love, sung with an angelic lilt to boot.

This was the first song we got from the soundtrack, and while it’s good, it’s not Noah Kahan at his best — if that tells you anything about the strength of Kahan’s latest projects. That noted, “Draw You Out” is beautiful and warbling, and most of all, it really nails what Haymitch must have been feeling after returning from surviving the Games only to lose his closest loved ones, too. Wrap that up with an Aaron Dessner production bow on top, and it’s the perfect song for the movie’s end credits. This song’s shining moment is its first verse. It’s beautifully wandering, and Kahan’s lyrical talent is undeniable on lines like “I’m in a song with one descendin’ note” and “I’ve been feelin’ like a wing-clipped bird.”.

This track’s cinematic opening is beautiful, as are the lyrics, which poetically capture grief. I’m particularly partial to the line “Moments were stolen, put in the frame,” which lends itself to a prevalent theme throughout “Sunrise on the Reaping”: personal moments, like Haymitch’s goodbye to his family, being used for Capitol propaganda. It’s angelic, haunting and near operatic. The lyrics are succinct and effective, perfectly balanced between the “la la la” refrains and tugging on the listener’s heartstrings with lines like “Silt in the meadow, salt in your eyes.”.

In a recent development, how can you not appreciate the work of the ultimate fangirl? From her press tour looks to her franchise knowledge to her portrayal of Maysilee (and Merrilee) Donner, Mckenna Grace has been at the top of her game. It somehow only gets better, with the second verse featuring the sucker-punch lyric “I was a sister once, I carry that love closely” and the warbling, defiant vocals of a girl who won’t be bowed on the final chorus and bridge. This is a character song executed to perfection by the actor in the role, and the overlapping dialogue that concludes the track is the brutal cherry on top.

This tune dances around the film’s title, with lyrics of “Open eyes are for the weeping/Let the sun rise, just for the weekend.” The haunting quality of Violet Grohl’s croon settles nicely on lyrics about Haymitch’s struggle to break the power generator in the Arena and his defiance when looking up at the “metal birds” coming to take fallen Tributes away. The vocals are patient, the lyrics are simple and poetic. There’s a dissonance in Grohl’s delivery and a gentle brutality in each line that makes this track an unassuming knockout.

Madeline Edwards’ song echoes elements of others that I like (i.e., the Haydove spirit of “Dove Song” combined with the grit of “First in Line”). I love the concept of Haymitch going toe-to-toe with Snow in a “wrestling with god” moment. And the contrast between the growl in Edwards’ voice on the final chorus and the gentler outro is incredible. The instrumental builds behind the bridge until she finally hits the growling final chorus and takes a deserved moment to rock out, giving this song an edge that she then reins in with the outro’s soft landing.

According to recent reports, this District 12 ditty comes at a particularly emotional moment during the film’s final act, and it makes me cry every time. The only thing that hits harder than this rendition is the TikTok-edited version stitching it to duet Rachel Zegler’s take from “Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.” Where hers is biting, this one is solemn but equally strong. Scot Greenan’s voice bears the kind of mournful restraint the song deserves in its scene, which lends this song the perfect near-tears tension that is bound to make any listener’s eyes well up when this track plays mid-album.

Industry observers note that this is the darker sister song to Sydney Rose’s “Dove Song.” It’s more mournful, but it also has the beautiful references to the dove that Haymitch can’t let go. Carter Faith’s gentle twang adds to that heartachey feel with an Americana edge the “Hunger Games” franchise does so well. Faith effortlessly toes the line between classic country and lyrics that are undoubtedly rooted in “Sunrise on the Reaping.” Take a line like “I can taste you in the shine,” which nails the textual references to Haymitch’s drinking with a delightful vocal flip from Faith.

According to recent reports, another song with great “Hunger Games” lore woven into the lyrics. Reading between the lines, I see parts of it as a take on what Merrilee might have said before sending Maysilee to (almost) certain death in the Arena. “Who will I be when you leave me?” as a chorus to Maysilee asking Haymitch if Merrilee will still be a twin after she dies in the Games. Bella Kay’s mournful performance makes this one what it is: sweet high notes, tense vibrato on the post-chorus, plus she goes big on the bridge with the gut-wrenching lyrics of “Who will I be when it burns down?/You and I are out of control now/I don’t know now.”.

To pull an old Stevie Nicks song for this ‘70s-inspired film is, well, inspired. Borrowing from Nicks’ discography makes perfect sense, though this 1989 track doesn’t have a novel take on the franchise. But still, it works in a way that emphasizes this franchise’s timelessness. I mean, “Fate calls this fortune and fortune takes it away” is just “May the odds be ever in your favor” to a different tune. And honestly, I’d accept more from Nicks and Fleetwood Mac on the soundtrack. “Hunger Games” to the tune of “The Chain,” anyone?

#163448. Industry News: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1481 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1481 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some of the smallest black holes ever proposed may be capable of destroying entire stars from the inside.
  • It has been revealed that researchers at MIT and other institutions have now identified a possible way to find them.
  • Their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal, describes a remarkable possibility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some of the smallest black holes ever proposed may be capable of destroying entire stars from the inside. Scientists believe these mysterious objects, known as primordial black holes, could have formed during the first fraction of a second after the Substantial Bang, when extremely dense regions of matter collapsed under their own gravity. If they exist, these ancient remnants could also account for a substantial portion of dark matter, the invisible material that makes up most of the matter in the universe.

It has been revealed that researchers at MIT and other institutions have now identified a possible way to find them. Using theoretical calculations and computer simulations in three dimensions, the team investigated what would happen if a primordial black hole became trapped inside a star similar to our Sun.

Their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal, describes a remarkable possibility. A black hole no larger than an atom, but carrying the mass of an asteroid, could gradually sink toward the center of a star and begin consuming it from within.

Industry observers note that if the star rotates rapidly enough, material falling toward the black hole would eventually form a spinning disk around it. That development could set the stage for a catastrophic explosion.

"Once the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star," claims lead author Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT.

Sources indicate that the interaction between the black hole and the surrounding disk could produce enormous jets of matter that punch through the star and cause it to explode within seconds. Researchers predict that the resulting outburst would emit intense blue and ultraviolet light, along with X-rays and gamma rays, potentially making it visible to telescopes already in operation.

Recent findings suggest that "There is hope for us to probe primordial black holes through interactions with stars," Gottlieb notes. "We expect this to be visible, and it's something we should look into.".

The research team also included Matteo Cantiello of the Flatiron Institute, Cameron Norton and Matthew Kleban of Latest York University, and Ken Van Tilburg of Stanford University.

Ancient Black Holes That May Have Survived the Big Bang.

Industry observers note that not every primordial black hole formed in the early universe would still exist today. According to a theory developed by physicist Stephen Hawking, black holes gradually lose energy through a quantum process called Hawking radiation. Over immense periods of time, this process causes them to shrink, and the smallest primordial black holes would already have evaporated completely.

Heavier primordial black holes, however, could have survived to the present day. Some might be approximately the size of an atom while containing as much mass as an asteroid (or about a millionth of the mass of the Earth).

According to recent reports, these extraordinary objects raise an intriguing question. If they are still scattered throughout the universe, what would happen when one encounters a star? More importantly, could the resulting interaction provide the evidence needed to establish that primordial black holes actually exist?

Recent findings suggest that to investigate, Gottlieb and his colleagues combined mathematical calculations with numerical simulations incorporating general relativity, fluid dynamics, stellar evolution, and particle physics. Their goal was to understand how a primordial black hole could become trapped by a star and what would happen afterward.

How a Tiny Black Hole Could Become Trapped Inside a Star.

The researchers found that a star acting alone generally could not capture a primordial black hole passing nearby. Its gravitational attraction would be insufficient to keep the black hole from escaping.

It has been revealed that the situation changes when another object is involved. A companion star or planet could alter the gravitational interaction enough to allow the primordial black hole to become trapped.

In this arrangement involving three objects, the black hole could repeatedly travel through the star. Each passage would create friction as it moved through stellar material, gradually draining energy from its orbit and drawing it closer to the star's center.

It has been revealed that the process could take thousands or even millions of years. Although that sounds extraordinarily slow, it is relatively brief compared with the age of the universe.

Eventually, the black hole would settle into the star's core, where it could begin feeding on the surrounding material.

"Then, this is where the action begins," Gottlieb states.

A Black Hole Could Slowly Consume a Star From Within.

Recent findings suggest that once the primordial black hole reaches the stellar core, its growth depends partly on what happens to the energy generated as gas falls toward it. Some of that energy can heat the surrounding material, potentially slowing the rate at which additional gas falls inward.

The team's simulations indicate that most of the energy would instead disappear into the black hole. This would allow it to accumulate matter more rapidly than earlier estimates suggested.

Over several million years, the growing black hole could consume approximately 1 percent of the star's total mass. At that stage, its fate would depend heavily on how promptly the star rotates.

According to recent reports, if the star spins fast enough, gas would no longer be able to plunge directly into the black hole. Instead, the material would gather into a rotating disk around the black hole, which would by then have grown to several meters in size.

Recent findings suggest that "Inside the star, you have a black hole with a disk," Gottlieb states. "The black hole is also spinning, and it's twisting space and time.".

According to recent reports, as the disk continues feeding the black hole, the extreme rotation twists the magnetic field threading the surrounding material. This process could generate exceptionally powerful jets that shoot outward from the black hole's poles.

"This twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole," Gottlieb explains. "And these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds. It's very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done.".

What began as a tiny black hole hidden inside an otherwise ordinary star could therefore end in a violent explosion, with the star's destruction unfolding in a matter of seconds once the critical conditions are reached.

Exploding Stars Could Reveal Primordial Black Holes and Dark Matter.

The researchers also calculated what these unusual explosions might look like to astronomers, estimating how their brightness and color would change across different wavelengths of light.

In a recent development, their models predict a recognizable sequence of emissions, beginning with high-energy radiation and progressing through other parts of the electromagnetic spectrum as the explosion evolves. The initial outburst could include intense blue and ultraviolet light, along with gamma rays and X-rays.

Recent findings suggest that "We would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions," Gottlieb says. "This is something we could potentially detect, if it's not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard.".

Such signals could be detectable with existing astronomical instruments, potentially allowing researchers to search for primordial black holes far beyond the Milky Way.

In a recent development, however, identifying one would not be straightforward. Other cosmic events can generate similar flashes of radiation, so an unusual explosion alone would not establish that a primordial black hole was responsible.

Astronomers would need to examine additional evidence, including the characteristics of the exploding star. One especially revealing clue would be an explosion involving a star that would not ordinarily be expected to meet such a violent end.

"For instance, if the star is a certain mass that is not supposed to explode, it must be something that is happening inside that is a sort of parasite that is consuming the star from the inside," Gottlieb says. "The broader impact is that we can now place constraints on primordial black holes, and their contributions to dark matter, using observations.".

Even if no convincing examples are found, the search could help scientists determine how common primordial black holes might be and how much dark matter they could account for.

For now, primordial black holes remain hypothetical. But the newly introduced research offers astronomers a possible observational signature to pursue, connecting the spectacular destruction of stars with objects that may have existed since the universe's earliest moments.

Ariana Grande was the newest addition to the Focker family this Thanksgiving.

Following a 16-year gap since the last film in the Meet the Parents franchise, Little Fockers, hit theaters, a fourth installment, Focker-in-Law, was released this week by Universal and Paramount Pictures. Grande stars as Olivia, a former FBI hostage negotiator who accompanies her boyfriend Henry Focker (Skyler Gisondo), the son of Greg Focker (Ben Stiller), to a family reunion celebrating his grandfather Jack’s (Robert De Niro) 80th birthday.

Grande’s performance has received raves, including from The Hollywood Reporter, where critic Frank Scheck called her “the best thing in the film, going toe-to-toe with her more cinematically experienced co-stars and displaying both formidable steeliness and deadpan comic skills.” Stiller, who shares multiple scenes with Grande as his character attempts to sabotage Henry’s proposal to Olivia throughout the film, wasn’t surprised by the Grammy winner’s acting chops. “I thought she was incredible in Wicked. It’s very specific,” he told THR of Grande, who’s returned to acting, alongside her music career in recent years, earning an Oscar nomination for best supporting actress at the 97th Academy Awards for Wicked. “She was great to work with and she’s just a really nice person and fun to hang out with.”.

Stiller also recalled one scene that put him in an interesting position: performing in front of the pop star. One of Greg’s attempts to stop Henry from proposing comes when he serenades his father-in-law, Jack, in front of the whole family, singing John Legend’s “All of Me” — the song Henry intended to sing to Olivia before popping the question.

“She was on set watching the whole time and she was incredibly generous and sweet and very supportive. I knew if I tried my best, it probably would be good enough for the movie,” Stiller mentioned with a laugh. “But it was interesting because I had to do it a lot in front of her. It was an interesting day.”.

Beanie Feldstein, who plays Henry’s sister Samantha, also had high praise for Grande. “Ari is the most incredible person on planet Earth. I love her more than life itself, and she’s a tour de force in this movie,” she said.

As the Fockerverse has spanned 26 years, Stiller isn’t convinced that John Hamburg’s Focker-in-Law will be the end of the franchise, though he’s leaving that decision up to audiences. “I think if the audience wants one, there is probably another story there,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that and it were up to Stiller? “I would do it for sure,” he quipped.

Focker-in-Law is now playing in theaters.

Industry News: Mysterious newly introduced viruses reveal a missing link in evolution

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1078 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at the University of Miami have discovered a previously unknown group of viruses that could help explain a missing piece of evolutionary history.
  • The research, published in Nature Communications, challenges the conventional explanation for the origins of cellular structures known as encapsulins.
  • The discovery could have vital implications for biotechnology and for understanding the origins and early evolution of life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at the University of Miami have discovered a previously unknown group of viruses that could help explain a missing piece of evolutionary history. The finding reveals an unexpected connection between viruses and tiny protein compartments inside cells, offering fresh clues about how some of life's earliest biological structures may have developed.

The research, published in Nature Communications, challenges the conventional explanation for the origins of cellular structures known as encapsulins. Scientists previously believed these compartments evolved from viruses. However, the latest evidence suggests a more complicated evolutionary relationship in which viruses and encapsulins may have repeatedly evolved from one another over millions of years.

The discovery could have vital implications for biotechnology and for understanding the origins and early evolution of life. It also raises the possibility that viruses have biological functions that scientists have largely overlooked.

Mysterious Latest Viruses Reveal an Evolutionary Connection.

It has been revealed that at the center of the discovery are proteins that fold into a distinctive three-dimensional structure known as the HK97-fold. These proteins can assemble into protective shells and are found in both viruses and encapsulins.

The newly identified viruses have smaller, simpler genomes than other viruses that produce HK97-fold protein shells. They also possess characteristics associated with both viruses and encapsulins, making them possible evolutionary intermediates between the two. Studying these unusual viruses could help researchers understand how increasingly complex biological systems first appeared.

In a recent development, "What makes the HK97-fold proteins so interesting is that they can form shells that enclose biochemical reactions in cellular lineages, archaea, and bacteria. But they also serve genetic purposes in viruses, storing and protecting their viral genome," noted Abelardo Aguilar, the study's first author and a Ph.D. student in the Department of Biology at the University of Miami College of Arts and Sciences.

"These proteins build compartments with two different roles, which connects directly with the study of the origin of life and its early evolution because if you think about it, life at its core is about enclosing reactions and also enclosing information that can be inherited so those reactions can happen in the future.".

AI Helps Discover Hidden Viruses in Billions of DNA Sequences.

To uncover these previously unknown viruses, Aguilar worked with Antoni Luque Santolaria, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Biology. Luque also holds secondary appointments in the Department of Physics within the College of Arts and Sciences and the Department of Chemical, Environmental and Materials Engineering in the College of Engineering. The project brought together collaborators from multiple institutions.

Recent findings suggest that rather than relying on laboratory experiments to grow viruses, the team searched enormous genetic databases containing billions of DNA sequences. They combined bioinformatics, models of protein behavior, and artificial intelligence tools, including protein language models and AlphaFold, to investigate the structures encoded by these sequences.

According to recent reports, the databases included IMG/M, a resource associated with the U.S. Department of Energy's Joint Genome Institute and the University of California, Berkeley. Its genetic information comes from environmental samples collected around the world, including soil, seawater, wastewater, the human gut, and numerous other locations.

This approach allows scientists to investigate viruses that have never been successfully grown in a laboratory, greatly expanding the number of organisms and evolutionary relationships they can study.

"The majority of viruses cannot be grown in the lab. But now through sequencing, we have access to information on viruses for which we don't know the host, that we can't culture in the lab, but that are everywhere," Luque explained. "That means there are multiple questions in relation to evolution and how viruses have adapted to the world that it's now possible to explore bioinformatically.".

Viral Protein Shells May Have Unexpected Functions.

Beyond identifying the newly introduced viruses, the researchers proposed a possible molecular explanation for how viruses and encapsulins could have evolved from one another.

Sources indicate that their model centers on procapsids, immature viral protein shells (capsids) that may provide a pathway between the two types of structures. These shells could potentially support both genetic functions, such as containing viral DNA, and metabolic functions involving chemical reactions.

In a recent development, this raises an intriguing possibility. Viral capsids are generally recognized for packaging and protecting genetic material, but certain forms might also help create environments where biochemical reactions can occur.

"One implication of this research is the possibility that viral capsids could also facilitate biochemical reactions, which would open up the potential roles that capsids have in environments as a whole," Aguilar explained.

Although further research is needed to establish these potential functions, the findings suggest that scientists may need to look beyond the infectious stages of viruses to fully understand their roles in nature.

"When we're looking at viruses, we tend to look only at the particles that are infective, and this study points out that we might need to start putting more emphasis on the non-infective versions of the virus and what other functions those viral-like particles may have that we have overlooked in the past.".

Latest AI Tools Open the Door to More Viral Discoveries.

Recent findings suggest that the research also demonstrates how artificial intelligence and computational biology are transforming the study of viruses. By combining powerful analytical tools with knowledge of protein structure and physical behavior, scientists can now investigate evolutionary questions that were previously difficult to explore.

Supported by the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation and the U.S. National Science Foundation, the project provides a framework for studying other poorly understood viruses and their biological capabilities.

The researchers believe these methods could also be useful beyond evolutionary biology, including efforts to understand newly emerging viruses and pathogens.

"If you have the right question and you pair it with the right tools and physical insights, it gives researchers an opportunity to look at viruses in a way that we didn't have an opportunity to do before," Luque said. "There are evolution questions, but there are also questions about emerging pathogens or emerging viruses. The set of tools that we use can be moved forward in different contexts.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Samir Guesmi joins cast as film gears up for April 2027 shoot.
  • Among the challenges facing Franco-Algerian filmmaker Rachid Bouchareb as he prepares to shoot his next feature, “Reggane,” are rebuilding a French military base in the Algerian Sahara, sourcing military vehicles dating back to the final years of French colonial rule and dressing some 2,000 extras.
  • Sources indicate that the three-time Oscar-nominated director, whose companion documentary short “Boomerang Atomic” is screening in the Ajyal Short Film Competition at the Doha Film Festival, tells Variety that the feature is now gearing up for an April 2027 shoot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Samir Guesmi joins cast as film gears up for April 2027 shoot.

Among the challenges facing Franco-Algerian filmmaker Rachid Bouchareb as he prepares to shoot his next feature, “Reggane,” are rebuilding a French military base in the Algerian Sahara, sourcing military vehicles dating back to the final years of French colonial rule and dressing some 2,000 extras.

Sources indicate that the three-time Oscar-nominated director, whose companion documentary short “Boomerang Atomic” is screening in the Ajyal Short Film Competition at the Doha Film Festival, tells Variety that the feature is now gearing up for an April 2027 shoot. “Each time, I discover that the scale of the production means preparation takes a little longer,” Bouchareb states. “We’re making a period film in the depths of the Sahara. There are surprises.” Related Stories Jennifer Lopez Teases 'Monster-in-Law' Sequel With Jane Fonda: 'We’re Talking About Maybe Doing Another One' Sheryl Lee Ralph-Produced ‘Until Everyone Is Seen’ Sets World AIDS Day Premiere on Hulu (EXCLUSIVE).

Set in 1960, two years before Algeria gained independence from France, the film follows an Algerian shepherd who dreams of becoming a fisherman but finds himself stuck on a French military base after the army requisitions him and his livestock.

Sources indicate that originally slated to begin shooting in September, the period drama is in preparation across a vast stretch of the Algerian Sahara, from south-central Timimoun, to Tamanrasset in the deep south and Djanet in the southeast. Some production locations are more than 1,200 miles from the coastal capital of Algiers, necessitating particularly complex logistical planning.

Algerian state-owned companies specializing in desert construction are working alongside the film’s art department to recreate the military base, while the Algerian army is supplying period vehicles.

Variety can exclusively reveal that French actor Samir Guesmi (“District B13”) is attached to the project. Further casting is underway to bring together professional Algerian and French actors alongside nonprofessional performers drawn from local communities.

Sources indicate that since Bouchareb unveiled the project to Variety last year, its financing structure has changed considerably. The feature is now financed entirely by Algerian partners, including the Ministry of Culture and Arts and the Algerian Center for Cinema Development (CADC), a public entity tasked with developing the country’s film industry. U.S.-based Cohen Media Group and Japan’s Kingyo Films are on board as co-production partners.

According to recent reports, “What’s most important for me, because I’m not in a hurry, is that I’m reassured that the film will be made. That’s one less source of anxiety for a filmmaker,” he says. “I haven’t had to go looking for financing here and there. Everything is secure.”.

In a recent development, bouchareb’s research for “Boomerang Atomic,” which revisits France’s first atomic bomb detonation in Algeria on Feb. 13, 1960, has also shaped his approach to the feature. He intends to move between fiction and archival footage, juxtaposing official declarations with images of the people living in the Sahara.

“It’s interesting to show these images, particularly to contradict what was being said, namely that there was no risk, that everything was fine, that they chose this place because there was nobody there,” he explains. “And then to show some faces, the few that I found, of Algerian workers at the time.”.

Recent findings suggest that the documentary has already forged connections between communities affected by nuclear testing. Its presentation by the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) in Hiroshima this past August brought together members of the film’s team, survivors of the atomic bombing and attendees from French Polynesia, where France conducted 193 nuclear tests between 1966 and 1996.

“The commemoration in Hiroshima was a really crucial moment,” he reflects. “All of a sudden, these memories were connected, between the survivors of Hiroshima, the Polynesians and Algeria, through the documentary.”.

It has been revealed that with potential school and festival screenings in French Polynesia, Bouchareb is particularly moved by the documentary’s reach. “Sometimes we don’t know where our films travel,” he says. “Having brought these memories together is wonderful.”.

He recalls a similarly powerful experience touring France with his Oscar-nominated 2006 war drama “Days of Glory,” which follows North African soldiers fighting for France during World War II.

It has been revealed that “The film allowed people to say to themselves, ‘Our ancestors participated in the liberation of France and Europe. They died by the thousands. They were heroes. So my place here is legitimate,’” he recalls. “Half the room was made up of children of immigrants. I felt that they had found something.”.

According to recent reports, the desire to tell such stories led Bouchareb to establish his own production organization, 3B Productions, in 1990. “I’m very happy to produce my own films because today I can tackle any subject,” he says. “I don’t think I would have had the career I have today if I hadn’t been my own producer. It simply would have been impossible.”.

“Boomerang Atomic” has been submitted for consideration in the documentary short film category at the 2027 Academy Awards, with Bouchareb hoping to bring greater attention to this little-known chapter of history. “The Oscar qualification opens up a few more possibilities for the film,” he says. “It allows me to talk about it through the press and make it better known.”.

Bouchareb remains open to collaborating on “Reggane” with Forest Whitaker, who boarded “Boomerang Atomic” as executive producer in October. Whitaker previously starred in Bouchareb’s 2014 drama “Two Men in Town.”.

“This important documentary made an indelible impact on me and needs to be seen,” Whitaker stated in a statement.

The director is also in discussions with Goodfellas for international distribution of the feature and is particularly keen to reach audiences in France, the U.S. and Japan. Though receptive to streaming platforms giving his films a second life, Bouchareb is adamant about where that life should begin.

“For me, first and foremost, it’s the cinema,” he states. “The movie theater is something magical.”.

You might have clocked it in the Season 4 premiere, but with episode 2 it's very clear: Molly Ringwald has joined Yellowjackets.

According to recent reports, the '80s icon who fronted movies like The Breakfast Club, Sixteen Candles, and Pretty in Pink takes over the role of Van's (Liv Hewson) mom, Vicky Palmer, from Deborah Vancelette. And this signifies a major change in Van's life, post-rescue.

Industry observers note that in the Season 1 pilot, Vicky (Vancelette) is presented as a bad mom. In a montage of the Yellowjackets readying for that fateful flight, Van walks through a dark, cluttered house to find her mom passed out on the couch, next to a nearly empty alcohol bottle. She tries to wake her, presumably because she needs a ride to the plane. But calling to her and shaking her isn't enough to rouse Vicky. So, Van slaps her, and she does so with a world-weariness that suggests this isn't an isolated incident.

Sources indicate that in Season 4, episode 2, Vicky (Ringwald) is transformed. The living room is sunny and tidy upon Van's return, with a wall of VHS tapes carefully preserved. Later, Vicky highlights she cares by assuring Van she taped every episode of The X-Files. To Tai (Jasmin Savoy Brown), she'll say of Vicky, "My mom is completely different.".

No shade to Vancelette, who got little to do in the role of Vicky. But if any Yellowjacket was going to get a mom played by a movie idol of the '80s, it ought to be Van. Her love of pop culture is a defining characteristic, as she'd quote and allude to movies and shows to brandish her wit and wisdom. Of course, if her mom's going to get a glow-up, she's going to become the "princess" from The Breakfast Club. Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1096 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that newly introduced archaeological research from Bournemouth University (BU) suggests that an influential Iron Age British ruler, long believed to have been a man, was actually a woman.
  • Industry observers note that verica ruled the Atrebates, a powerful tribe whose lands extended across much of what is now Hampshire and West Sussex.
  • The Roman historian Cassius Dio claimed that Verica's appeal was the reason Claudius decided to invade Britain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that newly introduced archaeological research from Bournemouth University (BU) suggests that an influential Iron Age British ruler, long believed to have been a man, was actually a woman. The ruler, known as Verica, played a pivotal role in events leading to the Roman invasion of Britain in AD 43. The findings challenge longstanding assumptions about early British history and the political influence of women during this period.

Industry observers note that verica ruled the Atrebates, a powerful tribe whose lands extended across much of what is now Hampshire and West Sussex. Around AD 40, Verica was forced from power and escaped to Rome, where the exiled ruler sought assistance from Emperor Claudius.

The Roman historian Cassius Dio claimed that Verica's appeal was the reason Claudius decided to invade Britain. If this account is accurate, Verica's actions may have helped set in motion one of the most consequential events in British history.

Ancient Evidence Challenges an Iron Age King's Identity.

Dr. Miles Russell, Director of Archaeological Fieldwork at Bournemouth University, led the research and argues that earlier historians incorrectly identified Verica as male.

Sources indicate that "Verica is assumed to have been male because of the patriarchal mindset of 19th-century classical historians. Verica was not only critical to the special relationship between Britain and Rome in the early first century AD but was indisputably female.".

Russell points to several pieces of evidence supporting this interpretation. One is the name Verica itself, which ends in the letter "a," a feature common among female names of the time. Other prominent examples include Cartimandua, who ruled the Brigantes (in Yorkshire), and Boudica, leader of the Iceni (in Norfolk).

All three rulers lived during roughly the same period. Boudica is the best known because of her rebellion against Roman rule in AD 60. However, Russell argues that Verica may have held even greater political power and influence.

Another important clue comes from coins issued under Verica's rule. These coins bear the Latin title "rex," traditionally translated as "king," which has contributed to the assumption that Verica was male. Russell explains that the title was not necessarily restricted to men.

"People also assume she was a 'he' because of the term 'rex' on coins, but rex is a non-gender-specific title; both male and female kings were recognized by Rome, Cleopatra of Egypt being the most famous.".

He continued: "The use of the Latin title rex on coins indicates that Verica ruled with the full authorization of the emperor.".

The artwork on Verica's coins provides another intriguing clue. Rather than depicting the masculine warriors commonly featured on coins produced by other British Iron Age rulers, Verica's coins show a figure with distinctly feminine characteristics.

"Whilst other coin-producing British Iron Age leaders portray obviously male warriors, Verica is depicted as a slender, feminine, bare-breasted figure riding on horseback.".

The Forgotten Ruler Behind Rome's Invasion of Britain.

Industry observers note that russell believes Verica's importance extended far beyond the ruler's identity. He argues that Verica may have been instrumental in helping Claudius successfully invade Britain.

Industry observers note that ancient Roman writers frequently portrayed Claudius as an ineffective emperor who was easily influenced by women and formerly enslaved people who had gained their freedom. This reputation may have shaped how historians described Verica's role in persuading him to invade.

Sources indicate that russell suggests that Cassius Dio's account reinforced this negative portrayal by presenting the invasion as a decision made under the influence of a woman. In reality, he argues, Verica may have been a valuable political and military ally who supplied the Romans with intelligence and practical assistance.

According to recent reports, "The story of Claudius committing to something only because a woman told him to fits the trope of this emperor as being submissive and henpecked. In effect, Dio was saying that the campaign was undertaken solely because of the whisperings of a barbarian femme fatale. Verica's role was rather more central to the British expedition. Having her on board ensured the project was a success, as she provided tactical information and support on the ground.

It has been revealed that "The invasion was Claudius' great triumph -- it being the only chance he had to prove he was a successful military leader. Verica provided the excuse for regime change, and the emperor seized it.".

In a recent development, for Claudius, the conquest of Britain offered an opportunity to establish his reputation as a successful military commander. Verica's removal from power gave him a political justification for intervening, while the exiled ruler's knowledge of Britain may have helped the Roman forces achieve their objectives.

Could Rome's Conquest of Britain Have Been Avoided?

Although Verica was an vital political figure in late Iron Age Britain, the ruler's influence has received relatively little attention compared with that of other prominent leaders.

It has been revealed that russell believes the archaeological evidence supports recognizing Verica as one of Britain's earliest and most significant female rulers. He also raises the possibility that the Roman invasion might never have occurred without Verica's exile and subsequent appeal to Claudius.

"We should take the archaeological evidence at face value" says Russell "and remember Verica as a female-king and one of the earliest and most important of British female leaders. Had she not been deposed, fleeing to Claudius for military support, Rome may never have invaded Britain in the first place.".

Upcoming Insights Into Women in Iron Age Britain.

The findings build on earlier Bournemouth University research exploring the position of women in ancient British society.

Sources indicate that last year, a study involving Russell and other BU researchers uncovered evidence of a matriarchal society in Iron Age Britain. The research indicated that husbands moved into their wives' communities after marriage, suggesting that women occupied a central position in the social structure.

Together, these discoveries are prompting researchers to reconsider the influence women may have exercised in Iron Age Britain, both within their communities and in the political decisions that shaped the region's future.

Russell's research on Verica is presented in the new book Caratacus: Great king of Britain, published by Bloomsbury in January (ISBN 9781350477902). The findings are also discussed in the latest edition of Current Archaeology.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Independent movie studio A24 has had a banner year at the box office, and HBO Max is set up to benefit from its success.
  • A24 is behind some of this year's buzziest films, including horror hit "Backrooms," dark comedy "The Drama" starring Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything," co-directed by Nathan Fielder.
  • The studio has generated more than $526 million at the domestic box office this year as of Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Independent movie studio A24 has had a banner year at the box office, and HBO Max is set up to benefit from its success.

A24 is behind some of this year's buzziest films, including horror hit "Backrooms," dark comedy "The Drama" starring Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything," co-directed by Nathan Fielder.

The studio has generated more than $526 million at the domestic box office this year as of Nov. 15, according to data from Rentrak. That's already roughly $290 million, or more than 50%, above its haul for all of 2025.

"They have an identity all their own, and just the mere mention of A24, the recognition that a movie is from A24, gives it instant credibility and provides a must-see factor, no matter what the subject matter," Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends at Rentrak, told CNBC.

Skydance co-CEO and Chairman David Ellison cited movie releases from A24 as part of the company's "unmatched portfolio" during its most recent earnings call.

A24 films released this year broke records at the box office, with "Backrooms" becoming the studio's biggest domestic opening to date and "You Can See Everything" notching the biggest documentary opening since "Fahrenheit 9/11" in 2004.

That success has already begun to translate to HBO Max's platform.

In a recent development, when "Backrooms" began streaming on HBO Max, it was the most streamed title on the platform for two weeks, according to Nielsen data. The film was also the fourth overall most streamed title the week it premiered, racking up 226 million minutes of viewing time.

After more than a year of competing bids and regulatory hurdles, Skydance now oversees two of the world's largest streaming platforms: HBO Max and Paramount+.

The tech giant plans to eventually merge the streaming services into a single platform. It will take the first step in that effort by offering a value bundle in early 2027.

The combination of the platforms "will drive stronger engagement and higher lifetime value," co-CEO Ynon Kreiz stated on the company's earnings call earlier this month.

In a recent development, paramount Skydance's direct-to-consumer segment, which includes Paramount+ and its free, ad-supported channel, Pluto TV, generated more than $2 billion in revenue during the third quarter, representing more than 35% of total revenue for the period. That segment revenue marked an 11% year-over-year increase, with revenue from Paramount+ up 21%.

The earnings do not reflect the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, since that deal closed after the close of the quarter.

Revenue growth in streaming will be key as it faces the daunting task of managing nearly $80 billion of debt.

The manufacturer has remarked it expects to realize $6 billion in cost savings over the next three years and has put a particular focus on consolidating its operations and streamlining its marketing spend.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are 44 movies that want it all.

That’s how many titles appear on BAFTA‘s draft Entered Films List for the 2027 EE BAFTA Film Awards, with submissions across every category open to them: best film, director, screenplay and all nine craft races, right down to special visual effects.

Industry observers note that there are 126 best film entries, up from 109 eligible titles a year ago. Across best film, director, the two screenplay races and the nine crafts, 213 features are in play. Count the titles entered only in specialty races such as Documentary, Animated Film or Outstanding Debut by a British Writer, Director or Producer and the list climbs to 235. Related Stories Andrew Scott on Starring in ‘Elsinore’ and Feeling ‘Very Grateful’ to Be an Out Gay Actor Jennifer Lopez Wears 186-Carat Diamond Necklace to 'JLo Show' Premiere: 'There's Security All Around'.

In a recent development, the list isn’t final. Distributors and producers have until noon GMT on Monday, Nov. 30, to request amendments and the official Entered Films List arrives Friday, Dec. 4, the same day Round One voting opens. Expect a few small corrections.

Among the list of films submitting in every category are Denis Villeneuve’s “Dune: Part Three,” Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” Emerald Fennell’s “Wuthering Heights,” Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day,” Robert Eggers’ “Werwulf,” “Project Hail Mary,” “Spider-Man: Brand Latest Day,” “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple” and “Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man.”.

Also swinging in all 12 categories are the Tom Cruise-vehicle “Digger,” “Verity,” “Send Help,” “Crime 101,” “The Death of Robin Hood,” “Heart of the Beast,” “Pressure,” “Ink,” “Tenzing,” “Wicker,” “The Sheep Detectives” and “Ghosts: The Possession of Button House.”.

Then there’s “You Can See Everything.”.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary is entered in best film, director, documentary and seven of the nine craft races, including costume design and makeup and hair. What it doesn’t have is a single performance entry, and that’s because BAFTA rules deem it ineligible.

Amanda Seyfried, who won an Emmy playing Holmes in Hulu’s “The Dropout,” returns to the role in the A24 film’s dramatized reenactments, a performance Variety right now projects to win the Oscar for supporting actress. BAFTA joins the Golden Globes and Actor Awards (formerly the SAG Awards) among awards bodies where Seyfried is ineligible for recognition. Critics Choice stands alone in deeming her eligible for supporting actress, making it the only televised stop on the precursor circuit where she can be nominated. Critics Choice Awards nomination voting is underway.

The four performance categories have 728 entries.

Six performers are entered four times apiece. Zendaya is submitted in lead for “Dune: Part Three,” “The Drama” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and in supporting as Athena in “The Odyssey.” Her “Drama” co-star Robert Pattinson matches her, entered in lead for that film and for “Primetime,” where he plays Chris Hansen, plus supporting turns in “Dune: Part Three” and “The Odyssey.”.

#163434. Industry News: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history

Industry News: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1061 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for billions of years, Earth's atmosphere contained almost no oxygen, making the planet vastly different from the world we know today.
  • Two geochemists from Chengdu University of Technology have presented this revised timeline in The Innovation.
  • Scientists have traditionally reconstructed Earth's atmospheric oxygen levels using chemical clues preserved in ancient ocean sediments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for billions of years, Earth's atmosphere contained almost no oxygen, making the planet vastly different from the world we know today. A latest scientific analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere during three major stages, while the deep oceans took much longer to catch up. In some cases, the delay stretched across hundreds of millions of years, with the final transition involving a gap of roughly 600 million years.

Two geochemists from Chengdu University of Technology have presented this revised timeline in The Innovation. Their findings challenge the traditional understanding of Earth's oxygen history by examining chemical evidence that reflects conditions in the ancient atmosphere rather than relying primarily on measurements of ocean chemistry.

Ancient Rocks Reveal a Different Oxygen Timeline.

Scientists have traditionally reconstructed Earth's atmospheric oxygen levels using chemical clues preserved in ancient ocean sediments. However, the amount of oxygen in seawater is influenced by many factors besides the atmosphere, including nutrient availability, biological productivity, ocean circulation, and the shapes of ocean basins. This makes ocean chemistry an imperfect guide to conditions in the air.

According to recent reports, the researchers instead focused on sulfate, a chemical compound that can preserve a distinctive signal from atmospheric oxygen. Reactions involving oxygen, ozone, and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere produce an unusual shortage of the oxygen isotope oxygen-17. When sulfide minerals undergo weathering, this chemical fingerprint is transferred into sulfate, which can eventually become preserved in sedimentary rocks. By examining these signatures, scientists can gain a more direct picture of how atmospheric oxygen changed over time.

According to this evidence, Earth's first major increase in oxygen occurred during the Great Oxidation Event, between 2.4 billion and 2.1 billion years ago. Atmospheric oxygen rose from less than one-millionth of today's concentration to somewhere between 0.1% and 10% of modern levels.

The second major increase took place approximately 1.3 billion to 1.0 billion years ago, followed by a third between 440 million and 410 million years ago. Both occurred earlier than conventional timelines suggest.

According to recent reports, under this interpretation, the well-known Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic oxygenation events, traditionally dated to 800 million to 500 million years ago and 420 million to 360 million years ago, mainly reflect delayed changes in ocean oxygen levels. The oceans responded roughly 200 million and 30 million years after the corresponding atmospheric increases.

Earth's Atmosphere and Oceans Did Not Always Change Together.

Despite these major increases, oxygen remained relatively scarce throughout much of Earth's history. Models based on the isotope evidence suggest that atmospheric oxygen during the middle Proterozoic reached only about 0.1% to 1% of present-day levels.

In a recent development, another clue comes from the fossil record of charcoal. Because charcoal formation requires atmospheric oxygen concentrations of approximately three-quarters of modern levels, its absence from older rocks suggests that oxygen remained too scarce to support widespread burning. Charcoal first appears in the geological record around 420 million years ago.

In a recent development, the researchers also highlight a surprising relationship between oxygen in the atmosphere and oxygen in the oceans. Over extremely long periods, the two generally increased together. However, on timescales of around a million years, they could move in opposite directions.

Industry observers note that when additional oxygen entered the oceans, it could react with accumulated organic carbon and sulfide, consuming oxygen in the process. These reactions could reduce the amount of oxygen remaining in the atmosphere.

Recent findings suggest that as a result, some chemical signals previously interpreted as evidence of rising oxygen may actually record periods when atmospheric oxygen was declining. This possibility could change how scientists interpret major fluctuations in Earth's ancient oxygen record.

Oxygen-Rich Oases Existed Billions of Years Ago.

The spread of oxygen through Earth's oceans was also far from uniform. The researchers describe two major sources of oxygen in seawater: oxygen produced locally by photosynthetic microorganisms and oxygen absorbed from the atmosphere.

The first process created isolated pockets of oxygen-rich water as early as 3 billion years ago, possibly even earlier. These small oxygenated environments existed during the Archean, when the atmosphere and most of the oceans still contained very little free oxygen.

According to recent reports, as atmospheric oxygen levels gradually increased, oxygen entering seawater from the air became more key. Eventually, this atmospheric supply overtook local biological production as the dominant mechanism driving widespread ocean oxygenation.

Even then, the transformation was remarkably slow. According to the proposed timeline, the deep ocean did not become fully oxygenated until approximately 410 million years ago, long after oxygen had begun accumulating in the atmosphere.

How Rising Oxygen Changed the Evolution of Life.

These findings also offer a newly introduced perspective on the relationship between oxygen and the evolution of complex organisms.

When Earth's atmosphere contained virtually no oxygen, its absence placed a major restriction on oxygen-dependent life. During the Proterozoic, increasing oxygen availability gradually made fresh environments accessible, although concentrations continued to fluctuate as early animals evolved.

Rather than acting as a single trigger for complex life, oxygen initially provided opportunities for biological innovation. Only after the third major atmospheric increase did higher oxygen levels become a powerful force supporting greater biological complexity.

This later transformation helped create conditions favorable for larger animals, more active predators, and organisms capable of occupying deeper marine environments.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers acknowledge that notable uncertainties remain. The available isotope record does not capture every change in detail, and absolute atmospheric oxygen concentrations after 1 billion years ago remain difficult to establish. Additional increases or decreases may have occurred without leaving sufficiently clear chemical evidence to identify them.

It has been revealed that nevertheless, the analysis proposes a major revision to the sequence of events that transformed Earth into an oxygen-rich planet. Rather than the oceans becoming oxygenated first and the atmosphere following, the evidence suggests that atmospheric oxygen increased well before the deep oceans responded.

That prolonged delay may have played an crucial role in shaping the environments where complex life emerged and evolved.

Germany: 2 arrested, suspected of plotting synagogue attack

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (570 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Germany's federal prosecutor's office on Thursday mentioned it had ordered the arrest of two Iraqi citizens in Germany who are believed to be members of a pro-Iranian terrorist group.
  • It identified the men as Mostafa Al-R.
  • Officers from Germany's federal criminal police force carried out the arrests.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Germany's federal prosecutor's office on Thursday mentioned it had ordered the arrest of two Iraqi citizens in Germany who are believed to be members of a pro-Iranian terrorist group.

It identified the men as Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J., and noted that they were arrested in Heidelberg in Baden-Württemberg in the southwest, and in Cologne, several hours' drive to the north.

Officers from Germany's federal criminal police force carried out the arrests.

Prosecutors also revealed searches and raids of 17 sites in total across three separate states, saying these were ongoing.

Sources indicate that after two suspects were arrested, Hendrik Wüst, the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, thanked the security agencies for their vigilance and dedication. "Protecting Jewish life is our shared responsibility," he wrote on X.

It has been revealed that "Jewish life must be able to flourish freely and safely in our country. Anyone who attacks it attacks us all," Wüst added.

Prosecutors remarked the two men were "strongly suspected" of membership in a domestic terrorist organization.

They noted that Mostafa Al-R. wa an associate of a man in the US known as Mohammad Al-Saadi, who is accused of setting up a group with the acronym HAYI (Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya) that is thought to be "responsible for a series of attacks against US, Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe from March 2026," in the aftermath of the outbreak of Donald Trump's war with Iran.

Industry observers note that mostafa Al-R. and Al-Saadi allegedly "founded a separate organization to prepare and carry out further attacks in Germany and Europe at the end of 2025.".

Recent findings suggest that prosecutors say Ameer J. joined this group. It gathered funds and "recruited several external people to carry out explosive attacks.".

"On the group's orders, unknown assailants headed on two consecutive nights in late March 2026 — presumably with explosives — to synagogues in Cologne and in one other European city," prosecutors wrote. "The blueprint was, for reasons as yet unknown, ultimately not carried out.".

Prosecutors stated that intelligence behind the arrests could be traced back to the federal domestic intelligence agency, the BfV.

More than 250 police officers from various forces were part of Thursday's operation.

Both suspects were expected to appear before judges later on Thursday for a decision on them being placed in investigative detention.

One other person is being sought as part of the investigation, with several others not at the moment suspected of criminal offenses affected by it.

The stated date for the plot to attack Cologne's synagogue, late March this year, would have roughly coincided with a series of crimes in Europe targeting Jewish people or institutions in the weeks after the outbreak of war with Iran.

These included an explosion in front of Liege synagogue in Belgium on March 9, which caused property damage but no injuries.

Police in the Netherlands investigated a fire at Rotterdam's synagogue a few days later. An explosive device was set off outside a Jewish school in Amsterdam soon after, prompting heightened security across the Netherlands.

In London, a Jewish ambulance service was targeted in arson attacks in March, not long before two Jewish men were stabbed in broad daylight in what investigators treated as a likely act of terrorism.

Several months later, in September, police in Wuppertal in Germany arrested an Afghan national on suspicion of trying to set a fire at the city's synagogue.
