📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SPOILER ALERT: The following story contains plot details from “I Learn How to Grow Zombies,” Season 3, Episode 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians,” now streaming on Disney+.

Seventeen-year-old Leah Sava Jeffries carries the weight of the world on her shoulders in Season 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” — literally. The story of Atlas, a Titan burdened by the unbearable task of holding up the sky, is one of the many Greek myths that serves as the basis for a Season 3 storyline. Related Stories ‘Artificial’ Star Andrew Garfield Recalls Believing OpenAI’s Sam Altman Was ‘Genuinely Great’ and Could Be ‘My Future Best Friend’ ‘Morning Show’ Star Mark Duplass and Katie Aselton Show Off Their Three Rescue Dogs in PETA Ad (EXCLUSIVE).

The Season 3 premiere saw Jeffries’ Annabeth kidnapped by a human-lion-scorpion hybrid monster called a manticore and taken across the country from Percy (Walker Scobell) and Grover (Aryan Simhadri). Annabeth faces her own struggles while her friends work to rescue her, which is latest for the show; the first two seasons followed the trio going on epic quests together. With Annabeth separated for much of “The Titan’s Curse” — the third book in Rick Riordan’s “Percy Jackson” series, which Season 3 is based on — Jeffries’ main scene partners now are Charlie Bushnell, who plays Luke, and Dafne Keen, who plays Artemis.

Sources indicate that that’s not the only way Season 3 is wading into uncharted waters. The first-ever screen interpretation of “Percy Jackson” was a pair of movies in the early 2010s based on Riordan’s first and second books. But Jeffries is keenly aware of the fact that “The Titan’s Curse” has never been adapted.

“It’s the first time anyone has ever seen it live action instead of just reading it in the book,” she notes. “I want to make sure that I’m still delivering how the description was as much as I can, but then also still giving my own little twist with it.”While dedicated readers of the “Percy Jackson” books love to see Easter eggs in the TV show, Jeffries never wants the show to be for those fans alone. She points out many viewers hadn’t read the books until Seasons 1 and 2 came out and aims to perform for that audience too — especially as someone who hadn’t even been born yet when the original novel was released in 2005, she points out.

Recent findings suggest that “Coming into these roles in the beginning was a tough thing because [the books] had such a significant fan base already, and so many people that already knew about them before me,” Jeffries indicates. “It was a lot to learn from, but I’m so excited that I was able to get this role and embody the character as much as I can.”.

In a recent development, jeffries notes she has learned a lot from Bushnell, 22, whom she acted opposite in several key scenes in Episodes 2 and 3 this season. She recalls him checking in after fight scenes or making sure he didn’t accidentally hit her during a take.

“He’s such a role model for people. I learned so much stuff from him. He’s just such a great person to work with as well as a scene partner,” Jeffries notes. “You could just tell he loves doing what he does, and that’s such a substantial thing to see because even before the show has come out, with criticism, sometimes I still get in my head. But when I watch him working, his confidence and the way he goes about things, it just makes me have a brighter day, so I’m very grateful to work with him.”.

Sources indicate that in Episode 2, Annabeth discovers that Luke has been subjected to the punishment that once burdened. Atlas, the Greek Titan: holding up the sky. She decides to takes over him, and when the weight hits her shoulders, she lets out a guttural yell that Jeffries claims was hard to find — and sounds different than she remembers. “The crazy thing is that it sounds so much more high-pitched on the show. I promise you, I have videos when I had a deeper scream and it was grittier, but I think I just lost my voice at that time,” she says, adding that the outburst didn’t come naturally to her: “I’m not a screaming person. Someone can ask me right now. like, ‘Hey, scream!’ I cannot just open my mouth and be like, ‘Ahhh!’ Like, I can’t.”.

In a recent development, so Jeffries devised a trick. If she needs to scream on camera, she pushes against something or strengthens her core with a quick sit-up beforehand. “I will growl before, and then go,” she states. “I have to know that my voice will hit it.”.

According to recent reports, in the show, when a character is carrying the weight of the sky, an eerie, gray haze spreads across their eyes — achieved with color contacts. That visual detail was actually Jeffries’ idea.

Sources indicate that she states she told Daphne Olive, one of the “Percy Jackson” writers, that using contacts would give more weight to the scene. “The grayness puts the strain on your eyes. It demonstrates that you’re in this different world and this different dreaming life,” Jeffries says. Eventually, Jeffries got approval from the production to move forward with her pitch.

In Episode 3, still stuck in the gray haze, Annabeth has a vision of herself holding onto Percy and Thalia (Tamara Smart) as they dangle over a cliff. It’s an emotional sequence — Annabeth has tears in her eyes — but Jeffries mostly recalls how awkward it was to film. On set, she was hanging off of a practically built cliff and was fitted with wires, “because obviously, they don’t want me to fall,” she states. And though Jeffries had Percy and Thalia on her mind, she didn’t have Scobell and Smart to look at. “Whenever you saw my face, they actually weren’t even there, and I wasn’t talking to them,” she says. “I was actually holding two weights while hanging over the top, which is the funniest thing ever. Everyone was staring at me. When I looked down — I always try to do my best, but — I was so nervous.”.

It has been revealed that at the suggestion of her acting coach, Jeffries took some quiet time to concentrate before her more emotional scenes. “It was hard because I love making jokes,” she says, “but the scene came out so beautifully. I just loved it.”.

It has been revealed that percy and Annabeth don’t share many moments together during Season 3, with the former going on a lengthy journey to rescue the latter. But Jeffries and Scobell spent a lot of time working together on Seasons 1 and 2, so when thinking about how to develop their relationship this season, Jeffries indicates they just went for it.

“It’s crazy because we really didn’t [talk], but in a good way,” she says. “I like the fact that we had our own assumptions of what it would be like, and then just see how we were going to play it on the actual day.”.

In a recent development, for their scenes together, the pair would just follow their instincts without a discussion for a few takes, then put their heads together to see what else they could build. “We just knew that if we were to leave it to ourselves, then it would be better when they say action,” Jeffries adds. “We were going to learn from there.”.

Sources indicate that from Jeffries’ perspective, the best is yet to come. She says she’s especially excited to see her work with Bushnell in Episode 5 — ”The improv we did was genuinely crazy,” she says — and teases that a big surprise is coming in the Season 3 finale.

The last episode “is something that literally means so much to me because I feel like so many people have asked for it,” she indicates. “I know so many people who wanted to see it, and that dream came true.”.

Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that some constellations are like old friends.
  • It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting.
  • But look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that some constellations are like old friends. You know them well, they're always there, and they never seem to change. A case in point is Cassiopeia, the queen. Its beautiful name comes from Greek mythology — the mother of Andromeda — and its shape is mentioned to represent a queen sitting on a throne. To a stargazer, Cassiopeia is best known as a prominent northern constellation shaped like the letter W.

It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting. It's so often a signpost, not a destination.

But look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone. The five stars are still there, but the shape you may have memorized looks like it's been picked up and turned over. It looks more like an E or an M, depending on when you look. Now try and look for the Significant Dipper/the Plough. It's gone.

Industry observers note that nothing mysterious has happened, of course. Cassiopeia is doing exactly what it always does, but it's a reminder that the northern sky is where you can easily watch the stars move — and the seasons turn.

According to recent reports, late November is an excellent time to reacquaint yourself with Cassiopeia from anywhere in the Northern Hemisphere. Look high in the northern sky during the evening for its five prominent stars — Caph, Schedar, Navi, Ruchbah and Segin. Depending on exactly when you look, it can look like a W, E, M or a 3.

Sources indicate that this is because Cassiopeia is circumpolar. Rather than rising in the east and eventually setting in the west like many familiar constellations, it circles the north celestial pole — a position currently held by Polaris, the North Star. From sufficiently northerly latitudes, its main stars never disappear below the horizon.

It has been revealed that this gives us a simple observing experiment. Find Cassiopeia in the early evening and remember its orientation relative to the horizon. Go back several hours later and look again. The constellation has moved around Polaris, and its shape has changed. The stars haven't changed their arrangement — Earth has simply rotated from west to east. We all know this logically, but watching the familiar pattern of Cassiopeia's stars apparently tip over during a single night makes Earth's rotation a lot less abstract.

Sources indicate that I'm going to observe Cassiopeia twice on the same evening this week, which is about as complicated as the experiment needs to get. The first time will be shortly after darkness falls. I'll find the W, note which way it seems to be pointing and use something fixed — a rooftop, tree or chimney — to give myself a rough reference for its position. I'll return to my backyard before bed, and see where the pattern has shifted. Cassiopeia's main stars are bright enough to survive urban and suburban light pollution, so you don't need a particularly dark sky or a telescope.

While I'm gazing at Cassiopeia, I'll try to see the stars as they really are, and not just how they appear to us. Check out the distances of its stars from the sun:.

Only Caph and Ruchbah are within 100 light-years — the sun's local interstellar neighborhood. Does that destroy the very concept of Cassiopeia as a group of related stars? Cassiopeia, like all constellations, is a mirage, with a capital M.

There's another reason I love Cassiopeia. Proxima Centauri, the closest star to our sun, lies just 4.24 light-years away. Travel there and look back towards our solar system, and our sun would appear as an extra star in Cassiopeia — effectively giving the constellation a sixth bright point. From a certain perspective, we are all Cassiopeians.

The last few evenings of November bring back darker early-night skies as the moon wanes from full earlier in the week and rises progressively later. It will rise in the middle of the night as it reaches its last-quarter phase on Dec. 1. It's an ideal time to sweep a pair of binoculars across the rich star fields around Cassiopeia and Perseus. On the boundary between the two constellations is the Double Cluster (NGC 869 and NGC 884), one of the finest binocular sights in the entire northern sky. These two dense concentrations of young stars sit side by side against the richer background of the Milky Way. Under a dark sky, you can see it with the naked eye. M52, NGC 457 (the Owl Cluster) and NGC 663 are other clusters also worth seeking out in Cassiopeia.

Get outside about 45 minutes before sunrise on Monday, Nov. 30, and look high in the southern sky for a fitting month-ending finale. A 61%-lit waning gibbous moon will appear alongside brilliant Jupiter, reddish Mars and Regulus, the brightest star in Leo. Together, the four objects will trace a striking crescent spanning just over five degrees of sky — roughly the width of three fingers held at arm's length. It's a much tighter version of a similar arrangement visible on Nov. 2, with Jupiter by far the brightest point and the contrasting colors of Mars and blue-white Regulus adding to the spectacle. No equipment will be needed, though binoculars will help you get a close-up of this rather unusual conjunction.

He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

The H3 Podcast has come to an end.

On Monday, Hila Klein announced on the show's Instagram account that she had "made the difficult decision to stop working on the fresh show." She had been developing a crew-led version of the podcast since her estranged husband and co-host, Ethan Klein, was pushed out of it last month after she revealed his affair.

According to recent reports, "I've come to realize that I can't continue down this path while also giving myself the space I need to heal and protect my mental health," she wrote. "Right now, I need to focus on myself, my healing, and what's best for me and my kids.".

The announcement closes out a month-long fallout that began on Oct. 22. That day, Ethan noted on Instagram Stories that the podcast was going on "indefinite hiatus." Hours later, Hila posted that he had been having an affair for more than six months. As Mashable previously reported, the crew said in a statement that they would not keep working with Ethan "involved or profiting in any way." Ethan said he was working to give up his financial stakes in the podcast and in the couple's businesses, including the clothing brand Teddy Fresh.

Industry observers note that complex reported that Hila filed for divorce on Nov. 2, listing their separation date as Oct. 13. The couple married in 2012 and share three children.

Since the news broke, multiple crew members have spoken out. On the show's Discord, longtime producer GirlWithAMicrophone (GWAM) remarked she would not work on a project with the rest of the crew. She thanked Hila for giving them "a shot during all this turmoil.".

Producer AB Ayad suggested on X that the obstacles were bigger than any one person. "There are certain people involved that were never gonna allow us to continue doing the show together," he wrote, adding, "I give Hila a lot of credit that she was able to do what she even did.".

Sources indicate that beyond the H3 Podcast, Ethan co-hosted Frenemies with Trisha Paytas, which became one of YouTube's most talked-about highlights before it ended acrimoniously in 2021. He later started the political show Leftovers with Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, which ended in 2023 over disagreements about Israel and the war in Gaza.

Since the announcement of the show ending, Ethan has broken his weeks-long silence. On Tuesday, in a series of Instagram Stories, he called the affair "the ultimate betrayal" to his wife and to the show's audience. He also remarked that "the show ending is entirely my fault.".

Industry observers note that however, he didn't rule out a comeback. "I will probably be back, but when and how, I can't tell you," he wrote, hinting at a solo show or a new project.

#163412. Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret

Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1398 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Carbon is essential to every living thing on Earth, from microscopic organisms to humans.
  • It has been revealed that A new study of volcanic rocks from Hawaii offers a surprising possible answer.
  • Recent findings suggest that the discovery centers on unusual carbon dioxide signatures preserved in volcanic rocks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Carbon is essential to every living thing on Earth, from microscopic organisms to humans. Yet scientists are still working to answer a fundamental question about our planet's history: Where did all this carbon originally come from?

It has been revealed that A new study of volcanic rocks from Hawaii offers a surprising possible answer. Researchers have uncovered chemical evidence suggesting that much of Earth's carbon may have arrived aboard ancient meteorites during a particular stage of the planet's formation. Even more remarkably, the findings suggest that some of this carbon became trapped deep inside Earth's core before eventually making its way back to the surface.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery centers on unusual carbon dioxide signatures preserved in volcanic rocks. Researchers believe these chemical fingerprints may reveal carbon that originated in Earth's core and traveled upward through the planet's interior.

"We think that we found evidence of carbon from Earth's core leaking into the core-mantle boundaries and traveling all the way to the surface," claims lead author Yves Moussallam, an associate professor in Columbia University's Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences at Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory.

The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

How Carbon Could Escape From Earth's Core.

To understand how carbon might travel from Earth's deepest interior to its surface, it helps to look at the planet's internal structure.

Beneath Earth's thin outer crust lies the mantle, a vast region of mostly solid rock extending approximately 1,800 miles downward. Below that is the outer core, a roughly 1,400-mile-thick layer of molten metal surrounding the extremely hot, dense, solid metallic inner core.

Scientists believe that most of Earth's carbon is stored in its core. However, directly examining this material is far beyond the reach of current technology, and researchers may never be able to obtain samples from such extreme depths.

Fortunately, Earth's volcanic activity offers another way to investigate what lies below.

Recent studies suggest that certain elements can escape from the outer core and enter the overlying mantle. From there, they may be transported toward the surface by enormous rising columns of hot rock known as mantle plumes.

These plumes begin near the boundary between the core and mantle. As they ascend, some of the rock partially melts, producing magma that can eventually erupt through volcanoes.

When that magma cools, crystals begin to grow. Occasionally, these crystals trap tiny droplets of molten material before dissolved gases have a chance to escape. The trapped droplets, known as undegassed melt inclusions, preserve valuable chemical information about the original magma.

"These melts are fossils of the magma," Moussallam notes.

Because magma contains dissolved gases, including carbon dioxide, these microscopic pockets provide scientists with a rare opportunity to study carbon that may have traveled upward from Earth's core.

Hawaiian Volcanoes Reveal an Unusual Carbon Signature.

Recent findings suggest that hawaii is particularly well suited for this kind of investigation. Previous research has established that its volcanoes receive magma associated with a deep mantle plume, potentially providing access to material originating near the boundary with Earth's core.

Sources indicate that moussallam and his colleagues examined volcanic rocks from eruptions at Kīlauea and the Tantalus Rift. Using a recently developed analytical technique, they measured carbon isotopes preserved inside undegassed melt inclusions.

Carbon isotopes are different forms of the same element that have slightly different masses. By comparing their relative abundance, scientists can identify chemical signatures that offer clues about where carbon came from and what processes it experienced.

Recent findings suggest that the Tantalus Rift samples are thought to represent magma originating near the outer margins of the mantle plume. Earlier research established that typical mantle carbon has an isotopic signature between approximately -5 and -7 per mil, a measurement expressing small differences in isotope ratios. The researchers found that the Tantalus Rift samples closely matched this expected range.

The Kīlauea samples, however, told a very different story.

Magma beneath Kīlauea is believed to originate closer to the center of the mantle plume, where material may rise from near the core-mantle boundary. In these samples, the scientists detected carbon with a much heavier isotopic signature of approximately -1 per mil.

This unusual value has rarely been observed before and differs substantially from the signature normally associated with Earth's mantle.

"This signature is very, very distinct from the normal mantle," indicates Moussallam. "This means it must have been contaminated by another carbon source and that source is probably carbon from the core.".

Industry observers note that although the team considers Earth's core the most likely source, Moussallam emphasizes that the evidence is not yet definitive. Additional measurements will be necessary to establish whether the carbon truly originated there.

Ancient Meteorites May Explain Where Earth's Carbon Came From.

The unusual carbon signature also provided researchers with a possible clue about events that occurred more than 4.5 billion years ago, when Earth was still forming.

According to Moussallam, the isotopic composition of carbon in Earth's core should preserve "the signature of the building blocks of Earth when it was created.".

To investigate that possibility, the team compared the distinctive Kīlauea measurements with carbon signatures found in ancient meteorites. They discovered similarities to a group of meteorites called carbonaceous chondrites.

Chondrites are among the oldest known materials in our solar system, dating back more than 4.5 billion years. They preserve clues about the primitive material from which planets formed.

Sources indicate that "All of Earth is made of chondrites," Moussallam explains. "They're the building blocks of all the terrestrial planets.".

Sources indicate that scientists generally distinguish between two broad categories of chondrites. Noncarbonaceous chondrites formed in the inner solar system, while carbonaceous chondrites, which contain more carbon, originated in the outer regions of the solar system.

Exactly how much each type contributed to Earth's formation has remained a subject of scientific debate.

The new findings support the possibility that carbonaceous chondrites made an especially vital contribution during the later stages of Earth's development.

According to the researchers' proposed explanation, these carbon-rich meteorites struck the growing planet at a time when it had become better able to retain carbon delivered by incoming material. Some of that carbon may have accumulated deep within Earth, eventually becoming part of the planet's enormous internal carbon reservoir.

Over billions of years, carbon from that reservoir could have migrated upward through mantle plumes and emerged in volcanic eruptions.

If the interpretation is correct, some of the carbon essential to life today may have arrived from the outer solar system aboard meteorites during Earth's earliest history.

A Remarkable Journey From Space to Life on Earth.

Despite the intriguing evidence, crucial questions remain unanswered. The researchers have not conclusively demonstrated that the unusual carbon came from Earth's core or established precisely how much of the planet's carbon was delivered by carbonaceous meteorites.

"We don't really know. We need more measurements," cautions Moussallam.

Nevertheless, the findings offer a fascinating possible connection between the formation of the solar system, the inaccessible depths of our planet, and the carbon that makes life possible.

It has been revealed that they also raise the possibility that some of the carbon found in living organisms today has followed an extraordinary path. After arriving on Earth billions of years ago, it may have become incorporated into the planet's metallic core, moved slowly upward through the mantle, and eventually returned to the surface through volcanic eruptions.

According to recent reports, "It's fun to think about. We're made of carbon, right? To think that some of this carbon might at some point have been linked to iron in the planet's core, made it all the way to the surface from out of a volcano, and is now part of the biosphere, is very interesting.".

Recent findings suggest that the study was coauthored by Guillaume Georgeais, HyunJoo Lee, and Bridgett Holman of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory; Damanveer S. Grewal of Yale University; Estelle F. Rose-Koga of Institut des Sciences de la Terre d'Orléans; Allan Lerner of the US Geological Survey; Paul J. Wallace of the University of Oregon; and Natália Gauer.

Materials provided by Columbia Climate School. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The starting gun of the Oscar season starts Monday, and by next Sunday, it will have a shape that many of us will be able to see clearly.

In a recent development, for months, the Oscar race has run on festival premieres, studio screenings and ever more elaborate predictions, mine included. This week, the people with ballots finally speak.

It has been revealed that the Gothams, the Newly introduced York Film Critics Circle, the National Board of Review, the American Film Institute and LAFCA each answer to a different electorate and each has its own complicated history with the Academy. None of them pick the Oscars, but they all shape the conversation that follows.

In a recent development, the question isn’t only who wins. It’s who wins where, and what each victory indicates about the corner of the electorate that handed it out.

Here’s what’s on the calendar this week.

Sources indicate that monday, Nov. 30: Gotham AwardsTuesday, Dec. 1: New York Film Critics Circle AwardsWednesday, Dec. 2: Film Independent Spirit Awards nominationsWednesday, Dec. 2: National Board of Review AwardsThursday, Dec. 3: AFI Awards honorees announcedFriday, Dec. 4: Critics Choice Awards nominationsFriday, Dec. 4: BAFTA Round One voting opensFriday, Dec. 4: Golden Globes nomination voting endsSunday, Dec. 6: British Independent Film AwardsSunday, Dec. 6: Los Angeles Film Critics Association Awards announcement.

Here’s how we see the opening week unfolding, with some commentary for each.

Recent findings suggest that the Gothams have long been a launching pad for independent cinema, a place for films that might otherwise get flattened by the studio machine. In 2023, the organization scrapped its $35 million budget ceiling and opened more categories to international titles. The result is a more eclectic ballot, one that puts established auteurs and first-time filmmakers side by side. This year, that means 42 features and 25 performances across 11 categories.

Sources indicate that that makes the Gothams a natural first stop for “The Invite,” which we expect to win best feature. Wilde’s ensemble piece, starring Seth Rogen, Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton, has the kind of dinner-party-argument appeal that plays well with this voting body. “Josephine” is my alternate and could follow some jaw-dropping selections like “A Different Man” two years ago. The drama took both the U.S. Grand Jury Prize and the Audience Award at Sundance in January, and the Gothams have never lost their appetite for championing a discovery.

Industry observers note that notably, a different set of industry professionals, five jury members each, for each category, pick the Gotham winners, while Gotham members vote on the audience award. A film can win a jury on artistic grounds while another finds its people in the wider membership.

Best Feature: “The Invite” (A24)Alternate: “Josephine” (Sumerian Pictures).

Director: Ryusuke Hamaguchi, “All of a Sudden” (Neon)Alternate: Mike Leigh, “Tender Loving Care” (Bleecker Street).

Lead Performance: Andrew Scott, “Elsinore” (Focus Features)Alternate: John Malkovich, “Wild Horse Nine” (Searchlight Pictures).

Supporting Performance: Tao Okamoto, “All of a Sudden” (Neon)Alternate: Kate O’Flynn, “Tender Loving Care” (Bleecker Street).

Breakthrough Performer: Guitarricadelafuente, “La Bola Negra” (Netflix)Alternate: Adia, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” (Amazon MGM Studios).

Audience Award: “You Can See Everything” (A24)Alternate: “La Bola Negra” (Netflix).

Breakthrough Director: Jordan Firstman, “Club Kid” (A24)Alternate: Aleshea Harris, “Is God Is” (Amazon MGM Studios).

Original Screenplay: “Tender Loving Care” (Bleecker Street) — Mike LeighAlternate: “Wild Horse Nine” (Searchlight Pictures) — Martin McDonagh.

Adapted Screenplay: “The Invite” (A24) — Rashida Jones and Will McCormackAlternate: “Minotaur” (Mubi) — Simon Lyashenko and Andrey Zvyagintsev.

Documentary Feature: “Naza” (The Guardian, MK2 and Neon)Alternate: “You Can See Everything” (A24).

International Feature: “Possible Love” (Netflix)Alternate: “Blue Heron” (Janus Films).

Founded in 1935, the New York Film Critics Circle is the country’s oldest film critics organization and one of the most influential early stops on the calendar. Its history is full of choices that challenged the Academy’s conventional wisdom. Many of them went on to become landmarks, even when they diverged from the eventual Oscar winner.

This year, we’re predicting “You Can See Everything” to show its strength by winning the top prize for best film, with “The Odyssey” as the alternate. Fielder and Oppenheim’s 174-minute portrait of Elizabeth Holmes premiered as Telluride’s secret screening and has drawn the kind of critical fervor usually reserved for narrative features. A best film win from New York wouldn’t automatically make it an Oscar best picture contender, but it would move the film into a different tier of consideration. “The Odyssey” is the more traditional choice: a major filmmaker, a sweeping production and a likely force in the technical categories.

In directing, Wilde could pull off a deserved citation ahead of Nolan, who has never won from the group before.

Recent findings suggest that andrew Scott is my choice for actor, with Robert Pattinson’s combined work in “Primetime” and “The Drama” as the alternate. Julianne Moore could win actress for “The Debut,” with Sandra Hüller for “Rose” as a real threat. In supporting actor, Guitarricadelafuente could keep building momentum for “La Bola Negra,” with a surprise citation for someone like John Cho of “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” (much like Regina Hall or Tiffany Haddish surprised in their respective years). Kate O’Flynn (“Tender Loving Care”) and Amanda Seyfried (“You Can See Everything”) could be in a battle for supporting actress, or someone else completely.

The screenplay prize could go to Jordan Firstman for “Club Kid,” with Cristian Mungiu’s “Fjord” as the alternate. “Tangles” is my animated film pick over Laika’s “Wildwood,” an interesting split between independent animation and a more established studio shop.

Best Film: “You Can See Everything” (A24)Alternate: “The Odyssey” (Universal Pictures).

Director: Olivia Wilde, “The Invite” (A24)Alternate: Christopher Nolan, “The Odyssey” (Universal Pictures).

Actor: Andrew Scott, “Elsinore” (Focus Features)Alternate: Robert Pattinson, “Primetime” and “The Drama” (A24).

The American Film Institute’s annual selections live in a different space from the critics’ prizes. There are no individual performances and no craft citations, just 10 films the institute considers culturally and artistically representative of the year. The Top 10 is restricted to American productions. Works that fall outside its criteria can receive an AFI Special Award, as Kenneth Branagh’s “Belfast” and Questlove’s documentary “Summer of Soul” did in 2021 and Jafar Panahi’s “It Was Just an Accident” did last year.

Sources indicate that that makes the AFI list a measure of which films have entered the industry’s broader conversation. There’s no single winner, and because the list is alphabetical, it isn’t a ranking.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Twitter’s traditional bird icon was booted and replaced with an image of a Shiba Inu, an apparent nod to dogecoin, the joke cryptocurrency that CEO Elon Musk is being sued over.

Musk addressed the change Monday afternoon, tweeting, “as promised” above an image of a year-old conversation in which another user suggested that Musk “just buy Twitter” and “change the bird logo to a doge.”.

Elon Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out one account.

The doge logo appeared on the site two days after Musk asked a judge to throw out a $258 billion racketeering lawsuit accusing him of running a pyramid scheme to support the dogecoin, according to Reuters.

Lawyers for Musk and Tesla called the lawsuit by dogecoin investors a “fanciful work of fiction” over Musk’s “innocuous and often silly tweets.”.

Industry observers note that it wasn’t clear whether the logo change was permanent. Musk has been known to use Twitter to troll both his fans and his critics.

Industry observers note that the price of dogecoin, which is typically volatile, was up more than 20% over the past 24 hours, to about 9 cents. It was trading just under 8 cents Monday morning.

Dogecoin was created December 6, 2013, by a pair of software engineers — as a joke. The name is a nod to the “doge” meme that became popular a decade ago. Its Shiba Inu mascot mimicks that meme: a dog surrounded by a bunch of Comic Sans text in broken English.

Recent findings suggest that the Richat Structure, also known as the “Eye of the Sahara,” is seen from the International Space Station as it orbited above on Nov. 14, 2026. It is an eroded geological dome about 100 million years old created by igneous activity and uplift in the nation of Mauritania. In this type of geologic structure, rocks exposed in the center of the “bullseye” are older than rocks forming the outer rings. This structure measures 45 kilometers (28 miles) across and is made up of igneous and sedimentary rocks.

Image credit: NASA/Luke Delaney.

#163408. Fresh nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1674 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Fresh nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1674 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that researchers at the University of Sydney have created experimental nose drops that significantly improved learning and memory in older mice, bringing their performance back to levels seen in younger animals.
  • The discovery, led by Professor Greg Neely at the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre, could open a new path toward treating conditions that affect the brain.
  • "If we can proceed quickly to clinical trials in humans, this approach could represent a world-first non-invasive delivery system to treat Alzheimer's that bypasses the blood-brain barrier," Professor Neely mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that researchers at the University of Sydney have created experimental nose drops that significantly improved learning and memory in older mice, bringing their performance back to levels seen in younger animals. The treatment also prevented severe memory decline in mice genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer's-like disease. Remarkably, the approach relies on mRNA technology similar to that used in COVID-19 vaccines.

The discovery, led by Professor Greg Neely at the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre, could open a new path toward treating conditions that affect the brain. Potential applications extend beyond Alzheimer's disease to other neurodegenerative disorders, stroke, traumatic brain injury, and rare genetic and developmental conditions.

"If we can proceed quickly to clinical trials in humans, this approach could represent a world-first non-invasive delivery system to treat Alzheimer's that bypasses the blood-brain barrier," Professor Neely mentioned.

The idea behind the research has an unusual origin. The team drew inspiration from Daniel Keyes' science fiction story Flowers for Algernon, which explores the limits of human intelligence through experiments designed to increase intelligence in laboratory mice and people.

How mRNA Nose Drops Restore Youthful Memory.

The treatment works by delivering messenger RNA (mRNA), a type of genetic instruction that tells cells how to produce specific proteins. These instructions are enclosed in tiny fat-based particles called lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), which protect the mRNA and help it enter cells.

According to recent reports, once delivered through the nose, the mRNA instructs cells to manufacture therapeutic proteins capable of reaching the brain. In effect, the nasal tissue becomes a small drug-producing factory, creating substances that can support brain function.

"In aged mice, we saw learning and memory significantly increased, returning animal cognition to its youthful prime," Professor Neely said.

"What's exciting is that this was achieved with a simple non-invasive nasal delivery system that builds on the same underlying mRNA-LNP technology platform many people became familiar with during the COVID-19 pandemic.".

It has been revealed that the study, published in Advanced Science, used mRNA to stimulate production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). This naturally occurring protein helps neurons survive, form connections, and adapt as the brain learns and stores memories. Levels of BDNF tend to decline with aging and are also associated with Alzheimer's disease.

In a recent development, the results were striking. Older mice that received the nose drops performed about as well as young mice in standardized tests of working memory, spatial memory, and object recognition. These tests measure abilities such as remembering recently encountered information, navigating surroundings, and recognizing familiar objects. Untreated older animals showed the expected age-related deterioration in cognitive performance.

Nose Drops Prevent Alzheimer's-Like Memory Decline in Mice.

To investigate whether the treatment might also protect against Alzheimer's disease, researchers turned to a widely used laboratory model known as 5XFAD mice. These animals carry genetic mutations that cause them to develop Alzheimer's-like brain changes and memory problems unusually early in life.

In this model, signs of Alzheimer's-related brain pathology can typically be detected by two months of age, with measurable cognitive decline appearing around four months.

It has been revealed that the researchers began administering the BDNF-producing mRNA nose drops when the mice were two months old, around the time the disease-related changes first appeared. Treatment continued twice a week.

By four months of age, the treated mice revealed no further cognitive decline, unlike the severe deterioration normally seen in this model. The findings suggest that supporting brain cells early in the disease process may help preserve cognitive abilities.

One of the most intriguing results was what the treatment did not do. Although memory and learning were protected, the researchers found no reduction in amyloid plaques, the abnormal protein deposits that accumulate in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease.

Sources indicate that that distinction could be important because many existing Alzheimer's treatments aim to remove amyloid. The newly introduced approach instead appears to help neurons remain healthy and functional despite the presence of these deposits. If the same effect can eventually be demonstrated in people, the two treatment strategies might be used together.

"Current Alzheimer's treatments largely focus on clearing these amyloid plaques," Professor Neely mentioned. "However, just under a third of Alzheimer's patients have serious plaques but do not suffer from dementia, and these patients show naturally higher BDNF levels, suggesting if we raise BDNF, it's possible to live with Alzheimer's disease pathology.".

"Our approach seems to work not by clearing plaques but by supporting the health, survival and connectivity of neurons themselves. It raises the possibility these therapies could eventually work alongside each other.".

Bypassing the Blood-Brain Barrier Through the Nose.

According to recent reports, getting medicines into the brain is one of the biggest obstacles in developing treatments for neurological diseases. The blood-brain barrier acts as a protective filter, preventing many potentially harmful substances in the bloodstream from entering delicate brain tissue. Unfortunately, it also blocks numerous drugs that scientists would like to use to treat brain disorders.

Industry observers note that the nose offers a possible alternative route. Connections between the nasal cavity and the central nervous system may allow certain therapeutic substances to reach the brain without requiring surgery or injections directly into the brain or spinal cord.

"This is a very exciting proof of concept for a method to deliver mRNA-encoded cargo to the nervous system directly through the nose," Professor Neely said.

The team adapted mRNA technology built on the same clinically validated BioNTech platform used for COVID-19 vaccination. Instead of delivering instructions that prompt an immune response, the modified system provides instructions for producing proteins intended to benefit the brain.

Recent findings suggest that first author Dr. Maria Bergamasco, from the University of Sydney's School of Life and Environmental Sciences, explained that the findings illustrate how mRNA technology could be used for purposes far beyond preventing infectious diseases.

Recent findings suggest that "The success of mRNA vaccines showed these systems can safely deliver genetic instructions to cells," Dr. Bergamasco said.

"We wanted to see whether we could adapt that technology to deliver beneficial proteins to the brain in a completely non-invasive way.".

Treatment Stimulates Latest Brain Cell Growth.

The researchers also detected increased neurogenesis, the process through which upcoming neurons are formed, in the hippocampus. This part of the brain plays an essential role in learning and memory and is particularly vulnerable to damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.

According to recent reports, the increase in upcoming neurons provides another possible explanation for the improvements in cognitive performance. By promoting the health and adaptability of brain cells, BDNF may help maintain the neural networks needed for learning and remembering information.

According to recent reports, the nose drops also appeared to be well tolerated. Researchers reported no major side effects in the mice during the study, although further testing will be needed to establish long-term safety.

Could mRNA Nose Drops Work in Humans?

Recent findings suggest that despite the encouraging results, Professor Neely emphasized that the treatment remains experimental. So far, its effectiveness has been demonstrated only in mice, and additional animal safety studies are required before clinical testing can begin.

In a recent development, "Before we can trial this therapy in patients, we need to perform a series of safety studies in animals," he said. "It is a very promising pathway, but human noses are different from mouse noses, so we will need to test our drugs in humans before we know whether it will work.".

That anatomical difference is a significant consideration. A delivery method that successfully transports therapeutic substances from the nasal cavity to the brain in mice may not work in exactly the same way in humans.

According to recent reports, nevertheless, the researchers believe the potential applications could be substantial. Beyond protecting against Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline, the technology might eventually help support memory and other mental abilities during normal aging.

"We believe our latest drug, if it works in humans, can promote general cognitive health as people age, should help treat a variety of neurodegenerative diseases, and may even increase cognitive abilities in healthy young people," Professor Neely mentioned.

In a recent development, the next steps involve refining the nasal delivery technology and conducting further studies to determine its safety and effectiveness over longer periods. The team hopes to advance toward human clinical trials as swiftly as the required testing allows.

"Based on previous clinical trials, we know the components used in this study to be safe in humans," Professor Neely stated. "We hope we can move rapidly through the requisite safety studies and trial this treatment in humans in the next two years.".

Although the individual components have previously been used in humans, the complete nasal treatment still requires its own safety evaluation. Whether it can deliver similar memory benefits in people remains an open question.

Research Funding and Disclosures.

The project brought together researchers from the Dr. John and Anne Chong Lab for Functional Genomics in the School of Life and Environmental Sciences, the Charles Perkins Centre, and the University of Sydney's Faculty of Medicine and Health.

It has been revealed that greg Neely and Maria Bergamasco are listed as inventors on a provisional patent application associated with the research. The other authors reported no competing interests.

It has been revealed that financial support came from the National Health and Medical Research Council, the NSW Ministry of Health, and an ongoing philanthropic contribution from Dr. John and Anne Chong supporting the Neely Lab's research. The authors also acknowledged the Sydney Imaging Facility for its assistance.

All animal experiments were approved by the University of Sydney Animal Ethics Committee and conducted in accordance with the Australian Code of Practise for the Care and Use of Animals for Scientific Purposes.

Materials provided by University of Sydney. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tanker carrying up to 7,000 metric tonnes (7,716 short tons) of diesel capzized off the Spanish island of Ibiza, local authorities noted on Thursday.

The ship's 17 crew members were rescued but one later died in hospital and another six suffered from hypothermia when the Maltese-flagged Med Emre capsized overnight, the government of Spain's Balearic Islands, remarked in a statement.

According to emergency services, the five further crew members were taken to Valencia and the remainig five were in good condition on a ‌rescue ​vessel.

The chemical tanker was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona when it capsized about 30 nautical miles (56 kilometers) off Ibiza's northwestern coast.

It has been revealed that according to Spanish authorities, the Med Emre was drifting upside down northwest of Ibiza after capsizing. Initially, they remarked the ship had sunk to the seabed in 1,000 metres of water, but later corrected this statement.

The nationalities of the crew or the cause of the incident was not immediately clear.

In a recent development, the Transport Ministry remarked the maritime rescue vessel Guardamar Talia had reported no wreckage, floating debris or signs of pollution at the site as of Thursday morning. It added that another rescue ship was heading to the area to continue monitoring the situation.

Spain's maritime rescue service deployed an aircraft and the Clara Campoamor, a vessel equipped to respond to oil spills, to inspect the area.

Spain's merchant marine authority ​has activated the national maritime pollution contingency initiative at level 2, the second-highest.

The Balearic regional government stated it was assessing the incident and its potential impact, including the risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures.

The waters surrounding Ibiza are a critical zone for biodiversity as they host sea turtles, dolphins and the ‌Balearic shearwater, one of Europe's most threatened seabirds.

The area also hosts vast Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows, which are essential for maintaining marine biodiversity.

Emilio Rodriguez Diaz, a maritime security expert at the University of Cadiz, told Cadena SER radio that the area affected was "particularly vulnerable.".

But he stated the Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkey in 2019, with a double hull to ensure that, "in the event of a leak (or) a collision, that intermediate part between the cargo hold and the outer layer would flood.".

"It's a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment," he said.

Spain's worst maritime environmental disaster happened in 2022, when the tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region. It spilled tens of thousands of heavy fuel oil and polluted beaches across Spain and France.

Former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra: "It's going to be tough.".

He should know. The 78-year-old businessman and U.S. Navy veteran helped with his own succession planning and recommended to GM's board in 2013 that Barra replace him as CEO. She has held the top job since Jan. 15, 2014.

Akerson mentioned Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence, vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles.

In a recent development, "It's going to be very, very dynamic," Akerson told CNBC during a phone interview. "It's going to be a significant change.".

Akerson declined to discuss potential internal candidates such as GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson, CFO Paul Jacobson or President Mark Reuss, but he noted the eventual successor needs to be dynamic and, if from the outside, "adaptable.".

In a recent development, his comments to CNBC follow a Wall Street Journal report on Tuesday that GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside candidates to succeed Barra, in addition to internal prospects. GM declined to comment on the report or Barra's succession.

Akerson, who came to GM as an outsider from The Carlyle Group in 2010, mentioned selecting an outside candidate might be risky if there are already executives within the organization who have similar leadership and technical expertise.

"Is there anybody in the organization that has that background that you know better day to day over a period of time? You may be taking a risk by bringing in an outsider," he said.

The prospect of an outsider leading GM would be unusual in the auto industry, where major automakers have generally promoted internal CEO candidates, apart from periods of exceptional disruption such as the Great Recession.

Stellantis, BMW, Toyota Motor, Nissan Motor and Hyundai Motor have all appointed internal executives to their CEO positions in recent years.

Barra has said several times that her successor and her longevity in the role would be determined by the board.

A notable influence is likely Hewlett Packard veteran Patricia Russo, GM's longest-serving board member who has been on the board since 2009 and leads its CEO succession planning as independent lead director.

GM's CEO succession planning is done "at least annually," according to the tech giant's yearly proxy filing. That process includes Barra providing the board "with recommendations for, and evaluations of, potential CEO successors and discusses developmental plans for these successors," according to the filing.

That is followed by board members engaging "with CEO candidates and senior management talent at Board and committee meetings and other forums to enable directors to personally assess candidates.".

When Akerson was preparing to retire, Barra was among a pool of four candidates — two longtime GM employees and two relative newcomers — who were finalists for CEO in 2013, he remarked.

Akerson remarked he put the finalists through an extended evaluation, asking how they viewed GM's strengths and weaknesses, how they would organize the firm, and their willingness to work together, potentially with other CEO candidates who didn't get the job.

Akerson said the final decision to appoint Barra was done at a day-and-a-half-long board meeting in Washington. The candidate field was narrowed to Barra and former GM executive Dan Ammann, an ex-Wall Street banker who was GM's CFO before leaving the automaker's Cruise unit, reportedly over a disagreement in strategy with Barra, in 2021.

"Mary's very deserving of all the accolades she's received," Akerson stated. "She's done a terrific job.".

Barra has been leading the automaker for nearly 13 years, which makes her the longest-serving CEO of the automaker since Alfred Sloan retired after a 23-year career as CEO in 1946.

Recent findings suggest that akerson mentioned he believes that, like he did, Barra will have major influence in picking her successor. He described that dynamic as integral to continuing her legacy leading the automaker.

Industry observers note that "This is crucial. I think if she doesn't pick the right person, in four or five years from now and things are back in the trough, that will tarnish her history. But I think she'll pick the right one," he mentioned.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, NBC has pulled an ad from a Middle East advocacy organization that calls for the end of U.S. military aid to Israel. The network will review its ad approval procedures after criticism from the Simon Wiesenthal Center and other organizations.

The spot, purchased by the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, pushes for the end of U.S. military aid to Israel amid the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. The spot titled “Every Three Seconds” ran Nov. 25 on NBC in primetime during the network’s “Saturday Night Live” Thanksgiving special. Related Stories Brad Pitt Claims 'Ocean's 14' Not Shooting Until 'Late' 2027 Sheryl Lee Ralph-Produced ‘Until Everyone Is Seen’ Sets World AIDS Day Premiere on Hulu (EXCLUSIVE).

The ad makes a jarring juxtaposition between the suffering in Gaza and scenes of a typical American preteen girl doing chores and odd jobs to save money for a bicycle amid tough economic times. Just as the American girl brings her jar full of money into a bike shop, the spot cuts to a scene of a girl standing in a pile of rubble in Gaza. As the camera pans back, the girl is revealed to be leaning on a crutch, having lost one of her lower legs. The spot tells viewers that “Every three seconds” the U.S. sends about $400 million in military aid to Israel under a long-term deal set to expire in 2028.

In a recent development, NBC’s top brass were unaware of the spot before it aired. As a result, there will be a review of the network’s ad approval processes, according to a person familiar with the situation.

Industry observers note that jim Berk, CEO of the Wiesenthal Center, issued a lengthy statement on Thursday questioning NBC’s decision to air the ad during an “SNL” entertainment special in primetime. He pointed to the ad’s potential to fuel hostility against Israel and Jews.

It has been revealed that “The advertisement’s imagery, an American child’s hardship set against the anguish of a child in Gaza, offers viewers a seductive but unsubstantiated narrative: that the struggles of American families are somehow bound up with U.S. support for Israel,” Berk stated. “In collapsing a complex foreign policy into a single, emotionally charged image, it erases the deeper realities, including the imperative to protect Israeli lives and the very existence of the country itself. By manipulating emotion and stripping it of context, this ad seeks to become a catalyst for hostility. … Without scrutiny, insinuations and half-truths are allowed to seep into the consciousness of millions, unchallenged and unchecked. Turning children’s suffering into a prop for political theater is an unacceptable manipulation.”.

Industry observers note that the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project did not immediately respond to a request for comment on NBC’s decision. It’s unclear how many more times the spot had been scheduled to run on NBCUniversal platforms. According to the organization’s website, IMEU “was founded in 2005 by a group of concerned Americans who want to foster an increased understanding among Americans about Palestine and the Palestinians.”.

Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1044 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at the University of Queensland have demonstrated an unusual fresh way to communicate, using gravity to send a message directly through a brick wall.
  • Recent findings suggest that the experiment took place inside UQ's Parnell Building.
  • Recent findings suggest that on the other side of a brick wall, a device called a gravimeter was positioned in a nearby bathroom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at the University of Queensland have demonstrated an unusual fresh way to communicate, using gravity to send a message directly through a brick wall. Instead of relying on radio waves or other electromagnetic signals, the team used an old elevator, a massive counterweight, and an extremely sensitive instrument capable of detecting tiny changes in gravitational pull.

Recent findings suggest that the experiment took place inside UQ's Parnell Building. Physicists repeatedly moved an elevator between two floors, shifting its 1.8-metric-ton counterweight between two positions. Each position represented a binary digit, either 0 or 1, allowing the researchers to encode information through the movement of the heavy mass.

Recent findings suggest that on the other side of a brick wall, a device called a gravimeter was positioned in a nearby bathroom. The instrument measured the extremely small changes in gravity produced by the moving counterweight. By decoding those measurements, the team successfully recovered a one-word message: 'Gravity'.

Why Gravity Could Succeed Where Wi-Fi Fails.

The experiment highlights a potentially crucial advantage of using gravity for communication. Unlike conventional wireless signals, which can be weakened or blocked by physical obstacles, gravitational fields pass through ordinary materials without being screened out.

Sources indicate that dr. Charles Woffinden from UQ's School of Mathematics and Physics explained why this property makes gravity an intriguing alternative to existing communication technologies.

"Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path," Dr. Woffinden remarked.

"Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.

"While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block.".

Sources indicate that the basic principle is surprisingly simple. Any object with mass produces a gravitational field, and moving that object changes the field around it. Although these changes are generally far too small for people to notice, sufficiently sensitive instruments can detect them. By controlling how a large mass moves, researchers can create a sequence of gravitational changes that represents digital information.

From Weighing Trucks to Sending Messages.

The idea for the experiment emerged from a separate research effort that had little to do with communication.

According to recent reports, dr. Andrew Groszek noted the team had originally been developing a contactless weighbridge, a system designed to measure the weight of vehicles without requiring them to drive onto a conventional scale.

"We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull," Dr. Groszek mentioned.

"Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realized the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information.".

Recent findings suggest that that realization opened the door to a different application. If a sensitive detector could measure the gravitational influence of a large vehicle, it could also detect deliberately controlled changes in the position of a heavy object. Those changes could then be used to represent the ones and zeros that form the foundation of digital communication.

Despite its success, the demonstration revealed a major obstacle to practical gravity-based communication: transmitting information this way is extraordinarily slow.

Professor Andrew White explained that the elevator's age and limited speed placed a severe restriction on how rapidly the researchers could send their message.

"Our lift was snail-paced - it's from the 1950s - so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word," Professor White said.

According to recent reports, for comparison, a bit is the smallest unit of digital information, representing either a 0 or a 1. Modern communication systems transmit enormous numbers of bits every second. The gravity experiment, by contrast, required an entire minute to communicate just one bit.

According to White, improving the system would require finding ways to produce detectable gravitational changes more quickly.

"The speed of gravity communication would come down to how substantial the mass is, how fast you can move it, and the sensitivity of the detector.

"It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future.".

Could Quantum Sensors Make Gravity Communication Practical?

Although the experiment relied on a conventional gravity sensor, the researchers believe more advanced technology could eventually make the approach faster and capable of operating over greater distances.

Professor Matthew Davis emphasized that the team's most notable achievement was demonstrating that gravity could be used to transmit recoverable information.

"It's not often that you get to demonstrate an entirely fresh way of communicating," Professor Davis remarked.

"We have shown experimentally that information can be encoded in the gravitational field and recovered at the other end.

"Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modeling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 meters and data rates of around 15 bits per minute.".

Quantum sensors exploit properties of quantum physics to make exceptionally precise measurements. In principle, their greater sensitivity could allow researchers to detect much smaller gravitational changes, potentially improving both the range and speed of gravity-based communication.

However, the team's projections depend on ambitious assumptions, and the suggested performance has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. Even at 15 bits per minute, the system would remain dramatically slower than modern wireless technologies.

It has been revealed that still, the potential applications are intriguing. A sufficiently advanced gravity-based communication system could someday transmit information in environments where radio waves, light, and other conventional signals cannot penetrate.

For now, an aging elevator and a gravimeter in a university bathroom have demonstrated something remarkable: information can be carried by changes in gravity and recovered on the other side of a solid wall.

The research was published in Science Advances.

Industry News: Childhood, Career Come Full Circle for Budget Analyst at NASA Goddard

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood.
  • Industry observers note that “I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled.
  • Her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood. Her parents worked at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and discussions about happenings at the agency continued even when they came home from the office.

Industry observers note that “I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled. “However, we talked just as much about the engaging work my parents were doing inside Goddard’s gates.”.

Her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources. They brought their daughter on center for Take Your Child to Work Day and other events, and over time she became hooked.

Sources indicate that “I saw the chambers where spacecraft and instruments were being tested, as well as other facilities used to help further space exploration. Above all, I witnessed the passion and collaborative spirit everyone had at Goddard,” Knight said. “As a child, I found it incredibly fascinating.”.

It all came full circle in late August when, after growing up around NASA and later working several contractor roles for the agency, Knight and a number of her colleagues in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer were sworn in as federal employees as part of a workforce directive to strengthen the agency’s technical core competencies by bringing mission-critical positions into the civil service.

She began her Goddard career more than two decades ago following graduation from the University of Maryland in nearby College Park. As the job search began after commencement, one organization inevitably stood out, along with one particular mission.

When she came across a contractor job opening at Goddard in support of the Hubble Space Telescope team, Knight jumped at the opportunity.

Industry observers note that “Hubble was doing amazing things, and I always admired how they fixed the faulty mirror,” she remarked, referring to how astronauts and team members corrected an early spherical aberration during the observatory’s first servicing mission. “It was exciting to become involved with such a flagship mission, especially coming right out of college.”.

As a project support analyst, Knight assisted engineers with test plans, data gathering, and hardware procurement for Hubble’s fifth and final shuttle servicing mission.

Following the mission’s completion in 2009 and subsequent end of the Hubble shuttle servicing era, she took on a similar role with the Robotic Refueling Mission in what was then the Satellite Servicing Capabilities Office at Goddard – now known as NASA’s In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing Capabilities Office.

Knight left Goddard momentarily afterward to perform contracting work in support of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory in Washington. After a phone call, she found her way back as a contractor program analyst in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, helping manage labor budgets within programs by avoiding funding lapses and ensuring employees received their paychecks on time.

Following the August ceremony, Knight now carries the title of budget analyst in the Program Analysis Office within the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, performing many of the same critical duties as a civil servant.

Recent findings suggest that “While many functions are similar, transitioning into the civil service makes it easier for my colleagues and I to help keep NASA’s missions going from the financial aspect,” stated Knight. “We have more autonomy to perform certain government-related tasks by being on the government side.”.

The civil service also provides additional training and growth opportunities for such positions.

Sources indicate that “Ashley is a great team player. This conversion is a fantastic milestone because it unlocks new avenues for her learning and development, and allows us to integrate her into new roles,” mentioned Linnette Morales, Knight’s supervisor in the Program Analysis Office. “I am thrilled she can now fully access the opportunities on the civil servant side, immensely benefiting both her continued career growth and our organization.”.

The workforce directive, entitled “Restoring NASA’s Core Competencies” and announced by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in February, is part of a broader effort to expand the agency’s critical institutional knowledge, increase resources essential for mission success, and maintain U.S. leadership in space exploration.

“The directive has given our office an opportunity to rebalance positions across the organization and remove limitations that were applied to those who were previously not government employees,” stated Lisa Kelleher, Goddard’s chief financial officer. “We are now better able to insource many of our experienced contractor staff, allowing us to build up our in-house core competencies in areas such as budget analysis and accounting, and in turn increase our support for mission success.”.

For Knight, she sees an increasing importance for her organization and hopes to make impactful contributions, especially as work taking place at Goddard helps NASA return a crewed mission to the lunar surface, build a Moon Base, and eventually send humans to Mars.

It has been revealed that “We’re the go-between between NASA Headquarters and Goddard programs, and it’s our job to make it a seamless transition for projects to use money they’ve been given to help get these projects off the ground,” she mentioned. “It’s both vital and exciting with the lunar and Mars endeavors, and I’m proud to play whatever role I can.”.

Decades after first following her parents around center, and now following in their footsteps as a NASA civil servant, Knight is as captivated by Goddard and its people as she was during her early visits.

“Through the years, I’ve noticed everyone remains driven by teamwork and achieving the mission,” she remarked. “Everybody wants to succeed together by working toward the same goal, and I’m grateful I can continue to be part of it all.”.

Farhan Akhtar, Ashutosh Gowariker and Madhur Bhandarkar Look Back at ‘Dil Chahta Hai,’ ‘Lagaan’ and ‘Chandni Bar’ at 25

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Variety

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2001, three films challenged familiar conventions of Hindi-language cinema in very different ways.
  • Farhan Akhtar‘s “Dil Chahta Hai” offered a new screen language for friendship and young adulthood; Ashutosh Gowariker‘s “Lagaan” turned a village cricket match into an epic about resistance; and Madhur Bhandarkar’s “Chandni Bar” took audiences into the largely unseen world of Mumbai’s dance bars.
  • One thread connected their stories: all three had encountered the expectations of commercial Hindi cinema before finding the conviction to make something different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2001, three films challenged familiar conventions of Hindi-language cinema in very different ways.

Farhan Akhtar‘s “Dil Chahta Hai” offered a new screen language for friendship and young adulthood; Ashutosh Gowariker‘s “Lagaan” turned a village cricket match into an epic about resistance; and Madhur Bhandarkar’s “Chandni Bar” took audiences into the largely unseen world of Mumbai’s dance bars. Twenty-five years later, the filmmakers revisited the films and the risks behind them at “The Legendary 25s,” a session at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa moderated by actor and producer Khushboo Sundar. Related Stories Sheryl Lee Ralph-Produced ‘Until Everyone Is Seen’ Sets World AIDS Day Premiere on Hulu (EXCLUSIVE) BMG’s Concord Originals Preps Supernatural Gothic Horror Pic ‘Wolf at the Door’ (EXCLUSIVE).

One thread connected their stories: all three had encountered the expectations of commercial Hindi cinema before finding the conviction to make something different.

Gowariker and Bhandarkar already had films behind them before “Lagaan” and “Chandni Bar” established their identities as filmmakers. Akhtar, making his directorial debut with “Dil Chahta Hai,” stated he had not been interested in making a film that conformed to the prevailing Bollywood potboiler template.

According to recent reports, for Gowariker, who is also the IFFI festival director this year, the turning point came after his first two films failed. Having initially tried to make commercial entertainers, he realized that “my next film had to be something I believe in, something that I want to make first, and then hope to God that the audience also likes it. So that’s how the genesis of ‘Lagaan’ happened.”.

It has been revealed that the idea was an unlikely proposition: a period drama built around a cricket match, with villagers taking on the British. Gowariker wanted to make a film about “a group of heroes.” He researched the British Raj, 19th-century life, cricket and village communities before taking the script back to star Aamir Khan, who had initially rejected the premise. Gowariker asked Khan for just three hours to hear the narration of “Lagaan” before deciding. “He heard it. He laughed, he had tears and he said, ‘I definitely want to do this now,'” Gowariker recalled of the film, which went on to receive an Oscar nomination.

It has been revealed that bhandarkar’s route to “Chandni Bar” was rooted in observation. A visit to a dance bar with a friend gave him the subject for the Tabu-starring film, which he researched by visiting bars across Mumbai for six months. “Even if, in retrospect, ‘Chandni Bar’ had not done well at the box office, I would still be happy because this is the cinema which I wanted to make, and this is the world which I’ve seen,” he said.

Industry observers note that his interest in underdogs has continued in films such as “Page 3,” “Corporate” and “Fashion,” which examined the worlds of the media, business and fashion respectively. He has also resisted pressure to turn women-centered stories into male-led films for commercial reasons. From Tabu’s vulnerable character in “Chandni Bar” to Raveena Tandon’s politically ambitious woman in “Satta,” he said he is drawn to complex women rather than idealized portrayals. “My movies are basically a mirror to society,” he said.

It has been revealed that with “Dil Chahta Hai,” a buddy movie starring Aamir Khan, Saif Ali Khan and Akshaye Khanna, Akhtar set out to bring a more recognizable version of friendship to the screen. He felt Hindi films’ depictions of male friendship did not reflect how people actually spent time together. “The relationship had become cheesy, filmy,” he remarked. He cited Mansoor Khan’s “Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak” (1988), which he watched as a schoolboy, as an key influence.

Asked specifically about the older-woman romance in “Dil Chahta Hai,” he said the inspiration for the relationship between the characters played by Akshaye Khanna and Dimple Kapadia came “from many crushes that I had on older women, that’s the honest truth.”.

According to recent reports, the filmmakers also reflected on how cinema is made and judged. Akhtar described a screenplay as “a living, breathing thing,” evolving through contributions from actors and crew members, sometimes well into the edit. Gowariker, discussing acting, said, “The true performance lies in the pauses where you’re not saying anything.”.

Industry observers note that on the industry’s fixation with box-office numbers, Akhtar stated, “Now the conversation is that I heard you had a great weekend. But I would rather know what you thought of the film.” Gowariker described every newly introduced film as “a reset to zero,” adding that the yardsticks had shifted over the years, from silver and golden jubilees to 100-day runs and opening weekends, making comparisons across films of different budgets and genres reductive.

Asked what they would change if they could revisit one another’s films, Akhtar stated he would leave “Lagaan” untouched, but if he were the producer, he would ask Gowariker to direct it again. Gowariker said he might add a soulful song to “Chandni Bar,” while Bhandarkar said he would find it difficult to remake either “Lagaan” or “Dil Chahta Hai.”.

On AI and visual effects, Bhandarkar remarked, “AI and VFX can certainly enhance the visual experience and expand the possibilities of filmmaking, but they can never replace the human touch.” Akhtar’s advice to younger filmmakers was to draw on their own unique experiences.

Latest Update: NASA Eyes Crop Candidates for Future Menus
