💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, as NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth.
  • Recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers.
  • In a recent development, while space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, as NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving.

Recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers. Space crops can absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water. These capabilities will become increasingly vital as crewed missions extend farther from our home planet.

In a recent development, while space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space. A latest investigation from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division is set to launch to the International Space Station, where the first-of-its-kind prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing crop production systems that could grow crops like these for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions.

Strawberries are among the few sweet fruits under consideration for spaceflight and are nutritious, aromatic, and self-pollinating.

Researchers at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida are growing strawberries in flight-like growth chambers to evaluate the potential space crop, and NASA partners at The Australian Research Council Centre for Excellence in Plants for Space also are helping expand knowledge of space strawberries.

Researchers at NASA Kennedy, the University of Melbourne, and the University of Western Australia recently tested a wild strawberry against NASA’s leading strawberry candidate, ‘Delizz,’ to see which thrived better under simulated space conditions.

According to recent reports, delizz and the wild strawberry produced very different fruits, according to a study published in September in the journal Life Sciences in Space Research. Delizz grew large, red fruit, while the wild strawberry produced small, yellow fruit due to a recessive genetic mutation.

Industry observers note that but looks are not everything. When grown from a seed, the wild strawberry produced twice as many buds, flowers, and fruit as Delizz. Ultimately, however, NASA’s pick kept its top spot, as the wild strawberry grew too many runners that would take up valuable room aboard a spacecraft.

Recent findings suggest that many crops have been grown in space, but none so far have come from the gourd family. Cucumbers could be the first.

Recent findings suggest that before crops like cucumbers can be grown and eaten in space, they must undergo extensive testing. NASA-funded researchers recently evaluated cucumbers for their growth, yield, and nutrition under spaceflight conditions.

The researchers found that while the plants showed some signs of enlarged leaves, they produced a steady stream of edible fruit, according to a study published in August in the journal HortScience.

Offering a variety of crops, such as cucumbers, not only benefits astronauts’ diets and mental well-being, but it also increases plant biodiversity, which can improve the likelihood of crop success on long-duration missions.

Herbs can spice up life in space, turning a bland meal into a bold one.

Lemon basil, an edible herb with a citrus scent and taste, is making strides in testing at NASA Kennedy.

Researchers report that lemon basil passed its preliminary round of space crop testing and successfully underwent seed sanitization, which is required before spaceflight to remove microorganisms from the seeds. Lemon basil’s next steps include assessing its growth in plant pillows, which can house plants aboard the space station.

Menu fatigue can swiftly become a problem for astronauts, but fresh herbs like lemon basil help transform packaged meals into something fresh and satisfying, supporting human health and performance in space.

NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division pioneers scientific discovery and enables exploration by using space environments to conduct investigations not possible on Earth. Studying biological and physical phenomena under extreme conditions allows researchers to advance the fundamental scientific knowledge required to go farther and stay longer in space, while also benefitting life on Earth.

Tech Report: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1393 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • About 2,000 years ago, the remnants of a massive ice sheet in the Canadian Arctic began expanding once again.
  • The findings suggest that global warming may have interrupted a upcoming ice age that was already getting underway, fundamentally altering a natural climate cycle that has shaped Earth for millions of years.
  • Industry observers note that "It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen -- and yet it stopped," notes Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia Climate School's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

About 2,000 years ago, the remnants of a massive ice sheet in the Canadian Arctic began expanding once again. According to newly introduced research, this slow buildup of ice may have marked the beginning of Earth's next glacial period, commonly called an ice age. But something unexpected happened. By the 1960s, rising summer temperatures had reversed the trend, causing the ice to retreat instead of grow.

The findings suggest that global warming may have interrupted a upcoming ice age that was already getting underway, fundamentally altering a natural climate cycle that has shaped Earth for millions of years.

Industry observers note that "It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen -- and yet it stopped," notes Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia Climate School's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "It's a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system.".

Ancient Arctic Ice Reveals a Surprising Climate History.

Industry observers note that in a study published in Science, Young and fellow Lamont geochemist Joerg Schaefer, along with their colleagues, investigated the history of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. This enormous mass of ice covered much of Canada and the northern United States between approximately 95,000 and 20,000 years ago.

In a recent development, at its greatest extent, the Laurentide stretched from north of the Arctic Circle all the way south to Illinois. In some locations, its ice was more than two miles thick. Although most of this enormous ice sheet disappeared as the climate warmed, one surviving piece remains.

Known as the Barnes Ice Cap, this ancient remnant sits on central Baffin Island in Nunavut, Canada, and covers an area roughly the size of Delaware.

"People always say that it disappeared, but that's not true," says Young.

Scientists already knew that the Laurentide Ice Sheet had repeatedly grown and retreated during the roughly 2.6 million years since extensive continental glaciation began in North America. What remained uncertain was whether the ice sheet had ever become smaller than it is today before expanding again.

Answering that question could reveal whether a newly introduced cycle of glaciation had begun much more recently than scientists previously believed.

(A note on terminology: Technically, we are still living in an ice age-the Late Cenozoic Ice Age-which started about 34 million years ago. Within it, colder glacial periods alternate with warmer interglacial ones, including the one we live in now. What people casually call an "ice age" is usually a glacial period. The last glacial period ended about 11,700 years ago.).

Ancient Plants Preserved Beneath Ice Hold the Clues.

According to recent reports, piecing together the history of an ice sheet is particularly challenging when researchers are looking for evidence of its smallest extent and earliest stages of regrowth. As glaciers advance, they frequently scrape across the land, destroying the geological traces that could reveal where and when the ice first began spreading.

The Barnes Ice Cap, however, offers an unusual opportunity to investigate this history.

Industry observers note that unlike most glaciers, it is frozen directly to the bedrock beneath it and does not slide across the landscape. As a result, plants that once grew in areas later covered by expanding ice can remain preserved in place for thousands of years.

Recent findings suggest that since the Barnes Ice Cap began retreating in 1960, previously buried vegetation has gradually emerged from beneath the melting ice. Researchers can collect these ancient plant remains and determine when they were alive using radiocarbon dating.

This technique measures carbon-14, a harmlessly radioactive form of carbon that living organisms absorb from the atmosphere. Once an organism dies, its carbon-14 begins breaking down at a predictable rate. By measuring how much remains, scientists can estimate when the plant stopped growing and became buried beneath the ice.

These dates provide a record of when the advancing glacier covered different parts of the landscape.

"If you do this enough times, you can actually develop a timeline of that ice margin systematically advancing over plants. You're actually tracking the expansion of that ice margin," claims Young.

Earth's Next Ice Age May Have Begun 2,000 Years Ago.

The research team examined ancient vegetation uncovered by the retreating Barnes Ice Cap, along with plant remains exposed beneath smaller ice caps that have recently melted in the surrounding region.

Together, these samples allowed the scientists to reconstruct thousands of years of glacial change.

Their results indicate that the Laurentide Ice Sheet reached its smallest extent approximately 3,000 years ago. Then, around 2,000 years ago, temperatures became cold enough for the remaining ice to begin expanding again.

Young and his colleagues argue that this renewed growth should be recognized as the start of Earth's next glacial period.

That interpretation differs from previous research based on climate models, which has generally suggested that the next glaciation would not begin for thousands or even tens of thousands of years.

Recent findings suggest that the disagreement partly comes down to how scientists define the beginning of a glacial period. Rather than waiting until enormous ice sheets have spread across continents, Young's team proposes that the first sustained expansion of an existing ice sheet should mark the starting point.

Under that definition, the next glaciation had already begun long before modern scientists recognized it.

The discovery also casts latest light on a controversial scientific debate from the 1970s, when some climate researchers suggested that another ice age might be approaching.

Recent findings suggest that "It actually was happening," Young indicates. "They couldn't quite prove it, but now we sort of have the evidence.".

However, this early expansion would not have produced an immediate or dramatic transformation of the planet. According to Young, it would have taken thousands of years for the cooling to become noticeable and roughly 30,000 years for the Laurentide Ice Sheet to regain its enormous continental dimensions.

The process was only in its earliest stages when the warming climate brought it to a halt.

Global Warming Reversed the Growth of the Ice Sheet.

By the 1960s, conditions had changed enough that the Barnes Ice Cap was losing more ice during the summer than it could replace through winter snowfall.

Instead of continuing to expand, the ancient ice began shrinking.

According to the researchers' interpretation, this reversal effectively ended the developing glacial period before it could progress into a full-scale ice age.

It has been revealed that the consequences may extend far beyond the present day. Models projecting the future of the Barnes Ice Cap indicate that it could disappear entirely within the next few centuries.

"That will be the true very last remains of the Laurentide, disappearing for good," Young claims.

The Loss of an Ancient Ice Cap Could Change Future Ice Ages.

The disappearance of the Barnes Ice Cap could also have implications for how future glacial periods develop.

In the past, the Laurentide Ice Sheet provided a starting point for renewed glaciation whenever Earth's climate cooled sufficiently. Because a large existing mass of ice helps create conditions favorable for further ice accumulation, it can trigger reinforcing processes that allow glaciers to expand.

Scientists describe this kind of process as a positive feedback. In this case, existing ice helps promote the growth of additional ice, allowing an ice sheet to become increasingly extensive as temperatures remain cold.

Without the Laurentide's last surviving remnant, a future glacial period might unfold differently.

Sources indicate that researchers cannot yet determine when another glaciation could begin under atmospheric conditions influenced by elevated greenhouse gas concentrations. If enormous continental ice sheets eventually start forming again, they may have to develop without the ancient ice that previously helped initiate their growth.

The findings suggest that global warming has done more than melt glaciers and shrink existing ice sheets. It may have interrupted a glacial cycle that was already beginning, while also removing a feature that helped sustain ice age cycles across North America for millions of years.

"What has been an extremely natural and predictable phenomenon is now gone," says Young.

How NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions through its recently renamed Small Business Supplier Development Program. As part of the program, NASA unveiled its latest Mentor-Protégé Agreement, this one signed between The Boeing Tech giant and GRACE Aerospace.

NASA is streamlining the application process for the Small Business Supplier Development Program, as well as reducing administrative requirements, accelerating review and approval timelines, and enhancing incentives for prime contractor participation. These improvements are aimed at making supplier development more accessible, efficient, and closely aligned with NASA’s mission needs.

“We have intentionally redesigned the program as a mission-focused tool for strengthening industrial base readiness and mission success,” said Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator, Office of Small Business Programs, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “By simplifying participation and focusing developmental assistance on the capabilities NASA needs most, we are helping build a stronger, more resilient supplier base that can support the agency’s highest-priority missions.”.

Recent findings suggest that under the new Mentor-Protégé Agreement, Boeing will provide structured assistance to help GRACE expand its capabilities as a supplier of mission-critical aerospace hardware. Boeing will fund the agreement, valued at nearly $500,000.

Sources indicate that “Boeing is proud to continue its longstanding relationship with NASA in support of its mission and the opportunities this agreement creates for Boeing, GRACE, and the broader aerospace industrial base,” noted Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager and small business liaison officer for Boeing. “Through this partnership, Boeing looks forward to sharing our expertise to support the continued growth and long-term success of a small business while strengthening our supplier base.”.

Building on two decades of experience supporting defense and aerospace customers, GRACE will use the partnership to prepare for increasingly complex aerospace and spaceflight programs.

“GRACE Aerospace is thankful and honored to participate in the program,” stated Pauline Sevigny, president and owner of GRACE Aerospace. “We look forward to growing and learning from industry experts and supporting the mission of resilience and space superiority.”.

NASA’s enhanced supplier program is part of the agency’s broader Office of Small Business Programs.

Bayern Munich's disappointing 2-1 Champions League defeat at Lille on Wednesday night – in which Jamal Musiala came on for the last quarter of an hour – was overshadowed by comments the club's captain made afterwards.

"It must never happen that something like this is played out at a player's expense. Of course, the club always comes first and is bigger than the player, but it's not bigger than the person," Kimmich told reporters in the mixed zone.

"That's an absolute no-go and not Bayern-like," he added.

Kimmich was responding to recent comments made by Bayern supervisory board members Uli Hoeness and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge.

"If he (Musiala) doesn't return to being the Jamal of old, then we need to have a conversation with his family, with the player, and, above all, with his agency – because, frankly, the current financial figures would no longer be justifiable," Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told Sky on Friday.

Honorary President Uli Hoeness has described the situation as a "dilemma" for the club, while CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen raised the prospect of talks with Musiala's management and family.

While theGermany player has struggled with a number of injuries over the past couple of seasons, his health came into sharper focus in August, after he collapsed on the pitch in a couple of preseason matches. He subsequently revealed that he had been diagnosed with a neurological condition which causes him to suffer from occasional "absence seizures.".

Kimmich added that criticism of a players' performances was legitimate, but that concerns about Musiala's situation should have been dealt with behind closed doors.

"That's something you should sort out internally, around a table, rather than trying to resolve it publicly," he said.

"It's not that he has problems because he's unprofessional. He's there every day trying to get the maximum out of himself.".

Meanwhile, Bayern bosses met with Musiala's agents on Tuesday, and clarified the timeline of events, dismissing speculation that the player could have concealed the condition when he signed his last contract extension.

It has been revealed that bayern remarked the two sides agreed that he was first examined for seizure symptoms in April 2025, two months after he had signed his contract extension, which makes him one of the club's top earners and is to keep him in Munich until 2030. 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers from “Twelfth Night,” the Season 2 finale of “Outlander: Blood of My Blood,” now streaming on Starz.

Recent findings suggest that “Outlander” was never a series to hold back on a brainy twist that took a minute to digest. But its prequel series, “Outlander: Blood of My Blood,” may have outdone its predecessor with a twist that rewrites at least one family tree.

Since the prequel premiered last year, it has always operated on its own narrative timeline, separate from author Diana Gabaldon’s book series. In those books, Julia (Hermoine Corfield) and Henry (Jeremy Irvine), the parents of original series heroine Claire (Caitriona Balfe), died when she was 5 years old in a car crash. But with “Blood of My Blood,” executive producers Matthew B. Roberts and Maril Davis ponder what might have happened if they actually time-traveled through the same magic stones their daughter would decades later, and were left to survive in 1710s Scotland.

It has been revealed that it has been one tragedy after another for the lovebirds, and that’s saying something, given that they weathered World War I. But one question has loomed large over the Beauchamps: What will happen to their son, William, with whom Julia was pregnant when they went through the stones? He’s not in Gabaldon’s books, so Roberts and Davis have a bit of freedom to play with his fate. And they seemingly gave fans their answer in the Season 2 finale.

Julia and Henry were dealt their biggest setback yet earlier this season, when a seer informed her she isn’t a time traveler, she was just pregnant with one. William has his father’s mystical gene, and now that Julia is postpartum, she won’t be able to go back to her own time unless they get pregnant again, which itself is a moral quandary. The news doesn’t stop them from trying to run away together again. But in the process, Henry is shot by Lord Lovat (Tony Curran) in a case of mistaken identity, and Julia’s attempts to flee Lovat’s henchman leave her lifeless at the bottom of a waterfall. Fearful for wee William’s life without his parents, Julia’s confidante Davina (Sarah Vickers) takes him to the safest place she can think of –– to her son Brian (Jamie Roy) and his new wife Ellen (Harriet Slater). Mere moments after Brian and Ellen’s long-awaited wedding, the Frasers have a new addition to their future home at Lallybroch. Related Stories ‘Golden Girls’ and 'Gilmore Girls' Writers' 'Silver Foxes' Screenplay Acquired by Alder Street Productions (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Morning Show’ Star Mark Duplass and Katie Aselton Show Off Their Three Rescue Dogs in PETA Ad (EXCLUSIVE).

According to recent reports, this is where the series goes for broke, and makes a frankly brazen claim. Brian and Ellen are, of course, the parents of future “Outlander” hero Jamie (Sam Heughan). According to Gabaldon’s original books, he had an older brother named William (aka Willie), whose death when Jamie was young forever affected how he saw the world and cared for those he loved. (Not for nothing, Willie was so formative for Jamie that fans latched onto the wooden snake he carved before he died, and the onscreen prop sold for more than $5,000 at auction earlier this year.).

If “Blood of My Blood” is to be believed, Brian and Ellen being given an infant named William could mean that Claire’s heretofore unknown younger brother was actually raised as a Fraser 200 years in the past. It’s a twist that completely alters how fans should look –– at least in the TV series’ timeline –– at Claire and Jamie’s relationship. Not only does the prequel depict their parents as unexpected allies, but it is now suggesting they may have even shared a sibling, not by blood thankfully.

Now before anyone gets too excited (or angry!), Roberts and Davis aren’t exactly making this twist official on a birth certificate just yet: Even when pressed multiple times for confirmation, they dodged answering whether this really is the Willie of the Fraser family tree. But with Season 2 coming to a close without news about a Season 3 renewal, it’s hard not to feel the impact of this twist, given it could be the revelation the prequel leaves fans as a parting gift. For now, Davis is tying it all back to the original.

“With Willie/William, even if they’re not the same person, I think it’s so interesting to think how these two stories are interwoven now,” she tells Variety. “It binds Jamie and Claire’s parents, and how will that affect them in the future? We always loved the idea that Jamie and Claire were meant to be, and we’re seeing how that fate all comes together.”.

In a recent development, roberts has a bit more fun with his response about the mystery of it all. “I feel like this is the natural place to go, and I like to manipulate people,” he says with a grin. “That’s my job.”.

Sources indicate that he isn’t kidding. Alternate endings were filmed for the finale, one where Ellen reveals to Brian that she is pregnant again right before they are handed William (an emotional beat, given that his father caused her miscarriage this season). So this could have been a case of two Williams. But Roberts suggests it was less of a possibility, and more of a security measure.

Recent findings suggest that “I like to do some alt endings to throw people off in case scripts get leaked,” he states. “I like to keep actors on their toes, too. I have something in my head that I want to put on screen, but we did multiple endings with the finale of ‘Outlander’ as well.”.

According to recent reports, but rewriting lore to this degree is risky business, especially given the series isn’t yet guaranteed to come back. Still, Roberts and Davis have already planned out what would happen next should they get the go ahead, and there is one thing audiences won’t ever see in this prequel: young Jamie.

While diehard fans have undoubtedly done the math to figure out just how soon their favorite Highlander could make his debut, Roberts states he is hesitant to bring the action too close to the stories told in Gabaldon’s books and the original series.

“It’s hard to think about the stories with young Jamie in them, because that feels like you’re starting to tread on ‘Outlander,’ and I don’t want to do that,” he indicates. “It feels like you want to get maybe as close to the birth of Jamie as we can, but that still gives us quite a bit of time.”.

If “Blood of My Blood” is at least in step with Gabaldon’s book series’ timeline, Willie is born in 1716 –– the same year of Brian and Ellen’s wedding, as seen in the Season 2 finale. Jamie will be born in 1721, so five years could be what’s left of the narrative runway for the series.

With those parameters in place, Roberts and Davis also continue to look beyond “Blood of My Blood” for future “Outlander” franchise opportunities. Even with the wealth of Gabaldon’s world building at their disposal (her 10th and final book has yet to be released), they continue to be vocal about a particular contender.

Sources indicate that lord John, a fan-favorite character played by David Berry in the original series, is the subject of Gabaldon’s companion series of novels, and Roberts and Davis previously tried to spin off those stories while the original “Outlander” was still airing. The series didn’t move forward then, but they seem to be actively hoping the franchise’s continued success will reignite interest.

“There are certainly other things out there for us to explore, and Lord John remains one of them,” Davis says.

2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1197 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea.
  • For as long as humans have traveled by sea, shipbuilders have faced the challenge of keeping water out while protecting vessels from saltwater, microorganisms, and marine creatures such as shipworms.
  • It has been revealed that yet until the mid-20th century, archaeological studies of ancient vessels largely concentrated on their wooden components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea. Researchers have discovered two distinct waterproofing recipes, including one that combined pine tar with beeswax. Even more remarkably, microscopic pollen grains preserved in the sticky coatings offer clues to where the ship was built and repaired during its lifetime.

For as long as humans have traveled by sea, shipbuilders have faced the challenge of keeping water out while protecting vessels from saltwater, microorganisms, and marine creatures such as shipworms. Despite their name, shipworms are actually marine mollusks that burrow into wood and can cause extensive structural damage.

It has been revealed that yet until the mid-20th century, archaeological studies of ancient vessels largely concentrated on their wooden components. The protective materials that made these ships seaworthy received comparatively little attention, and waterproofing substances remain an understudied aspect of ancient maritime technology.

In a newly introduced study published in Frontiers in Materials, researchers from France and Croatia investigated the protective coatings of Ilovik-Paržine 1, a ship dating to the Roman Republic that sank approximately 2,200 years ago off the coast of modern Croatia.

Recent findings suggest that "In archaeology little attention is paid to organic waterproofing materials. Yet they are essential for navigation at sea or on rivers and are true witnesses of past naval technologies," mentioned first author Dr. Armelle Charrié, an archaeometrist at the Laboratory of Mass Spectrometry of Interactions and Systems in Strasbourg. "Studying the coatings, we found two different kinds on this vessel: one made of pine tar, also called pitch, and the other of a mixture of pine tar and beeswax. Analysis of pollen in the coating made it possible to identify the plant taxa present in the immediate environment during the construction or repairs of the ship.".

Ancient Waterproofing Secrets Revealed.

Since its discovery in 2016, the shipwreck and its cargo have been the subject of several scientific investigations. However, this is the first study to combine molecular analysis with the examination of ancient pollen to determine both the composition of the ship's waterproofing materials and the types of vegetation growing nearby when those coatings were produced or applied.

The research brought together specialists from the Department for Underwater Archaeology of the Croatian Conservation Institute and the 'ADRIBOATS' program of the Centre Camille Jullian at Aix-Marseille University in France.

According to recent reports, "Some regions throughout the Adriatic have particular characteristics that led local populations to develop a specific shipbuilding style," said Charrié. "Only studies like ours offer an overview into these traditions which bear witness to genuine know-how and diverse traditions.".

To uncover the ancient waterproofing recipes, the researchers examined the physical structure, molecular composition, and pollen content of the coatings. Among the techniques they employed was mass spectrometry, a powerful analytical method that allows scientists to identify substances and measure their abundance based on the masses of their molecular or atomic components.

An Ingenious Combination of Pine Tar and Beeswax.

Sources indicate that the team analyzed 10 samples of the ship's protective coating to determine the biological origins of the ingredients. Distinctive chemical signatures characteristic of pine trees appeared throughout the samples, revealing that the primary waterproofing material was pitch derived from heated conifer resin or tar.

Pitch is a thick, sticky substance that has been used for centuries to seal wooden vessels and protect them from water. When heated, it becomes easier to spread over surfaces and into gaps between wooden components.

One sample, however, contained evidence of a different recipe. Ancient shipbuilders had combined the pine tar with beeswax, creating a protective substance known to Greek shipbuilders as zopissa.

In a recent development, the addition of beeswax made the coating more flexible and easier to apply while hot. Flexibility would have been a valuable property aboard wooden ships, whose timbers could shift and flex as they encountered waves and changing environmental conditions.

Ancient Pollen Preserves a Record of the Ship's Past.

It has been revealed that the sticky nature of pitch gave it another remarkable property that ancient shipbuilders probably never considered. It could capture tiny airborne pollen grains from surrounding vegetation and preserve them for thousands of years.

It has been revealed that different plants produce pollen with distinctive shapes and structures, allowing scientists to identify the types of vegetation present in an area long after the plants themselves have disappeared. By examining both the variety and relative abundance of pollen grains embedded in the ship's coatings, the researchers narrowed down the possible locations where the pitch was manufactured or applied during repairs.

According to recent reports, the pollen preserved aboard Ilovik-Paržine 1 pointed to a surprisingly diverse range of landscapes. Some of the plant species were characteristic of Mediterranean and Adriatic coastal areas and valleys, including forests dominated by holly oak and pine. Others were associated with matorral, a type of Mediterranean shrubland that can contain olive and hazel trees.

The discovery of alder and ash pollen suggested the presence of vegetation growing near rivers or coastlines, either close to the sea or farther inland. Smaller quantities of fir and beech pollen pointed to mountainous environments. Such vegetation is characteristic of the northeastern Adriatic coast, where the mountains of Istria and Dalmatia rise not far from the shoreline.

Evidence of Multiple Repairs Across the Mediterranean.

The distribution and composition of the protective materials also revealed that the vessel likely received four or five distinct batches of waterproofing coatings.

The stern, or rear of the ship, and its central section shared the same coating. At the bow, or front of the vessel, researchers identified three batches that differed from one another. These variations suggest that the ship may have undergone a series of repairs using materials obtained from different locations around the Mediterranean.

Earlier investigations of the ship's ballast, the heavy material carried aboard a vessel to improve its stability, identified the ancient city of Brundisium as its likely place of construction. Known today as Brindisi, the port city lies on the southeastern coast of Italy and was an vital maritime center in the ancient Roman world.

The new pollen evidence suggests that some of the waterproofing coatings were applied in the vicinity of Brundisium. Other layers may have been added along the northeastern Adriatic coast, near the region where the vessel ultimately sank.

The findings demonstrate how microscopic biological traces can reveal aspects of ancient maritime history that might otherwise remain hidden. Even when waterproofing materials appear chemically identical, the pollen trapped within them can preserve evidence of separate repair events and the environments in which they occurred.

In a recent development, "While it seems obvious that ships sailing long distances need repairs, it's simply not easy to demonstrate this," concluded Charrié. "Pollen has been very useful in identifying different coatings where the molecular profiles were identical.".

What’s So Great About Merino Wool?

According to recent reports, merino wool is great because you're stealing a sheep's ability to keep itself warm or cool based on the temperatures it's in. This is a process often referred to as thermoregulation. Merino sheep have thinner, softer wool than what most people think of when they think of wool. The sheep evolved this soft coat to keep them comfortable across a wide range of temperatures. The result is a fabric that's comfortable to wear next to your skin. For the softest tees, look for fabrics that are either superfine or ultrafine—anything 17 µm or higher—like Unbound's T-shirts.

Wool is sustainable, too. One sheep can produce 4 to 5 pounds of wool per year. While cotton has its place, and so does the occasional synthetic garment, merino wool is a remarkable fabric that's the cornerstone of my wardrobe. I don't think you can have too many merino pieces in your closet, but they’re not cheap, which is why we're featuring these deals.

What’s So Great About Unbound Merino?

I like Unbound's T-shirts because they're 100 percent merino wool, no synthetics involved. That means all the antibacterial, odor-resistant, moisture-wicking, temperature-regulating goodness of merino wool … just works. I've found Unbound's T-shirts in particular to be very quick-drying and wrinkle resistant, two of the reasons I think they're the best merino T-shirts for travel. The tech giant's pants also have a very high wool percentage (95 percent), and they roll up nicely, making them very packable. Do you need special travel clothing? No, but Unbound's merino wool is naturally odor-resistant, which means you need fewer pieces in your bag. The company also offers a 30-day guarantee. If you don't like it, you can send it back.

Most merino products come with care instructions. Unbound Merino's T-shirts should be washed cold with like colors, then laid flat to dry. Whatever you do, don't bleach them and don't tumble dry them. The latter is especially destructive. I do it to every wool T-shirt I test, and it makes me sad, but I know some of you won't listen and will do it anyway, so I have to know what happens so I can warn you. Don't tumble dry. Just put it on a drying rack. It doesn't take more than a day. Seriously, you just spent $80 (on sale!) on a T-shirt; take care of it. Properly cared for, high-quality merino clothing like Unbound's is incredibly durable and will last for years. Throw it in the dryer and the pilling starts almost immediately.

Do I always lay them flat to dry? No. When traveling I usually hand-wash in the sink and then drape them over the shower curtain rod to dry, which hasn't seemed to have much negative impact. The issues with hanging wool to dry is that it will stretch out from the water weight. This is particularly true with 100 percent merino, like Unbound's T-shirts.

Industry observers note that I've never had a problem storing merino in my closet between wears, but for long-term storage, I recommend you take precautions against moths, which are notorious for eating holes in wool. I have lost merino garments to moths. I make sure to wash and thoroughly dry whatever I am storing, then I seal it in a compression bag. Another option is to put your merino garment in a cotton bag or otherwise wrap it in cotton and then put it in a plastic bin. It's very vital to make sure that the garment is completely dry before using any of these storage methods; otherwise your wool will smell musty and moldy. Other options include storing your garment in a cedar chest, which is a good natural deterrent for moths, or use moth traps or lavender sachets, which will repel the moths.

Unbound Merino (Unbound Merino Women’s).

If they have a downside, it's that Unbound's T-shirts do need to be babied a little. To help them last a long time I recommend hand washing and line-drying. 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest Zealanders have long envisioned the island as a predator-free zone for native birds, but swimming stoats have shown a resolve of their own.

Industry observers note that in the late 1800s, wildlife conservationists in Fresh Zealand were recognizing how predators such as stoats, brought to the country to control other nonnative animal populations, were becoming a threat to native birds. Naturalists at the time surmised that some of the nation’s islands could serve as sanctuaries where endemic species could persist, free from the voracious newcomers.

Resolution Island, located in the Fiordland region along the rugged southwest edge of New Zealand’s South Island, was one of the first eyed for this purpose. Conservationist Thomas Henry Potts proposed in 1872 that the island could be a place where “wingless species, and birds of feeble powers of flight, might there find a refuge for some of their representatives.”.

Industry observers note that so began an early systematic effort to protect kiwi, kākāpō, and other native birds on Resolution Island, the largest of the approximately 90 islands in Fiordland National Park. This image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on December 12, 2025, shows the island’s setting amid a landscape of steep-sided valleys carved by glaciers and now inundated by the ocean.

It has been revealed that the uninhabited island rises from sea level to the summit of Mount Clerke at 1,069 meters (3,507 feet). Its diverse habitats and vegetation communities range from bogs and wetlands near the coast to widespread podocarp forests at middle elevations to tussock grasslands in the subalpine and alpine areas. Offshore, the Taumoana (Five Fingers Peninsula) Marine Reserve protects estuarine and wave-exposed rocky reef habitats at the entrance to Dusky Sound, east of Five Fingers Peninsula.

Farther into the sound, Pigeon Island was the onetime home of Richard Henry, who was named caretaker of Resolution Island after it was designated a reserve in 1891. In what some have called a “landmark effort,” Henry spent years transporting more than 700 birds, mostly kiwi and kākāpō, by rowboat to Resolution and other would-be island sanctuaries nearby.

According to recent reports, in 1900, however, people began spotting mustelids on Resolution. It turns out the island is within swimming distance for animals such as stoats. Henry was intent on trapping the interlopers but eventually abandoned the project and moved on to caretaking work on another island. The spirit of his efforts lives on, though. A Department of Conservation program started in 2008 aims to control stoat populations and bolster native species on Resolution.

Erdogan's political fate may be determined by Turkey's Kurds

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
  • In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month revealed that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.
  • “We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” remarked the HDP in a statement on March 23.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month revealed that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.

“We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” remarked the HDP in a statement on March 23. “To fulfill our historical responsibility against the one-man rule, we will not field a presidential candidate in (the) May 14 elections.”.

According to recent reports, it is a twist of irony for the Turkish strongman, who spent the better half of the past decade cracking down on the party after it began chipping away at his voter base. Its former leader Selahattin Demirtas has been in prison for nearly seven years and the party faces possible closure by a court for suspected collusion with the militant Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and affiliated groups. But its influence may nonetheless determine the course of Turkey’s politics.

Industry observers note that the HDP’s decision not to field a candidate came just three days after head of the Republican People’s Party (CHP) Kemal Kilicdaroglu, Erdogan’s main rival, visited the party’s co-chairs. He told reporters that the solution to Turkey’s problems, “including the Kurdish problem” lies in parliament,” according to Turkish media.

Sources indicate that kilicdaroglu, who represents the six-party Nation Alliance opposition bloc, is the strongest contender to run against Erdogan in years. And while the HDP hasn’t yet unveiled whether it will put its weight behind him, analysts say it is the kingmaker in the elections.

Erdogan's 'polar opposite' wants to replace him as president of Turkey.

It has been revealed that “It was a carefully crafted political discourse,” Hisyar Ozsoy, deputy co-chair of the HDP and a member of parliament from the predominantly Kurdish province of Diyarbakir, told CNN. “We are not going to have our own candidate, and we will leave it to the international community to interpret it the way they wish.”.

Experts say the crackdown on the HDP is rooted in the threat it poses to Erdogan politically, as well as its position as one of the main parties representing Turkey’s Kurds, an ethnic minority from which a separatist militant movement has emerged.

The party and the Kurdish people have had a complicated relationship with Erdogan. The leader courted the Kurds in earlier years by granting them more rights and reversing restrictions on the use of their language. Relations with the HDP were also cordial once, as Erdogan worked with the party on a brief peace process with the PKK.

But ties between Erdogan and the HDP later turned sour, and the HDP fell under a sweeping crackdown aimed at the PKK and their affiliates.

Kurds are the biggest minority in Turkey, making up between 15% and 20% of the population, according to Minority Rights Group International.

It is unclear if the HDP will endorse Kilicdaroglu, but analysts say that the deliberate distance may be beneficial for the opposition candidate.

It has been revealed that the accusations against the HDP place it in a precarious position during the elections. It at the moment faces a case in Turkey’s Constitutional Court over suspected ties to the PKK, which is designated as a terrorist group by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. Knowing it may be banned at any moment, its candidates are running under the Green Left Party in parliament.

If the opposition is seen as allying with the HDP, Erdogan’s AK Party may use its influence in the media to discredit it as being pro-PKK, remarked Murat Somer, a political science professor at Koc University in Istanbul and author of Return to Point Zero, a book on the Turkish-Kurdish question in Turkey.

Sources indicate that the HDP’s threat to Erdogan’s hold on power became apparent after the June 2015 election, the first general election it participated in. It won 13% of the seats, denying the ruling AK Party its majority for the first time since 2002. Erdogan, however, called a snap election five months later, which led to a drop in the HDP’s support to 10.7%, as well as the restoration of the AK Party’s overall majority.

“They are a kingmaker in these elections because the HDP gets about half of the votes of the Kurdish population in Turkey,” said Somer, adding that the other, more conservative Kurdish voters have traditionally voted for Erdogan’s AK Party. And last month, the Free Cause Party (HUDA-PAR), a tiny Kurdish-Islamist party announced support for Erdogan in the elections. The party has never won seats in parliament.

Erdogan's political fate may rest on his response to the earthquake.

The HDP knows that its position is key to the outcome of next month’s vote, but that it’s also in a delicate situation.

“We want to play the game wisely, and we need to be very careful,” said Ozsoy, adding that the party wants to avoid a “contaminated political climate” where the elections are polarized “between a very ugly ultra-nationalist discourse against Kilicdaroglu and others.”.

The party was founded in 2012 with a number of aims, mentioned Ozsoy, one of which was “peaceful and democratic resolution of the Kurdish conflict.”.

Somer remarked that the party was seen to be “an initiative” of the PKK, which later led to a heavy government crackdown on it in the name of counterterrorism.

Its former leader Demirtas remains an influential figure.

The Turkish government has been trying to link the HDP to the PKK but has so far failed to prove “a real connection,” remarked Asli Aydintasbas, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington, DC.

Sources indicate that A post-Erdogan Turkey may give some breathing space to the Kurds and Kurdish-dominated parties in Turkey, Aydintasbas told CNN, noting that many Kurdish voters have recently left Erdogan’s camp. “For HDP, this is more than just an ideological choice,” she said. “It’s a matter of survival.”.

Ozsoy notes his party understands what’s at stake, not only for Turkey’s Kurds but for all its minorities.

It has been revealed that “We are aware of our responsibility here. We are aware of our role. We know we are in a kingmaker position,” the HDP lawmaker mentioned.

In a tweet on Sunday, Iranian government spokesman Ali Bahadori Jahromi said the alleged Israeli attack wouldn’t go unanswered. “It was an opportunity for me to say, ‘let’s keep fighting,’” he stated.

#163385. What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach

What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (931 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The fundamental difference between human intelligence and artificial intelligence may have less to do with computing power than with the chemistry of memory.
  • Industry observers note that hearing a familiar song can transport someone back decades.
  • Like the human brain, computers can store and retrieve information.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The fundamental difference between human intelligence and artificial intelligence may have less to do with computing power than with the chemistry of memory. Researchers propose that the brain not only communicates through electrical signals but may also "write" and "read" memories through chemical interactions involving neurons, astrocytes, and the molecules surrounding them. By linking memory to emotion and thought, the theory raises an increasingly relevant question: Can computational power alone give rise to the kind of consciousness experienced by living organisms?

Industry observers note that hearing a familiar song can transport someone back decades. A distinctive scent can bring a forgotten person or place to mind, while recalling a terrifying experience can trigger both emotional and physical reactions within moments.

Like the human brain, computers can store and retrieve information. However, the mechanisms underlying biological memory may be fundamentally different.

Recent findings suggest that A new review by Dr. Gerard Marx of MX Biotech Ltd. and Professor Chaim Gilon of the Department of Chemistry at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem explores the physical and chemical mechanisms that could link memory, emotion, and thought.

In their paper, "Consciousness, Memory and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective," the researchers suggest that understanding memory requires more than studying neurons and their electrical activity. They argue that other brain cells, particularly astrocytes, and the intricate molecular environment surrounding them may also play essential roles.

Building on their previous research into the molecular foundations of memory, Marx and Gilon examine whether the processes responsible for storing and retrieving experiences could also shed light on the origins of intelligence, thought, and consciousness.

The Brain's Hidden Chemical Code for Memory.

Central to the researchers' proposal is a model known as the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory.

According to this theory, memories emerge from interactions between three major components: brain cells, especially astrocytes working alongside neurons; the molecular substances surrounding those cells; and various chemicals, including metal ions, neurotransmitters, and gliotransmitters.

Rather than relying exclusively on electrical communication between neurons, the brain may use chemical processes to encode and retrieve information.

It has been revealed that astrocytes, which are abundant throughout the brain and maintain close interactions with neurons, are particularly important to this proposed mechanism. Marx and Gilon suggest that groups of astrocytes help process cognitive information through their interactions with neurons and the extracellular environment, the space and molecular material surrounding brain cells.

In a recent development, the latest paper expands this hypothesis to explore the nature of thought itself. If the brain can physically encode an experience as a memory, the process of recovering that information, recognizing it, and interpreting its significance might contribute to the formation of thoughts.

Why Memories Carry Emotional Meaning.

One of the central arguments of the researchers' theory is that biological memories contain more than stored information. They are also closely connected to emotional experiences.

It has been revealed that A scent associated with childhood may spark feelings of happiness. Hearing a familiar voice can provide reassurance, while remembering a frightening event may produce an immediate physical response.

Industry observers note that marx and Gilon contend that a physical model of memory must account for these emotional associations. Their proposed mechanism incorporates neurotransmitters and other chemical messengers that may help encode cognitive information alongside its emotional significance.

This potential biochemical connection between memory and emotion provides a starting point for investigating larger questions about how the brain generates thought, intelligence, and conscious experiences.

What Human Consciousness May Have That AI Lacks.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence makes these ideas particularly relevant.

Although computers and brains can both retain and access information, the physical mechanisms behind these abilities may differ considerably. Computer memory is ultimately encoded in electronic hardware. Biological memory, the researchers propose, may instead depend on the intricate cellular and chemical machinery of living brain tissue.

This distinction becomes increasingly significant as AI systems grow more capable of performing tasks traditionally associated with human reasoning and intelligence.

Marx and Gilon challenge the assumption that simply increasing computational power and complexity will eventually produce consciousness comparable to that of a living brain. They argue that electronic systems lack the biological structures and emotional mechanisms found in living organisms.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers are not suggesting that AI cannot develop increasingly advanced intellectual capabilities. Instead, they question whether demonstrating intelligent behavior is equivalent to possessing the biological mechanisms responsible for memory, emotion, and conscious experience.

How Memory May Give Rise to Thought.

Marx and Gilon emphasize that their theory does not solve the enduring mystery of consciousness. They explicitly acknowledge that the nature of conscious life remains poorly understood.

It has been revealed that however, their proposed biochemical framework offers a different way to investigate the physical processes that may underlie mental activity. By examining interactions between brain cells and their chemical environment, the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory could provide researchers with another avenue for exploring how the mind works.

While their earlier research focused on how memories might be physically encoded within the brain, their latest work addresses a much broader problem.

Understanding how living brain tissue transforms experience into memory could eventually help explain how memories become thoughts, how conscious experiences arise, and what fundamentally distinguishes biological intelligence from artificial intelligence.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that the pandemic was a boom time for Domino's Pizza, Papa Johns, Little Caesars and Pizza Hut.
  • In a recent development, these days, consumers are watching their discretionary spending but have more delivery and takeout options when they do decide to order, thanks to the accessibility of third-party platforms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Big pizza chains are struggling as weaker consumer spending, a wider variety of dining options and the rise of GLP-1 medications weigh on their sales.

Industry observers note that the pandemic was a boom time for Domino's Pizza, Papa Johns, Little Caesars and Pizza Hut. But since dining rooms reopened, the biggest U.S. pizza chains have faced an uphill battle to retain their customers.

In a recent development, these days, consumers are watching their discretionary spending but have more delivery and takeout options when they do decide to order, thanks to the accessibility of third-party platforms. Plus, food quality and the customer experience have become more crucial to diners who are looking for value when they order from restaurants.

Sources indicate that as a result of pizza fatigue and challenges facing the broader restaurant industry, the number of U.S. pizza restaurants has tumbled. Since pizza locations hit a peak of 83,035 nationwide in August 2019, more than 9,600 pizzerias had closed their doors as of July 2026, according to data from Datassential.

In 2025, sales at U.S. pizza restaurants fell 0.3%, according to Technomic data. Sales at independent pizzerias slipped 0.4%. Chains, which account for about two-thirds of the domestic pizza category sales, saw revenue shrink 0.3%.

It has been revealed that papa Johns reported that North American same-store sales declined 2.5% in 2025. Pizza Hut's U.S. same-store sales fell 5%. Among the three pizza chains that were publicly traded last year, only Domino's posted annual same-store sales growth at its U.S. restaurants, with an increase of 3%.

It has been revealed that it isn't just diners who have lost their appetite for pizza. Since March 2020, Papa Johns stock has lost about two-thirds of its value. Even shares of Domino's, which dominates the category, have seen gains of only about 2% in that time. For comparison, the S&P 500 has climbed about 150% over the same period.

And Yum Brands sold Pizza Hut this year, offloading the laggard of its portfolio to LongRange Capital and Yum China after about two decades of stagnating sales.

"Pizza Hut has been a detractor for YUM ... Going forward, YUM won't be tripped up by pizza category dynamics (discounting, etc.), translating to stronger growth and higher concentration in higher growth industry segments and markets," Wells Fargo analyst Zachary Fadem wrote in a research note in September.

Recent findings suggest that pizza chains now have significantly more competition for diners' dollars than they did in 2020. Third-party delivery platforms, which grew in popularity during the pandemic, offer a wide variety of cuisines beyond the traditional pizza and Chinese. As a result, Domino's and Papa John's have to compete with other fast-food chains, like McDonald's and Chick-fil-A, for DoorDash and Uber Eats orders.

As pizza has grown more expensive, a pie seems less appealing to budget-conscious diners. The average large cheese pizza is now almost $17, according to the 2026 Pizza Power Report from PMQ Pizza, a trade publication.

Sources indicate that plus, frozen pizza is another convenient option, with a lower price tag. Retail sales of single- and multi-serve frozen pizza rose 2.9% in the 52 weeks ended Nov. 7 compared with the same period in 2022, according to NielsenIQ data.

"When the American consumer is focused on the least expensive eating occasion, the items that are in my pantry, my refrigerator and my freezer win every single time," noted David Portalatin, a food and food service industry advisor for Circana.

Convenience stores like Casey's General Stores have also won over customers with pizza at a low price point.

"We believe that [Casey's] has an advantage over [quick-service restaurants] and dollar stores, which have fewer options to navigate the persistent inflationary environment, while [Casey's] can offset food pressures with margins," Bank of America Securities analyst Sara Senatore wrote in a research note published in June.

She added that geographic overlap of locations suggests that Casey's is stealing share from Pizza Hut.

In a recent development, the biggest pizza chains have also been slow to adapt to shifting consumer attitudes toward nutrition. For example, of the four biggest chains, Papa Johns is the only one to even test a pizza crust with added protein as more diners prioritize it in their diets. And the test was only in one Atlanta restaurant — for a single day.

In a recent development, pizza's nutritional content more broadly is another drag for the category. Its carbohydrate and fat content, from its dough and cheese, respectively, can make it less appealing for consumers on GLP-1 drugs, which have skyrocketed in use over the last several years.

Spending on pizza quick-service restaurants has fallen 22.2% per GLP-1 household after six to eight months using the medications, according to a 2026 survey published by PwC.

It has been revealed that to be sure, pizza's recent struggles do not mean an existential crisis for the category. Total pizza servings are down only about 1% this year, Circana's Portalatin mentioned.

And chains are trying to reverse that downturn in servings. In August, Domino's rolled out the Domino, a customizable Detroit-style personal pizza to attract solo diners. In November, Papa Johns unveiled a newly introduced turnaround proposal focusing on improving food consistency and restaurant operations. And Pizza Hut is running a holiday-themed meal deal.

"Pizza's not going anywhere," Portalatin noted. "The American consumer loves pizza.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A pair of companies in Europe have signed an agreement to study the feasibility of developing weapons that can be dropped from orbit.

Atmos, a space manufacturer known for its Phoenix reusable reentry vehicle, will work with MBDA, Europe's largest missile manufacturer, on the new project.

In a recent development, "We are assessing how proven defense systems and fresh orbital technologies can be combined to strengthen Europe's conventional deterrence and enable future defense capabilities," Sebastian Klaus, the CEO of Atmos Space Cargo, stated in a statement on Nov. 18.

It has been revealed that the system that the companies are investigating is called Precision Orbital Deep Strike, or PODS. The companies noted that their initial scope will center on design and feasibility, as well as technology integration.

Atmos and MBDA also said this work could lead to demonstrations, but the companies' announcement makes it clear that any deployment or use would be subject to the approval of governmental and military authorities.

"The initiative also directly supports MBDA's broader strategic vision in the space domain, reinforcing both space for defense and the defense of space," Thomas Gottschild, MBDA Deutschland managing director, said in the same statement.

Sources indicate that this news comes a few months after Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess said that the U.S. Space Force operates orbital weapons.

It has been revealed that "Let me be crystal clear: Today, Guardians operate on-orbit weapons that can defend the joint force against space-enabled attacks," Schiess said during a conferenace presentation on Sept. 15 ("Guardians" refers to Space Force personnel.).

Last year, Atmos' Phoenix capsule got its first test run in space. The cargo-return technology launched aboard a Space X Falcon 9 rocket during a rideshare mission in February 2025.

Atmos tested out the inflatable heat shields it has been working on to help future space-manufactured cargo make it through Earth's atmosphere in one piece.

"Orbital transportation and return form a new layer of strategic infrastructure, and infrastructure determines what Europe can achieve on its own terms," Klaus said in the Nov 18 statement.

EU-Indonesia trade deal opens fresh markets, but challenges remain

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1066 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the European Union seeks to deepen its presence in Asia and diversify its trade relationships, Indonesia is emerging as an increasingly important partner.
  • At a signing ceremony in Brussels last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the bloc's trade agreement with Jakarta as one of its "most ambitious deals" in the region, linking markets of 730 million people.
  • The deal, the culmination of nearly a decade of negotiations, reflects the EU's efforts to diversify its trade partnerships, secure access to critical raw materials and reduce strategic dependencies on China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the European Union seeks to deepen its presence in Asia and diversify its trade relationships, Indonesia is emerging as an increasingly important partner.

At a signing ceremony in Brussels last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the bloc's trade agreement with Jakarta as one of its "most ambitious deals" in the region, linking markets of 730 million people.

The deal, the culmination of nearly a decade of negotiations, reflects the EU's efforts to diversify its trade partnerships, secure access to critical raw materials and reduce strategic dependencies on China.

For Indonesia, it offers opportunities to attract investment, expand exports and strengthen its position in global supply chains.

The agreement will gradually scrap tariffs on more than 98% of product categories, covering almost the entire value of bilateral trade over 15 years.

For the EU, gaining better access to critical raw materials, particularly nickel, and diversifying its supply chains are central to its strategic partnership with Indonesia, said Philip Schleifer, an associate professor of political science at the University of Amsterdam.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"The main strategic interests are opening up a large and growing market for European companies, diversifying and deepening its economic partnerships, reducing strategic dependencies on China, and securing access to critical raw materials," Schleifer told DW.

According to recent reports, indonesia's mineral resources are particularly important for Europe's green and digital transitions. Nickel, for instance, is a key material for batteries and electric vehicles.

The agreement also creates opportunities for European investment in strategic sectors, including electric vehicles, electronics and pharmaceuticals.

According to recent reports, but Indonesia has its own industrial ambitions. The government wants to move beyond exporting raw materials by developing domestic processing industries and retaining more value from its natural resources.

"The challenge for the EU is to reconcile its own interest in securing raw material supply with Indonesia's industrial development objectives," said Eline Blot, a senior policy analyst at the Institute for European Environmental Policy (IEEP).

Yose Rizal Damuri, an economist at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, noted his institution's study estimates Indonesian exports could increase by around 60% in the coming years.

"Not only can Indonesia increase exports to Europe, but it can also become more strongly integrated into the global supply chains of European companies," Yose told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Potential beneficiaries include labor-intensive manufacturing sectors such as textiles, garments, footwear and furniture, alongside other Indonesian commodities and manufactured products.

Recent findings suggest that the agreement could also encourage European investment and create employment opportunities. However, Yose stressed that access to the European market does not automatically translate into higher exports.

He identified three priorities for Indonesia: raising awareness of the agreement among domestic businesses, strengthening production capacity and improving the country's business climate.

"Various trade agreements signed by Indonesia have relatively low utilization rates. The value of exports using these facilities remains limited compared with overall export values," he remarked, emphasizing the need for better information and outreach to producers.

Syafruddin Karimi, an economist at Andalas University in West Sumatra, also highlighted the opportunity to diversify Indonesia's export markets and reduce dependence on major trading partners such as China, the United States and regional Asian economies.

However, he warned that Indonesian producers must improve their compliance with European standards.

"Products must be traceable, including whether their production involves environmental damage or labor practices that undermine human dignity," Karimi noted.

The expansion of trade and investment could also increase environmental pressures, particularly in nickel mining, palm oil production and manufacturing.

IEEP analyst Blot warned that increased production without stronger environmental safeguards could worsen pollution, ecosystem degradation and industrial emissions. "Nickel mining and processing can contribute to pollution and ecosystem degradation, while palm oil remains closely associated with deforestation," she mentioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The EU Deforestation Regulation presents another challenge for Indonesian producers, particularly small-scale farmers who may lack the resources, technical capacity and documentation needed to demonstrate compliance.

Blot acknowledged that these requirements could create disproportionate costs for smaller producers and potentially favor larger companies.

However, she cautioned against using smallholders' livelihoods as an argument to weaken environmental regulations.

"Rather than weakening environmental requirements, the priority should be to ensure that smallholders receive adequate financial and technical support to meet them," she said.

Schleifer at the University of Amsterdam also warned that growing global demand for Indonesian natural resources could create environmental and social problems previously associated with commodities such as timber, palm oil and coal.

While Indonesia has considerable bargaining power because of its mineral wealth, the challenge is ensuring that increased demand translates into domestic industrial development rather than simply expanding resource extraction.

Sources indicate that the agreement includes a dedicated Trade and Sustainable Development chapter covering climate change, biodiversity conservation, sustainable forest management and labor rights. It also provides mechanisms for cooperation and civil society participation.

Industry observers note that however, there is no guarantee these commitments will be implemented. "Experience with other EU trade agreements suggests that there is often a substantial gap between sustainability commitments on paper and outcomes on the ground," Schleifer remarked.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

For Indonesia, the challenge also lies in preparing domestic industries to compete. Karimi stressed that the government, both at national and regional levels, must work with businesses to improve production standards, particularly among small and medium-sized enterprises.

Yose also emphasized the importance of a predictable business environment, warning that frequent policy changes and regulatory uncertainty could discourage investors.

Industry observers note that "Without improvements in the domestic business climate, this will not become a reality. Everything will remain good on paper but will not turn into real momentum for change," he remarked.

Ultimately, the trade agreement offers Indonesia an opportunity to strengthen its position in international trade and attract investment from Europe.

But whether the agreement delivers broader economic benefits will depend on the country's ability to develop competitive industries, move into higher-value production, and ensure that environmental protection and workers' rights are not overlooked.
